speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am most impressed with the overall balance of the Budget measures and the clear roadmap articulated in the area of industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although there were no new big-ticket items introduced, the Budget actually went into the next level of the nuts and bolts of implementing the various policy measures that were introduced in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It shows continuity in the policy directions and staying committed to the overall game plan.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would also want to record our thanks to Deputy Prime Minister Tharman, the former Finance Minister, for instituting the timely and necessary shifts in the fiscal policy during his tenure and getting us towards more inclusive growth as well as strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Budget, in a way, also reminded us that we do have in place a comprehensive tool kit to deal with the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A number of life-changing measures were introduced in recent years and require steadfast and diligent implementation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I see this as among the important priorities of this year's Budget, which is to implement well the series of far-reaching social and economic programmes and to ensure they remain well-funded and sustained.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clearly, economic transformation is the priority focus for this year's Budget and, indeed, will be in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is the "get real" part for us as a country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are mindful that to achieve better lives and a stronger nation, we need to have the means and the resources to get there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Industry Transformation Programme is both an exciting roadmap to achieve quality growth as well as a practical organisation of the various efforts to help businesses deepen capabilities, scale up technology adoption and transform through innovation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Somehow, we cannot run away from tagging dollar values to important initiatives to show solid commitments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It goes some way to addressing the funding needs of companies seeking to grow their businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These new measures are tilted in favour of businesses that are looking to upscale, innovate and internationalise, the three important key words in the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is usual to expect individual businesses to have varying aspirations and perspectives with regard to future growth or expansions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some companies may be Page: 17 satisfied with the status quo and find no need to take on new risks or seek new growth markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But for those who are prepared to venture into new frontiers and have good business ideas and are willing to take on investment risks, we should do our utmost to assist them in a meaningful way so as to increase their chances of succeeding.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their successes will add vibrancy to the economy, create better jobs and grow value overall.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digitisation of the economy and the Internet of Things continue to proliferate at a very fast speed around the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is no longer just about setting up digital platforms for the purpose of gaining efficiencies and data management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, digital platforms should also spur innovations and co-creation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, in many platforms today, it is the apps that drive adoption and utilisations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global trading system has grown in complexity and we need to continually crowd source innovative solutions so as to stay in-game in the global trade flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A key ingredient for a vibrant startup scene is for the barriers to entry to be kept as low as possible, whether it is rental costs, red tape or others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I like the JTC Launchpad at one north – the now famous Blk 71 at Ayer Rajah.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is actually a very modest set-up but a very conducive environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would imagine that the maintenance cost for the place would not cost too much.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, in developing the next gen JID, we should bear in mind not to allow the cost of land and the cost development to be the de-enabling factor for startups or would-be entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the last decade, innovation districts have emerged in the Western economies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In many of the United States (US) cities, innovation districts emerged near anchor institutions – the universities – the midtown areas where economy shaping, learning, living and social networking are integrated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has helped cities move up the value chain of global competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Creating a new innovation district next to an established technological institute like the Nanyang Technology University (NTU) is an exciting idea.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides the innovation districts and launchpads, our neighbourhoods are also places where entrepreneurism and innovations can take root.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, Jack Ma started Alibaba at his humble apartment in Hangzhou.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already in the heartlands, we have seen smart work centres being set up at community locations like the community clubs and libraries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are meant to promote flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nonetheless, these well-equipped and broadband-enabled smart work centres can also serve as initial workspace for budding startups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Finance Minister spoke about revitalising Housing and Development Board (HDB) shops in his speech.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Much has been said about the need for a "more integrated approach" among the different agencies and support schemes, and a "more targeted approach" to develop each industry.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are very much the crux of implementing transformation on a national scale.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To transform at the enterprise level is already a formidable challenge.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To do it at the economy-wide level, the challenges just multiply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have seen promising adoption at the hospitals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is all very exciting, but I can imagine the various implementation challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first question is whether there will be a champion agency with deep enough knowledge and the leadership to drive and coordinate this programme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How would the robotics programme work along with the various efforts by the other agencies, like the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING), the Building and Construction Authority (BCA), the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), the Workforce Development Authority (WDA), and how will this agency be involved in the research and development (R&D), acquisition, standards and deployment of robotics in the enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or is this a case where the Government's role is primarily as the grant provider and to "let a thousand flowers bloom", with the hope that it will accelerate the use of robotics in the industry?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, how do we minimise wastage from duplication in R&D, share the limited robotics expertise and avoid fragmenting the robotics suppliers' industry?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we promote and incentivise the use of technology in enterprises, we should also synergistically grow our local technology providers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The transformation package is an excellent opportunity for our local technology industry to build credentials and expertise, which they can leverage to expand internationally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This should be the second order priority for the National Robotics Programme (NRP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Leveraging on the trade associations and chambers (TACs) to help transform industry is also a logical move.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government and businesses can work together to develop the industries, identify market failures and work out the most appropriate interventions, be it systemic or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should leverage on TACs to build interdependencies among industry participants and encourage the "win-win" culture of mutual harnessing and sharing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, it becomes trickier if the sector has more than one TAC representing them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It demonstrates commitment to the task and would help raise the partnership to new high levels.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also read from the news that a team of officers drawn from different agencies will be set up to serve each of the 20-plus sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These cluster champions will actively engage the industry to carry out the transformation roadmap.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such facilitation efforts, when backed by necessary Page: 19 resources will help kick-start and fast track the pace of transformation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clearly, in a Government-led transformation and where the agencies play a hands-on role to facilitate and enable transformation, we need to first get the bureaucracy right for the task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Agencies will have to work in a more integrated and networked rather than the hierarchical manner.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Public sector officers will also need to master the art of seeking aligned partnership with enterprises, something that is not written in the Public Service manual.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, importantly, in innovation-driven transformations, agencies administering the grants will need to move away from key performance indicator (KPI)-driven criteria to more outcome-based criteria in dishing out support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ticking of boxes approach would not achieve the outcomes that we want.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we seek new ways to grow the economy, it is also timely to take stock and review if the various economic agencies that were set up years ago are still well-positioned to carry out the transformation roadmaps laid out.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And whether we need a merger and acquisition (M&A), so to speak, among the agencies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is worth noting that our expenditures have grown to almost two-and-a-half times what they were 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And in the years to come, the rate of increase in expenditure will continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there are no new measures in this year's Budget to deal with the cyclical downturn, the Budget this year still presents substantial support for firms, especially SMEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although the increase in total expenditure amounts to $5 billion in this year's Budget, the overall injection to the economy is actually much higher if the net investment returns (NIR) contribution is taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This net injection into the Budget, which is not funded through taxes or tax leakages, represents a strong stimulus to the economy and helps to support overall growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Temasek's NIRC is now also based on expected long-term returns, like the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some would argue these are Page: 20 just changes to accounting treatment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is no guarantee that the expected long-term returns would not fall in the years to come, as it really depends on the prevailing yields of the financial markets and the global outlook.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already, we are seeing negative interest rates in countries like Japan and Europe and that we are entering into a world of low returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Uncertainties and downside risks in the global economy have increased.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, as China continues with reforms to rebalance the economy, there are concerns that the Chinese economy could slow down more sharply than expected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The services-driven nature of growth in the US and China, as well as the trends of in-sourcing in the two countries, may mean that external demand for our exports will remain subdued.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: China and the US are our top trading partners.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should watch closely how the lower oil prices would impact the marine and offshore sector as these could have negative spillover effects on other sectors supporting the oil and gas industry.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And we should also be concerned about the continuing shrinkage of the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government will lead and act, whether it is economic transformation or social uplifting.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can achieve better and with more sustainable outcomes if the stakeholders are in this together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last month, The Business Times conducted a pre-Budget poll.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the questions posed to the chief executive officers (CEOs) participating in the poll was whether businesses should rely less on the Government's help and more on their own efforts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that paper, almost all the recommendations that were put up asked for the Government to do more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In preparing this speech, I must admit I struggled quite a bit as to the role the Government should play in the next phase of our economic development.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the last five decades, we saw strong and direct involvement by the Government in industrialising the country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We achieved remarkable growth, very much engineered by the state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Government-linked companies, like Singapore Airlines (SIA), Sembawang Corporation (Sembcorp), Keppel, the Port of Singapore Authority (PSA), Singapore Technologies (ST) Engineering, were established which developed world-class capabilities for the economy and created good jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government's direct hand in the economy has enabled Singapore to progress and thrive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But my intuition tells me that in the next phase of development where the strategy is geared towards innovation, value creating and more entrepreneurship, the Government's hand in the economy should be less direct, though not necessarily less in terms of financial resources or administration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Page: 21 At least in the short to medium term, the Government would have to push urgently the various key horizontal enablers and to facilitate the realisation of a conducive ecosystem where innovation and entrepreneurship flourish.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Left to market forces, we may take a long while to transit or may not even get there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or we may have to do it in a more painful way at a later stage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, it is the businesses that must come up with the next "killer" product or services that can sell to the consumers of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government can help, but the Government may not always make the right business call.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the ideal state is for the Government to forge and sustain strong partnerships with economic stakeholders and, over time, with the stronger industry players and enterprises emerging, they can take the lead in driving the growth ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The gut instinct or the "animal spirit" is still very much needed to bring us to the desired state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, with the rapid technological development in the world, Singapore is also undergoing a necessary industrial transformation process.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What I am most concerned about is how this will directly impact our workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is the challenge that many developed countries are facing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The workers will end up like a "hero who has no place to show his prowess".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I hope that the Government will pay attention to this issue and give more support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, with that, I support the Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, some have expressed views that Singapore's early post-Independence economic philosophy had put an overly heavy emphasis on growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I think it was a choice for Singapore which the founding generation made and for which the founding leaders took responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They decided – correctly, in hindsight – on promoting growth and investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And because they took early and decisive action, Singapore gained a valuable lead over many other countries that subsequently took the same route.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Courageous decisions, not an endowment of natural resources, brought our economy to where it is today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The courage of such decisions bequeaths to later generations an expanded set of choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Today, instead of tearing everything down to remake the economy, we can choose to do so selectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And because we can do it with a high degree of penetration facilitated by depth of Page: 22 policy insight, we have more confidence that our economy's edifice will remain secure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Led by our founding Prime Minister, the early generation of leaders emphasised the need for an economy that continually updated itself and checked its relevance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order to remain updated and relevant, strong growth during the early days of development provided us with the necessary head-start.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If Singapore had commenced its pursuit of growth any later or grown any slower, imagine where we would be now in the face of the prevailing state of regional and global competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The basic principles of Singapore's economic philosophy have remained intact till now, but that can easily change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Just as natural resource endowments can be readily depleted through unrestrained profligacy, later generations of Singaporeans can easily end up with a vacuous foundation on which to erect their future economy if our economic philosophy shifts in the wrong direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: That is why I believe it is important at this point to recall these principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The first can be seen, in many ways, in our approach to economic partnerships within and beyond the region, as well as in our emphasis on communal effort and individual responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The second characteristic of openness is seen in our welcoming approach to foreign investment, both of money and talent, something that occurred from the very early days of Independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Today, there are few who seriously doubt the need for Singapore to continue to remain open and welcoming, especially to foreign manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The disagreement which exists has been about how much and in what manner to accommodate, not in the fundamental principle of being open to investment and talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is also openness to trade, which is why Singapore has always been exceptionally progressive in its approach to regulation, regionalism and globalisation, when compared to other economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is a philosophy which is reflected in our untiring pursuit of upgrading in every aspect of our lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This last one is also the one which I feel has been most taken for granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We enjoy good working infrastructure and roads without potholes, but it is also common to see frustration with what some regard as incessant upgrading works.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not uncommon to come across criticism about such things, without enough appreciation of the actual alternatives we could be presented with if we decide not to pursue continual upgrading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, Mdm Speaker, I believe this Budget goes beyond fiscal initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our development over the last 50 years into an advanced economy means that the policy approaches that were adequate when we were a Newly Industralised Economy (NIE) need to be supplemented with new policy innovations with sufficient penetration to deal with the deep level of sophistication that the economy has achieved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The most significant in this Budget relate to the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Labour market innovations have always played a critical role in Singapore's economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: That provided the framework for decades of strong labour market performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's outstanding record on employment growth, unemployment and income growth over the years is a testament to the efficacy of this and other supporting labour market policy innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we are not alone in these kinds of innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Other countries have also introduced innovations which have strengthened their labour market performance substantially.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One good example is Germany's introduction of flexible working time accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Often, reception to such innovations is mixed, at best.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They faced criticism and opposition, and only proved themselves over time, during crises, in particular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2008, another important labour market innovation was heralded by the introduction of Workfare by then-Finance Minister, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By encouraging workers at the lower end of the wage spectrum to seek employment and remain employed, Workfare has proved to be a forward-looking approach that helps the more vulnerable segments of our working population, and it does so in a fashion which is closely aligned to our economic principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Other labour market innovations include wage support measures, most notable of which was the Jobs Credit Scheme of 2009, the enhanced system of levies and dependency ratio ceilings (DRCs) on foreign manpower, the Jobs Bank and, more recently, the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By contributing to an increased range of policy options, such innovations equip the Government to handle increasingly complex labour market issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This system is vital for managing our long-term dependency on foreign manpower in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since its introduction at the recommendation of the Economic Strategies Committee (ESC), the current comprehensive system of levies and quotas has not been tested by a full-blown downturn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, beginning with last year's Budget, subtle changes have already been taking place in the way this system is applied without requiring recession as a precondition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In this manner, the Government is expanding the application of the system of levies as a policy instrument, allowing it to evolve into what could eventually become a very powerful tool for managing the labour market and one that is definitely more amenable to finetuning according to the degree and area of weakness in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Given the importance of this system of levies and DRCs, I believe it is important also to look out for possible signs of weakness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Where necessary, apart from an expansion in their application, such policy tools may provide improved performance with appropriate reconditioning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is Page: 24 especially so if there is clear evidence of unintended outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order for the system of levies to remain reliable and for its policy potential to be fully realised, we should re-examine the issue of whether and how quota restrictions should be imposed on top of the levies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: DRCs, which are quantitative restrictions, mean that aside from determining their willingness to pay, employers have to make a further determination of the numbers of workers they are entitled to hire under the quota.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Basic contradictions occur when both price and quantity restrictions are required to be fulfilled at the same time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Practically speaking, it is not possible for pricing and quota decisions to be made simultaneously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Consequently, the likelihood of such unintended outcomes is increased when employers approach their hiring decisions in a two-stage manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If they begin by determining the price they are willing to pay, one would expect that an employer would then proceed to optimise his entitlement under the quota.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order to reduce the likelihood of such unintended outcomes, it is timely to consider modifications to the system to eliminate the need for such a two-stage decision-making process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Such a two-stage process imposes unnecessary burdens on employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are alternatives that could potentially improve such a system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One possible solution is to forcibly reverse the order of the two-stage hiring decision process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In practice, a system that requires employers to decide the quota they want before pricing their entitlement would end up being quite similar to the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system for vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, this is a suggestion which commentators have raised in the past and which I am sure policymakers would probably have considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What I would like to point out and urge is a re-examining of its potential at this point in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I fully recognise that the implications of commoditising manpower services to such an extent should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Payment for manpower services is not like payments for vehicles, because it affects the livelihoods of workers and the welfare of their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Auctioning the right to hire also creates uncertainty for employers, possibly to an extent which would wipe out any efficiency gains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But the confidence with which the system is being used, at this point in time, is an encouraging sign that there is scope to alleviate the inherent contradictions that remain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Employers need some certainty in order to carry out forward business planning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the improvements in information sharing, including warnings about whether they have a weak core of Singaporean workers, are important improvements to our system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Here, let me be explicit about one thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My concerns about DRCs come from the head and not the heart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In my heart, I have no doubt why there was a need to resort to quantitative controls on top of imposing levies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I believe, for instance, that as a Singaporean worker, I probably benefit directly from such a system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But it is no use to have short-term benefits which diminish our long-term prospects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is in our interest to ensure that the system remains viable for the long term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Another area of concern which I had spoken about in this Chamber before and which invariably provokes a clash of emotions is prolonged forms of wage support, especially when these Page: 25 are not tied to clear rules for withdrawal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although I am opposed to extended wage support, I have no hesitation in acknowledging the Finance Minister for what can only be a decision made from his heart not to immediately discontinue such schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is no doubt that loss of jobs and the uncertainty associated with job search is an emotionally costly affair on those of our fellow Singaporeans who become affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the last few decades since our first recession, there have been many families whose lives have been severely disrupted as unemployment hit them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the process of searching for a new job, their decision about whether to accept lower paying alternatives or hold out for a similar position, and the anguish as the unemployment duration lengthens for them, are heart-breaking and anxiety-filled, not just for them but also for their family members, if they are the primary breadwinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, fellow Singaporean workers have remained stoic through each and every ensuing downturn, maintaining their faith in the almost unparalleled capacity of the Singapore economy to create jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is no mean feat to continue to generate jobs in an increasingly sophisticated economy packed into one of the most congested cityscapes in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, while saving jobs for the present, especially during times when the economy is weak and layoffs are mounting, is good, we should also have an eye for the preservation of the longer-term performance and vitality of the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although it is a difficult decision, I am certain that to preserve the policy effectiveness of these and other innovations, the Government must ensure that it is not just creating jobs, but continues to be focused on the more important task of creating longer term employment opportunities of value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The sector-specific approach that is introduced in this Budget could actually result in complications over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: While customising plans for each sector – whether in terms of manpower projections or business coordination – could potentially improve the fit to the specific needs of each sector, it may result in an entrenchment of sector-based interests and, ironically, could detract from overall coordination at the national level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This type of "spaghetti bowl" phenomenon is not unlike the complex maze of bilateral and multilateral relationships that analysts in trade theory refer to when analysing the impact of trade agreements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I support very strongly the switch away from a broad-based approach to a targeted approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should not rule out re-introducing broad-based measures later on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: After all, policy tools must be judged solely on the grounds of efficacy, and shying away from promiscuity is an unnecessary self-limitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite that, from a policy perspective, administrative ambitions have to be tempered as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As this Budget places us on the threshold of a technically more complex era of sector-focused planning, we should also guard against spawning a monstrous array of coordination challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 26 My question is: are there adequate assurances that sectors will not retreat into their own narrow outlook and compete for limited resources without an appreciation of national concerns?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The strong support from the Government and other stakeholders notwithstanding, resource constraints are a major factor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, in terms of the number of R&D personnel per million persons of the population, Singapore's figure, actually, has been consistently above those of the Republic of Korea, Japan, Germany and even the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Research manpower in Singapore has been growing rapidly, with the number of research scientists and engineers increasing 1.5 times between 1997 and 2012.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Such rapid rates of growth are not only difficult to sustain, they affect other sectors that compete for the same limited supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Industry Transformation Programme will further increase the scramble for already tight resources in this area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even as the outcomes from such efforts must be properly measured and assessed in order to justify public expenditures, we should avoid sparking off a chase for measured KPIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: They did so, keeping our core philosophy intact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Minister Heng is Singapore's eighth Finance Minister and is Singapore's first Finance Minister who was born after our very first Finance Minister took office in 1959.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our very first Finance Minister needs no introduction in this House.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Anecdotes of Dr Goh Keng Swee's frugality and thriftiness are legendary.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: His penny-pinching habits, including the state of disrepair of his car, have all been well-chronicled.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the context of Singapore today, our younger Singaporeans may not be able to relate to these stories personally and some may even find them laughable or ridiculous.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But thriftiness was the hallmark of our founding leaders.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not only Dr Goh, but then Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew and each and every one of our founding leaders.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We do so to secure the future of our children and grandchildren, just like the Pioneer Generation had secured for us what we have today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Page: 27 Mdm Speaker, this represented one of our core values and was also a reflection of Singapore's early history.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our fiscal prudence has put us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Educated guesses on the state of our reserves often arrive at a figure few could fathom or ascertain in an instance, the actual number of numerals involved.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am a chartered accountant by profession and I struggle also!

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is, however, a good thing, something we should be rightfully proud of.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But this has led to calls from some quarters for the Government to spend more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Calls for short-term fixes to stimulate the economy and to make the lives of Singaporeans easier and more comfortable.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: First Deputy Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Mr David Lipton, warned last month that the global risk of "economic derailment" has grown.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If true, this will certainly affect Singapore and calls for our Government to do more, spend more and help more will inevitably get louder and louder.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To be fair, the argument to assist those less privileged or to share some of our successes is not an unjust one and our Government has acknowledged this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Any further calls for more liberal spending by the Government, however, should be carefully considered and treated with great caution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we think we are safe and invulnerable because of the size of our bank balance and, therefore, can and should draw down on it to make our lives "easier" and "better", we are simply deluding ourselves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: History is there for us to learn from, not to repeat its mistakes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We should never deviate from our fundamental principle of "living within our means" and being financially prudent, no matter how tempting it might be to simply use money to solve problems that we are facing or will face.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In a recent interview with Channel News Asia, I highlighted the distinction between items that are "good to have" and "must have", the point being that the items that fall into the former category can wait while we allocate resources to achieve the latter first.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I said it because I believe in it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But it was also a good soundbite for television.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But carrying out the proposition is certainly more complex than delivering it on television.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In this, I do not envy the job of Minister Heng or any of our Ministers for Finance preceding him.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: How does one decide the arbitrary line that distinguishes the "good to have" from the "must have"?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As Singapore became more successful through the years, naturally, Singaporeans want more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is part of achievement and the fruit of hard work and ambition; key attributes to success.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: What is a "good to have" in the 1970s may very well be a "must have" today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Terminals 4 and 5 of our airport and their construction costs may seem extravagant to some, but is crucial when looked at in the strategic light of how Singapore Page: 28 hopes to position itself as a hub in this region.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Between 2011 and 2015, they have gone up by almost 10 million.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It has direct and indirect consequences for our economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am sure we all agree, without it, everything else really does not matter.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The recent bombings in Jakarta, Paris, Lahore and Brussels reinforce this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We also want a better and more efficient public transport system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We want the convenience of public transport at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We want sheltered walkways to take us from our towns to the various transport nubs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But looking at the heart of this Budget gives us an indication of a possible yardstick.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is meant to help firms and industries restructure, create new value and drive growth.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Government's role, after all, is to assist industries and firms to grow sustainably and succeed on their own accord in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that the Government will help firms and industries to transform, innovate and grow.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is, again, a future-centric development programme, beneficial to the long-term development of our economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, with limited resources, the transformation programme will encounter some difficulties.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: During the transformation process, pain brought about by change and trimming excesses should be expected.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the end, not all firms will survive and firms should not expect such support programmes to be permanent.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: After all, the Government's role is to help industries and firms to grow steadily.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Whether they can succeed in the future will depend on their individual efforts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: (In English): Folded into this is our Government's assistance to our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Again, these policies have been tailored with an eye for the future, to provide a helping hand to our SMEs gain a foothold in their respective industries on their own steam.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It aims to help those who need it the most but also assists us all in working towards a bright and sustainable and secure future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our needs and wants as a country will change.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is a principle that has been handed down to us by our founding leaders, and I urge all successive generations of leaders to keep to the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I want to begin by stating what I hold to be a hard truth about Singapore's survival and prosperity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And that truth is that Singapore must recognise our innate strengths and weaknesses and find ways to make up for and transcend our weaknesses and, at the same time, figure out approaches to propel ourselves ahead of the other nations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This has been and remains the only viable way to continue to make a good living and secure a bright future for ourselves and our children in an uncertain and turbulent world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For this reason, three things in this year's Budget speech resonated with me strongly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And by "us", I mean the companies or people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These three things are not only about specific Budget measures of where the funds and incentives are applied.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is not about where the money is going alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think these are three critical mindsets that all of us in Singapore must have, if we are to survive and thrive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Allow me, once again, to quote from our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think this particular quotation is by now very familiar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: He said, and I quote: "This country belongs to all of us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We made this country from nothing, from mud-flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over 100 years ago, this was a mud-flat, swamp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Ten years from now, this will be a metropolis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Never fear!" He said this at a grassroots event in Sembawang in September 1965.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Such was the boldness and audacity of the Lee Kuan Yew generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Always ready to look reality and obstacle in the eye, and then to find and fight a way forward through to victory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Today's challenges are no doubt different from those of the initial Independence years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But one must never underestimate the difficulties faced then, or to give ourselves too many excuses now for not driving harder and smarter to change with the times, to adapt and stay relevant – to not only be busy but to mean business − so that we can continue to have a reason to be useful to the world and, thus, a reason to earn a good keep.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Should that happen, then it would be a sad case of asking, "Who moved my cheese?" The Government is putting in place both constraints, for example, in a tighter foreign manpower policy, as well as incentives to nudge companies and industries away from overly manpower-intensive approaches towards manpower-lean ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government is also investing very heavily in spurring innovation, technology adoption and process remakes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is definitely pouring resources into pre-employment and in-employment training, skills upgrading and retraining, through numerous initiatives, including SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This would be money necessarily spent and spent right, provided we elicit the right responses from those who can make things happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we have to ask: are our companies responding fast enough, with enough hunger, with enough fervour?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Are our workers, at whatever level that they are at, clear enough about what they need to know, and fired up enough to take to learning what is required not only for now but for future employment and employability?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On top of positioning funds and setting up entities and processes, we must also ask what else must we do to tap constructively into our common imagination and anxiety, to unite our spirit and to unleash its power, to mobilise our people into real and impactful action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I firmly believe that it is the effectiveness of this mobilisation that will ultimately determine our progress and success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement is keenly aware of our role as a social partner in nation-building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To help workers maximise employment, minimise unemployment and have a fair go at good jobs and prospects are our constant goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Tripartism has been acknowledged as a significant national competitive advantage in attracting investments to create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The types of industries and jobs in our economy are changing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The nationality mix of the workforce is changing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: How people are earning a living – be it salaried, self-employed, hybrid – is changing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The platforms through which goods and services are traded and money is made are all changing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This means that we have to consider our approaches carefully and adapt our ways to ensure that the Labour Movement remains relevant and effective in standing up and speaking up for workers, employees, income earners of all types at all levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, we must continue to create this value for working people in ways that concurrently strengthen our national and sectoral tripartism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: My fellow Labour Members will elaborate on the respective segments of the workforce that they are championing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For me, I would like to devote the rest of my speech to mature workers, a Page: 31 segment of fellow workers that I have long spoken up for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It may appear odd for me to allude to a coming workforce shortage at this point when we are voicing concern about the possible increase in retrenchments and unemployment resulting from slower growth expected this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is because the Baby Boomers leaving the workforce by then are estimated to roughly match the local new job entrants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond 2025, more could be leaving than entering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Add to this is the need to maintain the local-foreign manpower ratio at a socially acceptable level, and you will immediately see that companies have to re-think their manpower strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the minimum, they have to ask themselves two questions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Any company that does not ask these questions or figure out good answers to them is doomed to fail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Clearly, if one has to do more with less, then productivity and capability become the lifeblood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And just as clearly, if one has to hunt for headcount, then keeping the capable headcount that one already has becomes an act of self-preservation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because there is no point losing what you have, or allowing what you have to waste away and then try in vain to recruit that younger person out there who may not be there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this area, I see that the Government is doing its utmost to help companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge the Minister for Manpower to make the specific announcement of when this will take place at the coming Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mature workers reaching age 65 working for companies that strictly follow statutory ages will greatly appreciate that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And, by my analysis earlier, I think companies ought to welcome such a move.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Referring to what Assoc Prof Randolph Tan has also mentioned just now, when he spoke about these being helpful measures from the heart, but what about the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I support this but, at the same time, my next point says that we have to balance these with continued investment in the skill sets of our mature workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Third, employers must not neglect the continued training and development of their mature employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Such employees are more likely to want to stay on with the company, compared to the turnover rates that have been observed through surveys amongst the younger cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This means that the effective runway for mature workers actually may not be shorter than that of younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If their skills are kept up-to-date and sharpened, they will be an asset to the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If they are neglected and rust away, then they lose employability and their companies lose capability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That would be a road that leads to mutual destruction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge every STC to also detail a plan to help their industry sharpen and tap the value of a skilled mature workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Each STC must go beyond recommending paying more in the hope of getting additional skilled headcount from somewhere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is also an STC for HR, and I urge HR STC to consider this demographic reality and see how best to equip and certify HR practitioners to help operationalise this for their companies and their industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These would include the redesign of HR policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, for example, where it makes sense, companies can consider retirement ages that are above the statutory retirement age, where it makes sense for the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are companies in Singapore already doing that, as a matter of strategic recruitment, retention, redesign of jobs and work processes, use of assistive technologies to help overcome some of the expected physical deterioration with age, considerations of enhanced lighting and safety to minimise unnecessary injuries and, therefore, maximise the ability of the workforce to continue working without mishap and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must make the working environment as ageless or age-neutral as possible, so that mature workers can be enabled to contribute as much as possible, for as long as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many of them want to and companies will increasingly need such employees very much, even if some of them have yet to realise it at this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I told this friend that, to me, the Budget had set the direction and positioned resources for companies and people to take advantage of, to help themselves, now and for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is not a question of whether the Government could have doled out more money here or there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is whether there is enough will; enough will to ride that rainbow and create that better future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Whether there is enough gumption to brave the challenges, and whether there is enough good sense to do it together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On 8 August 1972, speaking at the National Day Rally, founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew said this, and I quote: "A faint-hearted people would have given up long ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We never gave in, never mind giving up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is more than just a good thing to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Minister said in his Budget Statement, it is critical to the programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we fail at innovation, we will fail to transform our economy for the next stage of value creation for growth and this will endanger our very existence as a global city and an independent nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 33 Innovation is not an aspiration; it is a survival imperative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, important to get our innovation policy approach right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this respect, I have three issues to raise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Significant public monies are being invested by the Government in innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe most Singaporeans do not object to this necessary investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this does not mean that the Government should not account to Singaporeans that their money is well-spent and there are good results to show from the investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is crucial, as the Minister said, "to capture the economic and social value of R&D".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the public needs to know exactly how much of the value is being captured for the benefit of the Singapore economy and, I must emphasise, for the benefit of Singapore society, that is, Singaporeans ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The example of the Procter and Gamble Singapore Innovation Centre (SgIC), set up in collaboration with A*STAR and EDB, is well-worn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question is, as an "open innovation hub", how many Singapore enterprises is the Innovation Centre helping to facilitate research and accelerate product development?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not begrudge P&G for obtaining a large benefit from the Innovation Centre for their own product development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, P&G is promising to share valuable expertise and experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, Singapore enterprises should have a fair share of the R&D outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it has been two years since the Innovation Centre was set up, the Minister should be able to give the public a sense of how much of the economic and social value of R&D at the Innovation Centre Singapore enterprises has been and will be capturing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For sure, returns on investment in R&D and also tech startups are long term by nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, Infocomm Investments Private Limited, the venture capital subsidiary of IDA, has been around for 20 years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, the Government will be able to give us much more than a sense of the value Singapore enterprises are capturing through the funding from Infocomm Investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should be able to give us the actual return on investment (ROI) in innovation for Infocomm Investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is important because Infocomm Investments is the foundational model for SG-Innovate, which is a far more ambitious scheme to expand venture funding and accelerator and incubator support to new and emerging sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The success of Infocomm Investments should be detailed beyond a few anecdotal examples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of accounting for the investments to the public, explaining the ROI for Infocomm Investments would greatly inspire public confidence about the Government's present efforts in innovation and allay general cynicism about Singaporeans' ability to innovate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A more fundamental question then is whether the Government has any framework to measure and evaluate the ROI in innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Measuring ROI in innovation is fast becoming a norm internationally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a ready benchmark for us to adopt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I emphasise that I am referring to the general ROI in innovation and enterprise for the whole R&D sector and for key vehicles like Infocomm Investments, Biopolis and Fusionopolis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Investments in innovation and enterprise are inherently risky and fine-grained ROI with regard to individual investments and grants may stifle R&D instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government has an internal framework to measure and evaluate the ROI in innovation and enterprise, then it should share this with the public and let Singaporeans know how we are faring vis-a-vis international competitors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government does not have an existing framework, then now is the time to develop a framework to measure ROI in innovation and publicise it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not to embroil the Government agencies in the politics of blame and shame.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is to instil basic accountability for good governance as well as to mobilise Singaporeans for the innovation drive, which is a survival imperative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second issue is the development of a Singaporean Core in R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order for the economic and social value of R&D to be captured in the long run, we need to make sure R&D funding for scientific research is benefiting Singaporeans directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we invest heavily in deepening R&D capabilities, the corresponding focus should be to make sure these capabilities are anchored by a Singaporean Core in the R&D sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The NRF has been actively trumpeting the latest scientific advances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One such advance featured in the news in 2013, the invention of an invisibility cloak to make things disappear from view, quite literally caught my eye.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the stuff that makes for the thrill of Harry Potter fantasies and Star Trek science fictions and captures the public imagination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Scientific progress takes time and the translation from science to marketplace is an undertaking that requires patience and commitment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The team comprised six other collaborators from Zhejiang University in China and the Marvell Technology Group Boston in the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The global university field is characterised by the mobility of talents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though probably just a junior member of the team, the Singapore PR professor involved in the invention of the invisibility cloak is a young researcher under the age of 35 and has many decades of breakthrough research Page: 35 work in him yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to attract and retain foreign talents like him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Better still, we need to help him and his family sink roots in Singapore as a citizen, so that he will become a member of the Singaporean Core in R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are making progress in deepening our R&D capabilities, as the invisibility cloak example shows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the ideal would be that a cloak nearing industrial application be produced by a local industry-university team led by Singaporean scientists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My point and my plea are this: while the Government pumps generous funding into R&D to deepen innovation capabilities, that it does not ignore the social factor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not a matter of just plonking talents together and getting them to talk and work with one another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to focus on developing more Singaporean innovators as well as retaining non-Singaporeans who would help Singaporeans innovate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must strengthen and empower the Singaporean Core in R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only then will they continue to create value for the nation deep into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third issue is the risk of the innovation enclave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The industrial park model has been successful for us in the last 50 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is right we celebrate Jurong and how its success has benefited the country and our countrymen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The network of industrial parks merging into our heartland mobilised a generation of Singaporeans to become workers to transform the country and taught all of us the culture of hard work and perseverance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concept of getting researchers, entrepreneurs, industrialists and investors to live, work and play in the same mega-mall so that chance and choice encounters could produce new ideas, inventions and businesses is very plausible and attractive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research on science and technology parks and their influence on innovation has seen mixed results.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some studies show that science parks promote interaction between firms and research institutions, while others show that notwithstanding the increased interaction, geographical proximity does not seem to be an important factor for forging formal research links and innovativeness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question remains for researchers of science park innovation: are these parks "seedbeds" or "enclaves" of innovation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The science park, as "seedbed", would see the science park as providing the right environment to nurture new technology startups benefiting from technology transfer, research spinoffs and the development of innovative products.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But depending on a whole host of factors, the science park could very well end up as an innovation "enclave", where enterprises are attracted to the science park due to the status and prestige of being located in the exclusive park.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is, therefore, a precedent for the Jurong Innovation District.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is worthwhile for the Government to make its case to the public that the Buona Vista science parks work as innovation seedbeds and are Page: 36 not an innovation enclave detached from the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the Buona Vista science parks successful by measures of innovation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the ROI in innovation for the Buona Vista science parks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have Singapore enterprises and Singaporean innovators that relocated into the science parks become more innovative?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How have Singapore enterprises benefited from these science parks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the main beneficiaries vertically integrated foreign multinational corporations (MNCs) which have merely shifted their operations to Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the benefits to Singaporeans mainly trickle-down effects rather than improving Singaporeans' innovativeness?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have the science parks trained up a Singaporean Core of R&D professionals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the R&D leadership in the science parks still dominated by foreign scientists?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is that the Jurong Innovation District is going to develop into an enclave enveloping NTU.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such an innovation enclave would mean foreign MNCs and venture capitalists congregating in the enclave with more foreign researchers and managers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They would live, work and play with an exclusive group of local elites selected to interact with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is that the Jurong Innovation District, by virtue of its exclusive urban design, would become a high-tech island detached from the rest of Singapore, from the heartland estates where Singaporeans and Singapore enterprises are supposed to be beneficiaries of innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we creating mega-ivory towers, one surrounding NUS and the other surrounding NTU?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the science parks plug back into Singapore society to diffuse creativity and innovation into the rest of the city?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The benefits of this alternative model are these.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of hoping only for foreign know-how to somehow spread to selected local entrepreneurs, the heartland science parks will multiply and synergise local entrepreneurship, so that innovation will take off from a Singaporean base to engage the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
