text: The network of heartland science parks will bring a beneficial diversity to our public housing towns, making them more cosmopolitan than they already are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conversely, the rich heartland life worlds will expose otherwise isolated researchers to a grounded diversity that could generate interesting and relevant innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In time, the different science parks could evolve into diverse specialisations, creating experimental niches that will give local character to the towns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Bedok may well become a fintech powerhouse, while Bukit Batok becomes the cleantech town.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A positive side effect is urban renewal of our heartland estates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our heartland town centres will stay economically vibrant as local businesses provide services to the science park crowd.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will also increase the number of local jobs available in the heartland for those who find it difficult to travel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Overall, it may help solve the problem of ageing estates as older townships continue to Page: 37 attract younger families to move into them due to the heartland science parks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are now on the cusp of another industrial revolution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us be brave for a brave new world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seed innovation everywhere in Singapore and empower every Singaporean to pursue innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this note, Mdm Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Minister Heng worked hard at the Ministry of Education to ensure that every school is a good school, and now, with an even heavier portfolio, he has, in his first Budget, made his mark in attempting to make every industry a viable industry, every worker a valued worker, every family a stable family, and every Singaporean an important pillar of Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: His call to Singaporeans to come together to partner for the future is timely as we chart the path towards SG100.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is also reassuring that the Minister seeks to reassure all of us of it being prudent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we have arrived as a shining red dot because we have had a Government that has been accountable, innovative and yet prudent in our expenditure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although I am impressed by Budget 2016, please allow me to voice a few concerns.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I add my voice to the view that there is a need for long-term fiscal prudence both in Government and also in how society perceives the annual Budget.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although we have endowed future Governments with the creation of large endowments, such as those for the Pioneer Generation package, MediFund and Workfare, we need to keep our eyes on the horizon and ensure that we have enough for our children and our future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our Pioneers and founding fathers toiled hard to save us from seeing a rainy day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am concerned that we do not reach the stage that we develop the habit of giving out fish rather than teaching how to fish.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In trying to get feedback on the Budget, I received one email that simply said, "This year no ang pow".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot expect each Budget to be one bearing gifts aplenty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unlike Santa Claus, we need to work within the Budget and we certainly do not have an army of elves turning out gifts by magic.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, we need to be wise with what we spend and spend what we do well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Industries and businesses, especially the small and medium enterprises, should take the opportunity offered by this year's Budget to upgrade themselves and stay competitive and Page: 38 productive and be prudent with what they spend on.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: WCS is very much favoured by employers because it extends a lifeline to their businesses and also helps them retain and train their staff.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But my concern is: if and when WCS is discontinued, will these businesses, dependent on this scheme, therefore, fold?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should there not be some enterprise on the part of our enterprises to ensure their future survival without just depending on schemes and innovations?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope proper auditing is carried out to ensure that the money ploughed into this scheme is wisely used for the purposes intended.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, hope the Minister would be able to enlighten us on the actual number of businesses that have benefited and, most importantly, the number of employees who have benefited from this scheme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister share with us the statistics from these companies and the number of employees who were rewarded with larger wages?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This scheme, amongst many others, is not meant to be a panacea, but I hope that WCS does not instead become an opium.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will WCS be seen as a wise investment used well or will we be none the wiser on how businesses use the funds?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, it would be helpful for us to have a better in-depth view of how it has been benefiting companies and employees.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some are unable to successfully adjust to the pay cuts and a drop in their status from a change in their job scope.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the measures therefore taken by employers to retain these workers and how does the Government monitor if the money doled out is properly accounted for?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Employees should not be taken for a ride by employers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But authorities have also warned that false claims are being made.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I am sure everyone has read with interest that a recently convicted online pimp had applied and obtained PIC payouts!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The long-term investment by the Government is a wise one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But prudence requires us to ensure that it is used well and not well abused.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman, our former Finance Minister, had always had a very positive outlook in life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: His comments made during the recent Singapore Forum with regard to productivity growth were very encouraging.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The provision of platforms for industries and businesses to hop onto and overcome the productivity conundrum is timely but the question is, for how long?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Prime Minister Lee himself has also weighed in on this issue, saying all measures have been taken to boost productivity and to have more "faith".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 39 But again, for how long more?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should 2018 prove insufficient, would more tax dollars have to be spent to address this gap?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What would be tangible results for the average Singaporean?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They should be explained, too, in layman's terms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the onus is also on our businesses to innovate and be productive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If they do not, and if their businesses suffer, who is to blame?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot drink water on behalf of the horses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the name of prudency, we cannot also drink water that does not already exist.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I especially like the comments made by the CEO of Qian Hu, Mr Kenny Yap, in a recent interview with 938LIVE.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The outspoken ornamental fish exporter was reported to have said that an enterprise that shuns innovation will not survive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Allow me to quote him: "Any enterprise that does not embrace innovation, especially in Singapore, will not survive in the next three to five years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in this area, my worry is not just about revitalisation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we simply look around us and our estates, shopping malls are popping up like mushrooms after autumn rains, they are competing for the same consumer pie.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And every single mushroom mirrors the other – same type of shop mix.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the news last week was also a big head-on clash between two behemoths on Orchard Road – Ngee Ann City and Takashimaya; even Orchard Road is not unaffected by the challenges of productivity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from the industry-based boost to transform our industries, I welcome the focused support that Budget 2016 offers to the people of Singapore – be it the young, the old, families, the needy or the disabled.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lifelong learning is a culture that should take hold in each and every one of us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the credits only began in January this year, I think we need some sensing on the progress and usefulness of the scheme to date, despite the very short period of time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With a large number of courses being made available, although we say hobbies would not form any part of this scheme, my fear is that some of these courses could become dominant within the course structure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During a recent dialogue session held by the PAP Seniors Group last week, seniors who participated in the session stated that more information is also required on some of the schemes, and more of their key concerns are with the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the need to sustain daily living expenses, participants felt that a constant monthly supplement for the elderly is in need and would be more helpful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same discussion also focused on the establishment of Community Networks to help seniors discover health issues earlier and address them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The seniors in the discussion group urged the Government to pilot it in more than three to five precincts for there to be a better Page: 40 understanding of issues in different estates.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am glad the scheme will help such families to own a 2-room flat with a shorter lease.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the concerns, which I shared before, still remain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also believe that the flexibility in the scheme for shorter leases will provide the impetus for younger families to upgrade to housing on full leases when they are ready and where possible.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Overall, to me, this Budget, even if skewed towards the industries, is a welcome and necessary change – a very slow and silent revolution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Businesses and industries fuel our growth and it is only right that we shower them with more care amidst a possible downturn.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I only hope that business owners and industries do not become too dependent on initiatives and funds from the Government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We hope these measures are temporary and wish that they serve as a catalyst for Singapore's growth. "Every School is a Good School" was Minister Heng's mantra when he was our Education Minister from 2011 to 2016.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: His tenure there left an indelible imprint on the education sector as his vision sought to bring out the best in every child.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He has just started his innings at the Finance Ministry and I am sure his vision will also be embedded there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The current Budget runs in a similar vein, ensuring every industry is a viable one, re-emphasising that every worker is a productive worker, and every Singaporean an equal partner in Singapore's growth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And again, with an eye always on prudence, may every Budget be a balanced Budget.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mdm Speaker, Members of Parliament, good afternoon.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: When delivering the Budget Statement, Minister Heng Swee Keat quoted one sentence that I was particularly struck by.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This was: "There is no such thing as a sunset industry, only sunset thinking!" The two points I will be raising today are centred on this sentence.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In general, people tend to term sunset industries as those deemed to have no future and where profits are not easily forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As a matter of fact, those so-called sunset industries could thrive as long as they clearly understand market changes, discover changes and address them, and succeed in restructuring and upgrading their industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the local food processing industry, furniture manufacturing industry and garment fashion industry are examples of success.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: What they share in common is that their industry leaders are united, have vision, courage and determination; they seek a way out amidst changes and have the gumption to try.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Not only have they led their industries from the bleak winter into the spring, but they also managed to uplift the image of the entire industry, hence attracting young people to join the industry, bringing with them new ways of thinking and new ways of doing things.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 41 Given the rapid changes in the current business environment, bottlenecks could occur in the development of any industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even those industries which are doing fairly well now may face new challenges five or 10 years down the road.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Traditional industries are mainly involved in the areas of clothing, food, accommodation and transportation; they will continue to have demand even as time evolves.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We live in an era where infocomm technology is already a norm.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, some shops still operate like before by waiting around for customers to drop in, hence have little business; some industry players adapt to the change by using online sales to expand their market reach, and do very well.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Just as mindset influences thinking, thinking determines the solution.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Whenever changes appear in the marketplace, enterprises need to embrace their customers' needs, make adjustments to their business model and undertake the necessary transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the past few years, the Government has provided many assistance schemes to support enterprise transformation and productivity improvement.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is essential for enterprises to be self-reliant.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, Government assistance cannot be viewed in terms of whether it is sufficient but whether it is truly effective.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that some industry players have no confidence in their own industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of mindset is, in fact, sunset thinking, which would sooner or later lead to their elimination.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even as we emphasise creating value-add, we should not ignore the value of their existence.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Having been in business for many years, I am deeply aware that traditional industries that wish to innovate and achieve growth will encounter countless bottlenecks.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, for these traditional industries, the value of their existence lies in being able to survive well and service the society at large.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We should realise that industry development has its own rules and process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some gradually evolve, some involve major reforms while some undergo complete changes altogether.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The role of Government officials in economic transformation is to gather resources and promote industry development through policies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I hope that Government officials could understand the uniqueness of each industry and be open-minded and inclusive in guiding industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They should not have preconceived notions on the industry potential.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: While some of these methods have worked in the past, they may not necessarily be effective in the future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Heng has said, industry transformation is a very long-term strategic plan and the crux is how to implement this plan.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: It has also affirmed the contributions of TACs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: TACs have intimate knowledge of their specific industries and, moreover, have industry leaders with deep experiences Page: 42 in restructuring.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This would be able to help their member companies effectively.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's Public Service standards and efficiencies are world famous.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the past, Singaporeans have benefited from the 3P model, which is, the close cooperation among the Government or "Public", citizens or "People" and enterprises or "Private".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Companies will have to transform to stay competitive through adoption of technology, optimisation of manpower and streamlining of work processes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But in this transformation process, there will be workers – Singaporean workers – who will be affected by the changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must understand that some jobs will disappear and no longer be available.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some will take on added functions and a broadened scope.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With this structural transition, our workers will have to adapt quickly and be equipped with new skills at a much faster pace than before for the new jobs ahead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, transformation is necessary, but we must not forget our workers in this transformation journey, our workers who are the bedrock of our economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to ensure that no one is left behind as the changes gather pace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to ensure that our workers, both young and old, can maintain a sense of job security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When there are structural changes, it can result in a "chain effect" on three fronts – jobs, workers and skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These changes can spread from one function to another within a company, essentially, changing with it, the requisite skill-sets required for each role.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, when a retail company adopts an e-commerce platform and reduces its physical shop fronts, certain job functions would change.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: New processes will have to be introduced and implemented.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What this means is that workers who used to take on specific job functions may suddenly find themselves having to move to new or expanded job functions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In that sense, it is not only about one worker, but rather, all the workers along that value chain will also have to transition into other job functions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This may occur both upstream and downstream within a company, from one company to another, within an industry or even across industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Changes are never easy to deal with, but they also present an opportunity for our workers to undergo training and upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While today's economic conditions are difficult, there are Page: 43 still jobs available – good jobs, new jobs, different jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Certain industries are growing and require more manpower.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, the public transport industry is looking to hire thousands of drivers, engineers and technicians.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The key challenge is to improve on our job matching.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to create better awareness of where the available jobs are and what skill sets are needed for these jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To that end, we need to better coordinate and bridge the manpower demand and supply chains so as to improve the chance of a suitable match between job and worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, when there is a retrenchment exercise by a unionised company, the union would coordinate efforts with the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute, or e2i, and e2i would assist in job matching for the affected workers after assessing their profiles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During the process, there would be in-house training and coaching for the workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where needed, these workers would be advised to go for further training to enhance their employability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Place-and-Train programme is another way of job matching to help displaced workers secure suitable jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the programme, workers receive training while in employment with the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Companies resolve their manpower shortage issue and workers enjoy job progression and, more importantly, job security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to create more meaningful internship attachments and apprenticeship programmes to allow students to gain valuable hands-on experience at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would help channel students with the relevant skillsets and requisite experience to the appropriate industries, minimising post-school "talent leakage".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government and employers can do more to improve job matching.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to encourage more employers to embark on Place-and-Train programmes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides providing funding support for these programmes, the Government needs to work closely with the industries to identify future jobs so that we can better prepare our younger generations and equip them with the relevant future skills to meet the needs of these future jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many times, the jobs that they have been doing are no longer in demand and they do not have other skills or relevant experience to perform another job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, not having a second skill deprives our workers of the opportunity of promptly finding alternative employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The longer it takes to find a job, the harder it gets for a successful job match, the higher the stress for the individual and the family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to help our workers attain a second skill, but not only when they face a risk of displacement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even before the risk of displacement becomes real, we should help them acquire relevant skills to help them move ahead into new jobs, different jobs, future jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our strong tripartite partnership, I believe we can and will manage the change well.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together, we will come out stronger, as we have time and time again.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Small businesses, particularly, are very worried about their outlook; so, too, are the workers on their job prospects.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Finance Minister has been very reassuring in his speech and I am confident that, once again, as long as we band together as one, we will tide over the difficult year ahead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In today's speech, I will highlight and put forward a bold proposal for an uncertain future ahead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second, I will talk a little bit about what I like and what I do not like about this Budget, and third, I will talk about learning from a crisis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In preparing for an uncertain future ahead, truth be told, for all our accomplishments as a nation, we are still very vulnerable to global economic and political storms.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, how can we survive as a small country in this turbulent world?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: History has never been kind to small countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How do we ensure our continued existence in this big chaotic world?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have grown from an entrepot trading centre to manufacturing, to a thriving global city, actively engaging in regional and international dialogues from social, political to medical science; we are plugged in to the global network.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our manufacturing industry was once filled with vitality.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even Apple opened a plant in Singapore in 1981 to manufacture circuit boards and computers for several years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Between the 1960s and 1990s, we had high economic growth and Singapore was recognised as one of the four Asian Tigers, along with Hong Kong, South Korea and Taiwan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How do we maintain our relevance to the world?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If I may use a biological analogy: we could learn from the small organisms as to how they have survived and thrived over the millions of years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The mitochondrion is a very unique organelle within the cell and it is the only organelle within the cell that has its own DNA and genes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is found in all cells, hosting critical biochemical Page: 45 processes like respiration and energy production.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In short, the mitochondrion is the powerhouse of the cell.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Because it has a structure that is very similar to a bacterium, many scientists believe it started off as a free-living bacterium many million years ago.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Over time, it evolved and became incorporated into the Eukaryotic cells.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And now, all cells cannot survive without a mitochondrion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, we need to make Singapore a country such that we are very much needed in the modern scheme of things.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a democratic, secular, multiracial society with good political stability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have well-developed infrastructure and good diplomatic relationships with all countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are strategically located as an air and sea transport hub, as well as a leading financial, communications and arbitration centre.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yes, we are small, but that also means we are no threat to the others as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since 2002, we have hosted the annual Shangri-La Dialogue which is attended by defence ministers and defence chiefs from 28 Asia-Pacific countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have also successfully hosted many important global meetings, such as the first World Trade Organization (WTO) Ministerial Meeting, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) meeting, as well as the World Customs Organization (WCO) meetings.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We even played host to the historic landmark meeting last year between China’s President Xi Jinping and his Taiwanese counterpart, President Ma Ying-jeou.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the same year, we saw the opening of INTERPOL Global Complex for Innovation (IGCI), which complements INTERPOL's headquarters in Lyon, to enhance its presence in Asia and support policing efforts to tackle international crimes around the world.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are at least 70 resident foreign embassies and high commissions, 43 foreign consular posts and 11 international organisations in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Recently, we saw the opening of the China Cultural Centre as a bridge for people around the globe to get acquainted with China and vice versa.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Orthodox Metropolitanate of Singapore and South Asia has its headquarters in Singapore, of which 12 countries, including some of our neighbours and parts of Asia, are under its spiritual jurisdiction.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, from political to culture and religious organisations, we are clearly the choice for them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, UN has permanent offices in New York, Geneva as well as Vienna, Austria, and in Nairobi, Kenya.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Surely, this is the millennium for Asia; and should UN not have a better presence in this region?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Asia is not only the most populous region in the world, but it is one of the biggest markets for global trade and an engine of growth for the world economy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The list should include the International Labour Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization and even the UN International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF) as we have the expertise and the ability to house them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If Singapore is the home to UN bodies, then we can be even more well-plugged into the global network to see us well through beyond our next 50 years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The opening up of UN offices in Singapore would also provide good employment prospects for Singaporeans from across various sectors here.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Page: 46 UN Park in Geneva is a tourist attraction.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am sure if we were to have a UN Park in Singapore, it would be a tourist attraction, too.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, to the layman, it looks like we are spending a lot on defence.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, it is because we have a small population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you look at the list of countries by total military expenditure, we are far from the top.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They are now ranked number 30 in terms of military expenditure, just six places below us.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Defence spending of our neighbours, given their growing economy and population size, will outstrip us soon.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am not saying this to get us into an arms race, but I raise this so that we know that there is a limit to what we can do, given our small size and small population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need a new defence strategy, apart from maintaining a strong deterrent armed forces.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What I like and do not like about the Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am pleased that in his maiden Budget, the Minister for Finance has given focus to the elderly and the needy in our society.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Silver Support Scheme is the latest addition to our social safety network providing support to our needy senior citizens.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is like an extension of the current Public Assistance Scheme rather than what some perceived as an extension of the Pioneer Generation scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Resources needed for the Pioneer Generation Package are finite and the last Government has already set aside money for it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The number of Pioneer Generation citizens will decrease with each passing year while the number of recipients for Silver Support Scheme is likely to increase with our ageing demographics.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Resources needed to fund this recurring and perpetual scheme will have to come from the Government of the day.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many have upgraded to 5-room flats to accommodate a bigger family and the price difference between 4- and 5-room flats was not that great decades ago.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we include the 5-room owners, how many more seniors will be eligible for the Silver Support Scheme?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The three qualifying criteria are reasonable, simple and practical to implement but there will always be deserving cases that may not qualify.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is there an appeal mechanism for those who do not meet the criteria and feel that there is a case for them to appeal?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If there is none, I hope the Minister can consider setting up one.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Within the 140,000 recipients who qualified for the Silver Support Scheme, some may already be on the Public Assistance Scheme and some other welfare schemes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How will the new Silver Support Scheme affect the current assistance that they are receiving?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What I do not like about the Budget this year is very simple – there is nothing "green" about it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is no mention of climate change mitigation and what we are doing to reduce greenhouse gas Page: 47 emission.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Although we do have green car carbon emission rebates, I am disappointed that there are no further enhancements to it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Government can put more focus on this and develop our green industries further.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is a whole slew of schemes to help businesses, particularly SMEs, to face the challenges ahead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, if I may briefly raise this point as I do not know if we are doing good if each time when we anticipate an imminent economic turbulence, everyone would look to the Government for shelter.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Businesses are always hopeful and confident that the Government will introduce measures to help them tide over the crisis and, indeed, the Budget always delivers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the last crisis, the Government introduced and enhanced many policies to retrain workers and help employers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But there are also situations that, if we over-shelter, we may end up with an over-reliance on the Government and businesses may become like plants growing in a sheltered greenhouse – they will not have the resilience to withstand a storm or winter.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Economic crises are cyclical occurrences, just like the seasons.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With every crisis, we are supposed to emerge stronger and more resilient from the last one.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But that would not happen if companies do not feel the pressure to improve, innovate or adapt.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Business leaders who have the foresight will take advantage of the crisis to learn about the weaknesses of their set-up, resolve them quickly and accordingly.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some workers will learn new skills and become more employable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But there will be that few who do not learn from these lessons and take for granted that there will always be help available.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In other words, "The plum only blooms in the harsh coldness of winter." It means success comes only with hard work and labour.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But I believe that with wise leadership and the diligence of our people, we will all live to smell the fragrance of the plums.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I will focus my speech on our economy and jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I fully subscribe to this spirit of collaboration, which is critical in this increasingly complex world where the Government cannot be expected to know all and do all.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We Page: 48 are most effective when working together, leveraging one another's strengths.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Corporations and individuals alike need to take greater charge of their own destinies, even as they look to the Government to foster a nurturing and enabling environment in which to thrive and grow.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We will get to SG100 in better shape if we each focus on our strengths, align our goals and resolve to support one another in the journey there.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I am concerned about the underlying structural deficit.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, crucial that we enter into careful consideration and robust debate over our country's spending plans to ensure that every dollar is well spent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is to ensure that these multi-year schemes achieve their policy intent and deliver the expected outcome, namely, the boost that is needed for our capabilities and competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What lessons have we learnt from our experience of years past, where well-intentioned productivity schemes, costing billions of dollars, ultimately failed to lift productivity levels?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have been on this restructuring journey for some time now and, with each passing year, the urgency to show results grows whilst our margin for error shrinks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The introduction of a one-stop Business Grants Portal is timely.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And two thumbs up for the shift from the broad-based PIC scheme towards a targeted and sector-focused approach to support schemes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, perhaps because the new schemes that have been announced have been targeted, many SMEs have the impression that they will not benefit much from this Budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should remember that, apart from these new schemes, SMEs can continue to take advantage of many broad-based schemes that were previously introduced, such as the Transition Support Package, Infrastructure Projects and SEC.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Execution will be more complex as success will depend on multiple partners pulling their own weight.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government agencies will need to work closely with enterprises at the industry level in order to develop transformation maps tailored for each sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They will need to come up with different support schemes, tailor-made for different industries, and they will need to look afresh at specialised infrastructural development for each key sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Trade associations will need to proactively step up their outreach to member firms, develop capacity and capability-building in their respective industries and lead the development of industry-wide solutions that address common challenges amongst their members.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These are all steps in the right direction but the journey will take time and success is not guaranteed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These initiatives require extensive planning, coordination and execution, but we must not be deterred.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge all parties to seize this opportunity to embrace a new era of collaborative Page: 49 ventures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If it all sounds familiar, perhaps it is because we hearken back to a time when our Pioneer Generation, faced with great uncertainty in a new land, depended on one another to make what they could of the little they had.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They were inventive, determined and they were a team.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But even while we foster a healthy environment for startups to succeed, we should not forget to also help long-established companies continue their success and thrive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of these home-grown companies,老招牌 big or small, are ageing family businesses, where longevity depends on conscious and deliberate efforts towards a successful handover of the business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These SME bosses often share the strain on them to continue managing the day-to-day business when age catches up, yet they are unsure how they should go about structuring a smooth transition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For some, their children are either not ready or disinterested to carry on the family business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For many family businesses, succession represents a "make or break" crossroads in the company's history – and many do not make it across.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must, therefore, put in place measures to preserve and build on the precious value of these companies accumulated during Singapore's growing years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should learn from the best practices in Europe, home to some of the world's oldest brands, many of which started as small family enterprises.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should provide counselling services to prepare family businesses for succession, advice in the transfer of ownership between generations and trade-offs to be considered when choosing between future managers from within or outside the family.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should set up a market place and also financing schemes to connect owners, potential successors and investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our learning institutes may also offer strategic and business expertise to these family businesses to help them refresh and reinvent themselves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With such support, perhaps we could help the likes of Mrs Kwan of Lana Cake Shop ensure that her amazing chocolate cake remains a treat for generations of Singaporeans to come.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If Singaporean candidates possess the necessary capabilities for the jobs they aspire to do, then they should be given greater consideration than foreign candidates.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Page: 50 As for those who have lost or at risk of losing their jobs due to restructuring, we must do everything we can to help them get back into the workforce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have focused our efforts so far on SkillsFuture to help PMEs learn new skills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But many employers believe that no amount of new knowledge and skills can help displaced PMEs restart if they do not, first, have the right mindset.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As for us jobholders – whether PME or otherwise – we will need to adapt to a new paradigm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: No one can promise us a job for life.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When Steve Jobs, in his commencement address at Stanford, told his audience to "Stay hungry, stay foolish", he was advising them to take control of their own destinies, to be vigilant and open to new possibilities, to never be complacent, and never too comfortable.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is an uncertain and fast-changing world that we live in.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Hope for the best but plan for the worst.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Try and put aside some savings to tide you over tough times.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Take advantage of SkillsFuture and be ready to seize new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Look forward and put yourself out for the new possibilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Build bridges, cultivate and maintain a strong network of friends and contacts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is a significant challenge at the best of times – and these are certainly not the best of times.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should lose no time in taking the first determined steps forward, looking out for perils and pitfalls, ready to make course corrections, and always, always watching out for one another.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue should not be framed in terms of just providing state support to help companies survive, but in terms of providing enablers to help companies to develop their own competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state has a vital role to play in countering some of the downsides of our economic environment like high costs, but it should also act as a catalyst to help our SMEs identify, develop and maintain their own critical competitive success factors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially so in regard to developing productivity, where Singapore is still struggling in certain sectors, especially in services, construction and other domestically-oriented ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 51 To this end, our main focus should not be only on short-term props like ensuring more public sector construction projects, even if those are necessary, to smooth out short-term fluctuations, but on making SMEs more competitive and more productive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I used to take my children for breakfast before taking them to swimming class when they were much younger.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Near the swimming class, there were two cafe outlets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One frequently had five, six or seven staff present, many of whom were standing around with nothing to do much of the time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, many dishes were not available or took a long time to prepare.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other cafe outlet had two to three staff and yet, all the food and drinks were prepared fairly quickly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No prizes for which one we went to for our breakfast most of the time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, companies do not all know how well they are performing vis-à-vis their industry peers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not have the visibility about the rest of their industry and often do not have the resources to understand what productivity levels are like in other developed countries and how those are achieved.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is available is public information which tends to be about larger, public-listed companies and industries dominated by these larger companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt, the National Productivity Council and SPRING do work with SMEs to raise productivity, disseminate best practices and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But nothing beats a simple quantitative ranking to focus minds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would be similar to how our household utilities bills show a chart of our electricity and water consumption, compared to similar-sized households and the national average.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Economic promotion agencies or the Government can agree on a company-level standard for, for example, "poor", "average", "good" and "excellent" productivity for specific industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Government agencies could then automate the extraction of data from financial statements filed with the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA), even for private-exempt companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This data analysis could be used to derive the average figure within the industry and the figure for each company.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: ACRA, SPRING or another Government agency could then write to each company each year to inform them of their level of productivity, where it is ranked versus the industry average and where it stands relative to the benchmarks which have been derived from global analyses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Improvement in a company's productivity ranking could be used as one criterion or one forward-looking condition, not the only one, to grant access to Government incentive schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second suggestion is to create an R&D-matching facility to allow SMEs to work with autonomous universities (AUs) and national research centres (RCs) and research institutes (RIs) under the A*STAR umbrella to call for tenders, as it were, for standalone R&D projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can do even better in intermediating between the R&D sector and local SMEs to allow synergistic projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The example of Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), Germany's Fraunhofer Network or even how some Japanese MNCs collaborate very closely with Page: 52 Japanese universities to outsource part of their R&D work is interesting in this regard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a project is agreed between the parties, A*STAR and/or other relevant agencies could provide co-funding in exchange for job creation commitments or some form of modest profit-sharing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would appeal to SMEs which seek R&D support for ideas they may have but lack in-house R&D resources and who may not want to go down the path of the Get-Up Programme, which allows researchers to be seconded to companies, since their needs are more project-specific.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mdm Speaker, I would like to speak on sector-specific measures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The services and construction sectors are two sectors which are still grappling with productivity issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need both carrot and stick for these sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may also have been the case with some firms that PIC was not used to make game-changing investments in technology in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For these two sectors, to help them transition to a higher productivity future, we should pay careful attention to ensure that funding support is available to make transformational game-changing investments in technology and work processes, either using the Automation Scheme provisions or some other incentives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, SMEs still face problems to do with high cost, problems attracting talent and access to finance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these issues were highlighted in the Singapore Business Federation's January 2016 report on "A Vibrant Singapore Private Sector".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government needs to help level the playing field.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to discuss the Jurong Innovation District.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will take up the issue of access to finance in the Committee of Supply (COS) and access to talent later on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the Jurong Innovation District, one of the key challenges that SMEs face is rental costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More broadly, the issue of high rentals has to be addressed as it is a bigger and more fundamental impediment to startups and SMEs evolving innovation capabilities as opposed to gaining access to innovation districts with purported network effects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleagues will have more to say on this issue of rentals during COS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, the Workers' Party suggests that we create a mechanism to ensure a high-level whole-of-Government approach to SME development that goes beyond just the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we see local enterprise development as a critical priority, as I believe we should, we should create a national secretariat for local enterprise development, one that brings together multiple Government departments and Ministries and which can create and execute goals for different Government agencies to nurture local enterprises in their spheres of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the same vein, the Singapore Business Federation has suggested creating a Minister for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, on nurturing SMEs, the pool of local enterprises is also not equal in terms of their goals and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some aspired to become world-class whereas others aspired to maintain Page: 53 themselves as SMEs indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our approach to incentives should reflect this inequality very strongly, as was practised by Japan and Korea in their early days of post-war development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The support should be conditional on hitting goals in terms of revenue, investment, job creation and so on, as determined objectively by audits or checks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The support should be unequivocally withdrawn if results are not achieved within a certain timeframe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The genuinely entrepreneurial and ambitious SMEs that we have would welcome this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, Mdm Speaker, and briefly, making SMEs more competitive is also about unlocking talent in Singaporean entrepreneurs and workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a pragmatic case for egalitarianism as unlocking hidden talent, particularly for our local enterprise sector, which needs it most.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CareerBuilder Singapore's Employer of Choice 2015 survey showed that sectors like the Government and Public Service, airline and travel and banking and financial services are the top industry sectors that millennials want to work in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, many of our young Singaporeans are drawn to work in the Public Sector, banks and large enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This draws talent away from startups and local enterprises, particularly SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To tilt the playing field so as to nurture our local enterprises, we should consider a few possible actions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also teach our children about the contributions of entrepreneurs and local firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SME Talent Programme (STP) helps local SMEs attract talent from local educational institutes by co-funding internships, study sponsorships and fresh-hire training.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More publicity should be created around existing SME Talent Schemes among both SMEs and students to drive the take-up rate even higher, which I believe is possible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be done in terms of media awareness programmes as well as school events.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SMEs should also be encouraged and supported to develop employee branding initiatives so as to be more successful in hiring.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, we should do more to measure and raise social mobility to provide more educational support to persons with disabilities to develop their talents and to work with ex-prison inmates to support their entrepreneurial dreams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall have more to say on these topics in COS and future debates, but the reason I raise this subject in the context of a discussion on local enterprises is that future entrepreneurs and innovators can come from such backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):  : Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We heard earlier a Workers' Party Member of Parliament mentioned about the help needed for bosses of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will address my speech on how workers in SMEs will benefit.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This year, the Minister for Finance announced many measures to help SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are helpful but for them to be effective, we have to ensure that the bosses and workers understand how they can benefit from these measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, the publicity efforts should not be aimed only at the business.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think the Government and the employers should explain in detail to the workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should understand whether the workers appreciate what these measures mean to them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Workers, in looking for a job, not only consider the salary, they also consider whether the jobs are challenging and whether the career will have progression.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, we have to ensure that we continue to attract people to work for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government can work with the SMEs in two ways.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In optimising the business, if more SMEs can get help from the Government, their operations will be optimised.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some workers may feel that the bosses are trying to help them, but some others may be worried that they will lose their rice bowls.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should consider how to improve the communication with the workers and before the introduction of automation, let them understand the goals of this automation and how they can benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will remove their worries and will be more effective.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If robots can help them improve their effectiveness and make their work safer, more productive and more innovative, then workers will be more willing to accept.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this process, I suggest that the automation and the Adjust and Grow upgrading scheme should be implemented together.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, in implementing the robotic scheme, we should also improve the attitude and adaptability of the workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the Government, in assessing the schemes, should understand whether the enterprise can apply the schemes and whether the enterprise has given sufficient help to the workers, so that they will understand how these schemes can benefit the workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SMEs do not have enough resources and they may not understand how to seek help.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them feel that to submit the application forms to many different agencies, they are quite troubled by this process.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them may not understand the schemes.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them may have to seek help from intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But with companies that have a shortage of resources, the application for help actually has become a burden.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SMEs can also seek help from U SME under the NTUC and the trade associations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help them to implement their projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I took part in a seminar conducted by U SME recently for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides explaining to SMEs how they can innovate and revamp, it also helped them to interact among one another.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, many of the SME bosses are relatively older and their educational level is not high.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that this LEAD+ scheme will have a Chinese version in explaining the contents of this scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The officials should have proficiency in Mandarin so that they can help the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A good package must be repeated three or four times to be effective.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we provide help to SMEs, we must repeatedly explain the good points, so that they will receive the help just as how we implemented the Pioneer Generation Package through different channels and repeatedly explained the benefits to the Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope more employers and graduates will be able to benefit from this scheme and that businesses will be able to attract more young graduates to help them expand their business.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the frontline, the supervisor may not be able to guide and communicate with the new workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the one hand, we try our best to send graduates to the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope under this Earn and Learn Scheme, we can ensure that the supervisors and the workers will have good communication through proper training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this way, we will have a good system for them to welcome the new workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides new workers, when they decide to expand the business, there are some old workers who will feel worried because the ability to adapt to new technologies, the new skills, they need more help.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some old workers resist change because they have a sense of fear.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are afraid that they will not be able to do the job, they will not be capable of completing the work, and they may lose the job to the younger and new colleagues.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The companies and the Government must give more time for training, so that they can adapt to the new technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just like the story of Travel to the West, there are many difficulties and our opponents are powerful.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I echo the Finance Minister's call for Singaporeans to work together in new ways to transform our economy and strengthen our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Finance Minister said, and I quote, "Everyone has a role, and together, we are weaving a rich tapestry – each thread a different colour and texture, but woven together to give strength and resilience to our economy and our society." To have a strong resilient tapestry, we cannot reinforce one part and allow another to fall apart.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It may sound trite, but our individual destinies are interwoven, and how our individual and collective destinies play out will, to a large extent, determine the destinies of our future generations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we need to be responsible for one another: the Government for its people, and the people for themselves and their country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Undergirding this relationship of interdependence and cross-responsibility is accountability: the Government to its people, and the people to themselves and their country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should, therefore, approach Budget 2016 with this sense of responsibility and accountability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome the measures, but because we are using public funds, I would like to see that our funds are prudently disbursed, responsibly utilised and effectively achieve the expected and intended outcomes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: By way of illustration, Madam, allow me to address the drive for innovation under the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to declare my interest as a partner of Yusarn Audrey, which is a law firm specialising in intellectual property and the commercialisation of intellectual property.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There should be a few key observations on the innovation drive.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These would be: (a) the purpose of innovation is to meet the needs of people and industries better; (b) innovation is the engine of value creation and growth; (c) there is economic and social value in R&D; and (d) ownership of IP allows companies to realise the value of their efforts.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In order to achieve the outcomes, we are: (a) making a concerted shift towards innovation and enterprise; (b) placing great emphasis on industry-research collaboration; (c) spending billions of dollars on this; and (d) in this for the long term.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And for that, we are investing billions of dollars and we will be in this for the long haul.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: With the foregoing as the background, I will now address two fundamental issues which, ideally, we should tackle.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure that we can effectively do so, we need to own the IPs or, at least own the rights, on a sustained long-term basis to achieve that impact.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of ownership of IPs is particularly important in research collaboration.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be clear as to who owns what IPs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This issue should be considered even more carefully where the parties to the research collaborations involve non-Singaporean entities and that happens pretty often.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I think we would all agree that unless we own something, we do not have full rights to do whatever we want with it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I am using a borrowed mobile phone, I have no rights to sell it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do not even have a right to lease it to another person.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am currently using a dictation software which I bought.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I have no rights to reverse engineer, I have no rights to copy or to make improvements.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I cannot even install it beyond a stipulated number of devices.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot generate recurring revenue through royalties and licence fees.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, unless we own the IP rights or have meaningful rights to the IP in the innovation, we do not have the rights to deal with the IP in the way we want to.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Unless we own the IP rights, we would have to be bound and limited by terms of licences and permissions granted by the IP owners.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Would we think it is odd for us to pay billions of dollars and not have full or have meaningful rights to our IPs in our innovations?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that we cannot have our way always, particularly in collaborations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The good thing about IP is that rights are a complex bundle and there are strategic structures that can be customised in dealing with this bundle.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, we would be like the man who owns the land, pays the builder to build a house, but stays in the house as a tenant of the builder.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: No, Madam, we want to use such intellectual property for value creation and growth so that we can harness the economic and social value of such a property.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In order for us to generate value creation and growth for the relevant industry and ultimately our economy, we must identify the measurable outcomes to be attained.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Tangible outcomes should be differentiated from intangible outcomes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should ensure that we are in a position to correctly identify the outcomes which are impactful and strategic to the industry and direct the research accordingly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The collaboration has to be conducted at a high level with mutual respect and understanding between the industry and research institutions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that the industry plays a more active role than that of a mere feedback provider.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The industry and research institutions should collaborate to identify the outcomes that are impactful and strategic and cross-validate each other's inputs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should not be content with just filing patents.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to see the tangible economic and social impact from such innovations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, in order for the IPs created to be more effectively exploited and applied within the industry, the IPs should be owned by the industry or the commercial entity, possibly either represented by the TACs or, as I had said, by the company itself.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To encourage further research, we could have schemes for the licence back of such IPs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We would require cross-licensing to other entities within the same industry, and we could commercialise and derive revenue from them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, suggest, for the consideration of this House, a structured framework wherein the industry-research collaboration proceeds on the basis of the industry specifying, validating and accepting the outcome of the research, whilst the research institutions use their expertise to achieve the desired outcomes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This structured framework differentiates the industry as the client, as opposed to a feedback provider, and the research institution as the expert adviser, researcher and developer.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a client, the industry will be better able to communicate its greater insights to direct the outcome of the research.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I also believe this framework would result in the creation of IPs that would be relevant to the industry, which would, in turn, create an intangible impact on the Singapore economy and community.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This framework, I believe, will enable the industry to enter into other collaboration agreements with its members, or with other industries, and to proliferate further value creation and growth.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, it would be able to monetise the economic value in the IP, be profitable and competitive.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the benefits will be shared by the Singapore economy and community.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But suffice it to say that the agencies administering the grants, the industries and research institutions must see themselves as being in partnership for Singapore's future, beyond their respective KPIs, beyond the granting of patents, for the future of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As the Finance Minister says, "We must remain prudent in expenditures, and ensure every additional dollar spent is spent responsibly." Indeed, let us move forward on this issue courageously, decisively and responsibly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I declare my interest as President of the Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and board member of SG Enable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In this portion of my speech, I will be referring to persons with "disabilities" or "special needs", but they will all be the same group.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged that the Minister makes specific mention early on in this section, of the three groups of special people within the Singaporean society: those who have special needs, those who are less well off or who have fallen on hard times, and seniors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome Budget 2016 for its Page: 59 inclusiveness and initiatives to empower persons with disabilities, the seniors and the economically disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have come a long way, since the Prime Minister's National Day Rally speech in 2004, in taking care of vulnerable groups in our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
