text: The second Enabling Masterplan ends this year, and the steering committee for the third Enabling Masterplan has been appointed.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have made great improvements in infrastructural accessibility.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is greater breadth and depth in our programmes for persons with special needs, the seniors and the economically disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The appointment of Deputy Prime Minister Tharman as Coordinating Minister for Economic and Social Policies sends a strong message that economic policies cannot be segregated from social policies and affirms the Government's commitment to include vulnerable groups in national planning and nation-building.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service initiative to employ persons with disabilities is another important milestone in the Government's walk of the talk.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These enhancements show the Government's recognition that persons with disabilities can be economically productive, and its flexibility in providing for the limitations and needs of persons with disabilities in the support for their employment progression.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Because I believe that the Government has set a good framework and built a good foundation for the cultivation of a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond this framework, beyond all the financial measures, we need people to make this successful.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we have discordant voices and there will always be.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans, on the whole, are known for their kindness and generosity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have experienced that through the years in my personal journey.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In terms also of relationship, we are not really too remote from persons who may have some form of special need.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It could be a child, sibling, spouse, parent, grandparent, friend, colleague.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Or we may know someone who is related to or associated with such a person.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For some of us, by reason of illness or accidents, we acquire some form of disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And for all of us, as we age, we slowly lose our vision, hearing, speech, mobility.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When we buy insurance, there is a category of protection for permanent disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The insured can claim insurance payout if he or she suffers permanent disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is a reminder that any of us could suffer a permanent disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a wheelchair user, I do not relish the thought of having more persons on wheelchairs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But it is not for me to wish otherwise, because there are things beyond our control.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I have recapped what the Government has done.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken about the culture of kindness and generosity, and I have spoken about the form of experience that some of us had, either personally or distally, with disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And we know that we can suffer disability at any time.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 60 So, why then do persons with disabilities still not feel included in our society?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot be that it is because people are not kind.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Could it be that it is because we have a lack of awareness?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Could it be that it is because there are disabilities that are not visible?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Could it be that it is because there are disabilities that are perceived as disabilities?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to share some small voices: "We hope for you to be patient when we are slow in entering the elevator.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We do not like to hold up others. "We hope for you to be accommodating when we make strange loud noises.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot control our muscles. "We hope for you to give up your seats in the train.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We feel bad for you not to have a seat, but our ankles are weak and we cannot stand for long. "Please understand if I refuse to communicate; sometimes, I am afraid and confused from the many voices I hear in my own head. "Do not be offended if I do not respond to your greetings.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot hear you. "Give us a chance to train and upgrade our skills so that we can work.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We cherish our hope for a brighter future. "Give us a chance to work, so that we can be less of a burden to our families. "Let my son have flexible working schedules so that he can accompany me for my medical and therapy sessions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do not want him to sacrifice his career development or lose his job because he is looking after me. "Be kind to my parents when I throw tantrums.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not because they did not teach me well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I simply cannot comprehend my external environment. "Please play with me.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My legs are weak, but I still have a sense of adventure. "Thank you for accepting me." Madam, a disability is not caused by a medical condition per se.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have people who do not feel included because they do not know what disabilities and what challenges we have.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Can we ask this House to be that platform to convey the little voices that I have just shared?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let our people know that there are disabilities they cannot see, they cannot perceive.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We will then have a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It matters not then whether our society is rich or poor; we will all be rich.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I am sure the House will respond accordingly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, we see a continuation of some existing schemes to support businesses, such as the Wage Credit Scheme and an extension of the SEC which provides a modest offset for wages paid to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These measures benefit employers and employees still on the payroll.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The painful reality is that there is a significant proportion of Singaporeans who have lost their jobs or are at risk of losing their jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said that unemployment remained low at 1.9%, but this percentage included foreigners in the computation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These figures paint a worrying picture but, in all likelihood, under-represent the problem.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is due to the definitions adopted in compiling the data.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the definitions used are in line with international norms, it is useful to elaborate briefly why unemployment statistics likely under-represent the employment landscape.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, a person is considered unemployed only if he is out of work and actively searching for work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If a job seeker is unable to find work and decides to give up the job search or to go into training, he is not considered unemployed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, a person is considered employed in Singapore so long as he has worked for just one hour in the period in question.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, a general manager who loses his job and works just five hours a week at a fast food chain counter is considered employed and off the unemployment statistics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the plight of this general manager deserves attention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of my residents recently shared with me his worries about employment in security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of his friends in their early 40s had recently lost their jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They had decided to dumb down their expectations and found jobs in other industries, but the reduced pay was insufficient to meet their commitments, leaving some of them to become Uber taxi drivers to supplement their income.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such persons are not captured in our statistics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But are these displaced workers not worthy of attention?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What stress befalls a breadwinner who loses his job at a stage of life when he has to support children or elderly parents, service a mortgage and more?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These stresses, in turn, have ripple effects on the quality of family life and the ability of children to concentrate on their studies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unlike unemployment, which refers to the extreme situation of a total lack of work, measuring underemployment will indicate to what extent a person is suffering from a partial lack of work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), measuring underemployment is Page: 62 increasingly relevant for industrialised countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: ILO noted that many countries were facing changes in the employment situation, labour market flexibility and the rise of various forms of non-standard employment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, new situations have emerged that can be regarded as under-employment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the 16th International Conference of Labour Statisticians, underemployment reflects an under-utilisation of the productive capacity of the employed population.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Measuring under-employment usually starts off with time-related measures, namely, the hours worked versus the hours that the employee could be available and willing to work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We note that the Government has been putting up some statistics on time-related underemployment in its Labour Force Reports.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While looking at underemployment based on time is certainly useful, it does not present the full picture.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Returning to the general manager example, the fact that he works five hours a week, as compared to a full 50-hour week, is one indicator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But it is also relevant to consider whether he is now drawing a pay at a rate below what is commensurate with his qualifications and experience.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A person's earning potential is just as relevant as the hours spent at work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order for us to better understand the phenomenon of underemployment in Singapore, I call on the Government to do the following.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Putting these three measures in headline numbers will ensure that public attention will be focused on these.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, employment income versus the median income for that academic qualification and age, or versus the previous employment income.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will give some idea of the extent to which people are downgrading expectations and taking up jobs that are below reasonable labour market expectations just to make ends meet.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the Budget measures, what does this Budget do for workers who lose their jobs?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is an Adapt and Grow Initiative and the TechSkills Accelerator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The emphasis is on inducing employers to hire through wage support to the employers and on retraining and job matching assistance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are certainly laudable, but it may take some time before the job seeker is able to find meaningful employment, through no fault of his own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for TechSkills Accelerator, it is not clear whether it is meant only for those already from the information and communications technology (ICT) sector or has a broader catchment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I concede that I am no ICT professional, but TechSkills Accelerator assumes that technical skills learning can be accelerated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For simple level skills, that might be the case, but for specialised knowledge, I can imagine that it would take years of experience to master, just like other professions, say, engineering or law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Page: 63 In this economic transition, there are hardworking Singaporeans and their families being pushed into limbo.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a society, we should devise some safety nets to give them some peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the individual, he would seriously have recourse to this buffer which he contributed to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He may not need to queue up at the social assistance agency and tap on public monies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He also need not grab the first job opportunity that comes along but be able to take a bit of time to hold out for a suitable job, enabling a better employee-to-job-fit and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As pointed out by the panellists at the Economic Society of Singapore post-Budget roundtable, better cushions for the unemployed will also encourage more people to venture out on their own and become entrepreneurs, an essential element of an innovative society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also inevitable that if we succeed in our productivity and automation drives, people will be displaced from their jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should devise a feasible scheme to tide our fellow citizens through these difficulties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This year's Budget stood out for the futuristic new economy it painted while taking care of the humanistic immediate needs of our families and our workers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A new world where robotics and other forms of automation become core factors of production, industries are transformed and local firms scale up and internationalise.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But also a new world where our children benefit from the First Step Grant and the KidSTART programme, and our seniors get help through the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is a lot that we wish to do: to improve education and opportunities for the less advantaged, to take care of our elderly more and to have social safety nets to cushion Singaporeans impacted by a restructuring economy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a world with unlimited resources, we can strive to do everything.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But alas, we do not have unlimited resources.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would thus like to focus my speech today on the economy and I will take up issues pertaining to individuals and families in the COS debates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But these are supply-side mechanisms, and supply and demand forces are closely interwoven.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The role of the Government is critical in the Singapore Inc model.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Jurong Innovation District and Smart Nation are initiatives which play a role in creating demand for new products and services and drive change through being lead users of technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together with the Punggol Creative Cluster, these platforms allow local technologies to be test-bedded and this opens up opportunities for exports if they are successful.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And just as we had adopted a targeted approach in our early years of economic development, the need to identify core areas of competencies, strategic strengths and invest in our capabilities in them, has grown even more acute, given the increasing contribution of technology and knowledge to products and services.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to build deep verticals and competencies, for only then will our products and services be sought after by international markets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have existing competitive advantages and we should build on them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some competitive strengths arose out of scarcity or needs that we have.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our land scarcity, for instance, led us to create giants in urban planning, infrastructure and city management solutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our water treatment competencies arose out of a need for self-reliance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies in strategic industries will continue to innovate and be competitive because the problems that they solve for are integral to us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we embark on the Jurong Innovation District, Punggol Creative Cluster and Smart Nation initiative, new competencies will emerge.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Exploration of the use of data analytics and seamless Internet of Things technologies will add to our urban solutions capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Energy-efficient green buildings, urban greening or farming will add to our offerings as a green and liveable city.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And with greater connectivity arising from Smart Nation, all our critical sectors of power, security, water, telecommunications, banking and finance, transport will be linked up, and competencies in cyber security will emerge to safeguard the resilience of our system.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Next, we can look to grow markets by working with emerging champions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Singapore Inc model of economic development has always been one where we are open and aspire to work with the best in the world.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By working with emerging champions − companies with leading technology or new business models that are rapidly disrupting traditional businesses and creating demand with their new products and services – we can share in their IP, people and networks and ride the megatrends with them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can gain access to emerging champions via M&As or through partnerships.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our corporates can also work with emerging champions via a partnership model as many emerging champions start out as small companies looking for partners to trial their products and services.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To encourage such partnerships, our two economic agencies, EDB and IE Singapore, need to tie together more strongly the efforts of attracting inward-bound investments with internationalisation of our local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another area that Singapore can leverage is in the speed and scope of our policy support.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last year, it was worth $50 billion and had expanded to 63 countries − a growth of 800 times in five years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Airbnb was a $100-million company five years ago.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A year in the lifecycle of a technology-driven company can be worth a difference of 10 times in valuation and the outcomes can be quite binary – all or nothing.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a small nation, speed of adaptation and adoption should be our strength.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We had a Singapore Inc model of industrialisation in the past and we had put everything on the table to attract foreign direct investment (FDI).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A one-stop window for speedy approvals to enable rapid startups was the key then.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we are to be an early adopter or test bed from which new businesses can grow, our policies need to react to companies quickly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the new tempo of the market.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Government agencies need to adopt a faster process, perhaps a one-stop window, when looking at licensing requirements for new technology and business models.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can, and we should, upgrade our Singapore Inc model so that it is more likely that the "next big thing" grows from our shores.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, we have always leveraged our role and connectivity in the region.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can leverage the promise of the Southeast Asian market to attract investments, partner players and internationalise.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But changing geopolitical situations, changing trading patterns and a new narrative coming from China warrant a constant reassessment to see how best we can position ourselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are a key node along OBOR in the centre of Southeast Asia and we can be a gateway linking the South China Sea and the Indian Ocean Basin and be a place for businesses to embark on partnerships and expansion into the region.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As China looks to Southeast Asia for opportunities, particularly in the area of infrastructure development and production capacity cooperation, Singapore can play a role as a project development hub and provide a financing platform for China's new initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are, of course, always risks in overseas projects, especially when commercial projects can be thwarted by diplomatic tensions and idiosyncratic problems.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what we can try to do is to focus on projects which have strategic value for us and provide services where we have expertise, as this will allow us better control of project risks.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But there are strengths that we can leverage on, new partnerships that can be formed and new opportunities that we can seize.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Singapore Inc model was one where we put our minds and our resources singularly behind the need to provide good jobs and a good standard of living for our people.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can and should upgrade our Singapore Inc model to forge a new path forward.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.55 pm until 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This year's Budget continues to strengthen the foundation for Singapore's future growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It gives Singapore's longer-term economic transformation added impetus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Both businesses and workers need to transform for a new economic model.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to help them to be ready for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Much has been said about helping companies to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will address how we must transform the way we help our workers, especially younger Singaporeans, to prepare for this new future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Budget offers hope to industries and some individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, some already have a difficult time looking for one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Page: 67 Some of these youths have asked me, "With all this gloom, is there still a rainbow for me to chase after?" This reminds me of a recent encounter during a house visit with a young resident who is not more than 35 years old.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Naturally, I asked him how was his job and if times were tough.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Surprisingly, he said, "Yes, it is tough in the manufacturing sector but I'm okay." This is quite different from the many conversations I have had.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two years ago, because he was worried about job security in the traditional manufacturing sector, he started looking for alternatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He chanced upon a write-up on 3D printing, researched into it and was convinced about the prospects of this industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He tapped into his informal networks to understand more about the industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He left the familiarity of his old job and got a new one with a 3D printing company developing prototypes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The company is doing brisk business and he is now doing well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He has found his rainbow and is riding a new wave of growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even in an industry beset with growth issues, there are many opportunities for those who can seek them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question is: can we help young workers and millennials discover their own rainbow, especially when our younger Singaporeans will have more than one career throughout their lifetime and many students struggle with the paradox of choice?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An industry-led integrated career counselling system can help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It starts from preparing students in schools, then to their workplaces so that they can constantly stay relevant to the global marketplace of jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry of Education's (MOE's) strong career counselling initiatives are a good step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, it is not possible for counsellors to have up-to-date knowledge on all industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, the need to help these youths with career navigation post-graduation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: MOE can partner the Labour Movement in the latter's broad economic representation to guide our youths in choosing the right paths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government can have the Labour Movement to run their career counselling services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This then allows students the opportunities to tap on the unions' extensive network to understand jobs and entrepreneurships through industry networking, workshops and workplace visits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Post-graduation, this relationship continues seamlessly into the Labour Movement's network of career development opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must also bridge the gap between training and industry needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Jobs are being transformed so quickly that employers are finding it difficult to find workers with the right skills while, at the same time, students find their school knowledge quickly redundant once they step into the working world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the German and Swiss style of apprenticeship, students not only learn realtime industry-relevant skills, but also work habits from mentors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They also pride themselves equipping apprentices with problem-solving skills on the shop floor and not only in the classrooms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government consider further incentivising companies, especially promising SMEs, to start apprenticeship schemes, as opposed to just internship programmes commonly implemented today?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employees and unionists can be trained to become certified mentors and appraisers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And because students and workers know that what they learn is practical, there is good career path, they will more likely stay on the job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can create an ecosystem of continual training and upgrading that is truly win-win-win.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In preparing workers for Page: 68 the future, a tripartite partnership is and will be an important catalyst.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed Industry Transformation Programme, especially in the ICT sector, embodies many important elements in helping workers to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Minister for Finance Mr Heng Swee Keat proposes for transformation through innovation and for innovation to be pervasive across all segments of society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a point well picked up by hon Member, Mr Thomas Chua, that there must not be sunset thinking and that change is needed in every firm, every segment, and he used the food industry as an example.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need pervasive innovation to help our workers to get good jobs continually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The ICT sector will be an apt sector to test bed new ideas and catalyse innovation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, Minister Heng's proposal for the ICT sector addresses many of millennials' desire for continual innovation, definable skills level and broad-based level application of their skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the TechSkills Accelerator programme would identify the skills needed in the industry, match them with specialised training providers and chart a clearer path for careers in the sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The success of the ICT sector is, indeed, critical because ICT skills and innovation are strategic competencies for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are the engine of value creation and growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we all know that competencies, such as data anaIytics, cybersecurity and applications development, require extensive and lengthy training.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we help the displaced professionals to quickly get into these new jobs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we scale up the professional conversion programmes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To our workers, a good career is not only a challenging one that brings back the bacon, but also where there is relative security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For the ICT sector to attract local talent, our workers in the industry can be afforded better employment security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Singapore branch of Double Negative was responsible for some of the visual effects in several Hollywood blockbusters, such as "Man of Steel" and "The Hunger Games".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was, indeed, an important symbol of a thriving media ICT industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was not a unionised company and workers were offered retrenchment terms less than market practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The young employees' faith in the sector might be shaken.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is certainly much easier for technology and media companies like Double Negative to uproot itself, compared to a manufacturing plant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also true, lest we forget, that the only job security is not unemployment or redundancy insurance, but value-add and mobility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, how can we put in place strong employment facilitation and reassure our workers that this is a good industry despite its volatility?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage the Government to work with the Labour Movement to better provide workplace support and care for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Out of this group, most of these are Employment Pass holders holding on to good jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps what is most critical, beyond good school-to-work preparation and apprenticeship systems, we need our millennials and Generation Z to have that sense of adventure and gumption to take on the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to have the mindset that even in a period of slow growth, there can be many bright sparks, if we choose to look for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are rich findings for those who decide which rainbow to pursue and work at it with gumption to make it truly theirs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I support the key thrusts of the Budget in forging strong partnerships to transform our economy and build a caring society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Finance Minister has highlighted that our economy and ageing population are facing new challenges.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: He has emphasised that we must find new ways to grow our economy, educate and train our people, and forge more partnerships to encourage firms and community organisations to work together to take care of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the complexity of these new challenges, I agree with the Finance Minister that we need to adopt a targeted and prudent approach to help our businesses, workers and seniors in our community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Global competition and fast-changing economies have affected our SMEs adversely.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, many have closed their businesses while others struggle to sustain their business operations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government can increase its efforts to provide SMEs with information on emerging markets in our region, including information regarding the ASEAN Economic Community, free trade agreements and new industry growth clusters in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: A business opportunities portal can be set up to provide updated information on new business opportunities both in Singapore and the region.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: More seminars, workshops and networking sessions can be organised by various Government agencies, together with trade associations, to provide more opportunities for SMEs to meet up with MNCs and GLCs operating in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, incentives can be given to bigger firms to adopt and nurture SME subcontractors for long-term partnerships.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a practice in Japan where MNCs have long working relationships with their subcontractors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some MNCs provide scholarships to the children of their subcontractors' employees or owners, so that these children can continue to run their family businesses and support the MNCs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, help SMEs to improve productivity and the quality of products and services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Page: 70 We need to ensure that the use of PIC grants will actually increase production capacity or reduce manpower or improve the quality of products or services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must focus on helping SMEs achieve quality growth and develop niches to remain competitive.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To further improve the business processes of SMEs, the Government should partner trade associations to develop and document best business practices.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will raise the overall skill levels of our workforce and shorten the learning curve of new staff.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three, help SMEs to recruit and retain talent.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: SMEs face tremendous difficulties in attracting and retaining talent to ensure continuity and quality of their products and services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The turnover of staff has also made it difficult for SMEs to build capabilities and grow.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With a tight labour situation, it will be more difficult for SMEs to attract talent to restructure and grow.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would urge the Government to help SMEs attract and retain talent.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This could be in the form of Government-funded co-payment of SME scholarships or gratuity performance and loyalty bonus for long-serving staff, for SMEs to reward and retain their staff.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In schools, students must be given more opportunities for experiential learning, such as service learning projects, internships and applied research projects.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will narrow the gap between theory and practice, and enable our graduates to be more industry-ready when they enter the work environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As for working adults, they face various challenges in upgrading their employability skills, such as language barriers, family commitments and even lack of support from some employers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must find new ways to facilitate and encourage SkillsFuture learning among workers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These centres of excellence must be conveniently located for easy accessibility.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For instance, the centre for excellence for finance must be at our business and financial district.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, some schools within HDB housing estates can be designated as SkillsFuture centres for generic skills training, such as language, IT or office administration skills.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans who are more able must step forward to lend a helping hand to those in need.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Companies should exercise more corporate social responsibility and do more for the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is, indeed, a big setback in building a caring society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these charities are small outfits with limited capabilities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I urge the Government to consider merging or clustering the charities so that they can enjoy better economies of scale and develop capabilities to sustain their operations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Rather than having many charities scattered all over Singapore, it may be more efficient to co-locate them to support various towns.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, these co-located charities can consider providing "mobile services" to serve more people, especially those with mobility problems.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is no point building a wealthy Singapore if our people are not healthy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Without health, Singaporeans will not be able to enjoy the fruits of Page: 71 our labour and have a good quality of life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many have had to downsize and recalibrate their business model.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The prudence of the Budget is apt as it keeps some dry powder for potential off-Budget measures, if needed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a Budget with a social focus, extending help to the lower-income groups, families with children and the elderly, but also professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) to some extent via or through efforts helping to adjust to changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are groups that are especially affected both by the cyclically slowing economy and by the structural shifts affecting a number of sectors in the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may say this Budget is sombre and lacking in "goodies".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think otherwise and believe that, in the context of past Budget measures which are still being implemented, this Budget is measured and well-calibrated to take on the storm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Singapore economy is in transition and some in the workforce are experiencing rising incomes and even employment volatility.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This issue has been discussed slightly more than a decade ago by some economists.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I refer to the summary report of a workshop on "PAYE Taxation System" jointly organised by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) and the Economic Society of Singapore (ESS) on 23 October 2004.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While discretionary fiscal or Budget measures we are seeing now could be seen as a macroeconomic stabilisation tool, its effectiveness may be limited by the long lags between fiscal policy decisions and their impact on the economy, and also the difficulties in determining the optimal amount of Page: 72 transfers, disbursements and rebates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, the aim here is to do a little bit more from a tax payment perspective to allow Singapore to have a slightly stronger foundation to better withstand global economic shocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rationale for considering the current year basis is to enhance the effectiveness of the tax system as an automatic stabiliser and to help taxpayers better manage their cash flow by matching tax payments and incomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, a shift to the current year basis could increase the compliance burden of the tax system, cause uncertainty for some taxpayers, and also reduce cash flow flexibility for others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An accurate system of assessing current year income is also important for a successful PAYE scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the macroeconomic benefits of shifting to a current year system or scheme may have added support now as, under the preceding year basis, tax is paid on income earned in the year before – which would hit the newly retrenched or those who just had a pay cut or even those with a wage freeze amidst rising costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is likely that as we restructure and face increasingly volatile global business cycles, income streams for both individuals and companies will become more unpredictable, making it more difficult to plan for deferred tax payments as per preceding year basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may yet be too soon to react and stave off a recession.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And yes, we are not in sight of a recession but we may see zero growth and, with this, comes cyclical and, potentially, structural unemployment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to monitor very closely the pattern of retrenchment and shuffling of workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must ensure that the connection between hard work by Singaporeans and the fruit of their labour remains intact.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, those who have been toiling day after day at the shipyards, factories, hotels, retail stores, offices, banks, trading houses and airports should not be unfairly treated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must not allow foreign employers to furtively downgrade and reshuffle local staff under the guise of economic restructuring such that they create openings in senior ranks for expatriates to take over from the locals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To those who harbour such intentions, let this be a shot across the bow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I have mentioned this in my speech during the Debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am all for introducing wider laws to protect against discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our entrepreneurs and their businesses are one of our engines of growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All said, our economy inevitably transforms, and they, too, have to transit and shift their mindsets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a senior oil trader told me, I quote: "If I can't sell one petroleum product because of market change, I will look for other products to trade.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a long chain of by-products from a barrel of crude and it requires the same skill set except that I have to learn something new, get out of my comfort zone, understand the next product and its uses, its price and market share, and start to go overseas to talk to new customers." And that is the entrepreneurial mindset.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have many small entrepreneurs and these include retail outlets in the HDB heartlands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Already we have seen the demise of the mom-and-pop shops.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us not allow our town centres to turn into shuttered centres.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Government will look into sustained measures to revitalise these centres.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also applaud the Budget's focus on "transforming through innovation" by creating an open and innovative urban environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope we can see more JTC efforts to agglomerate certain industries together leading to innovative and sustainable infrastructure solutions which may bring about overall cost savings for businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similarly, I am especially excited about the "blue ocean" approach to pioneer new industries and create the industrial park of the future at Jurong Innovation District.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I do hope more of this can be replicated in other areas in Singapore, hopefully, maybe in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think that is a bit of a stretch.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe that by creating the right environment, we can turn it into the right ecosystem for an innovative and creative industrial sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From the workers' standpoint, this Budget's social measures do have a sharp focus on helping low-wage workers relative to PMETs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the vulnerable group in this current environment of structural change would also include those who are in their mid-careers and higher up the corporate ladder.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are graduates, earning higher salaries, in their 40s and are often targeted for lay-offs as part of cost-cutting measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Others are let go because they become redundant as their skills are no longer relevant or required.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This applies also to those who are non-graduates, diploma holders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They would have housing loans, renovation loans and car loans to service.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And then there are children's school fees, school transport, three square meals a day for the family.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are very daunting demands when you do not have a job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are already retrenched and taking jobs with lower wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A small number would have taken up driving taxis or joined the Uber or GrabTaxi operators.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A few more were fortunate enough to find jobs but in postings overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have to sacrifice family togetherness in order to stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, I hope that the Government and society do not discriminate those who hold part-time degrees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, the Government should regard them as people who took up the torch to improve themselves at their own pace.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are the lifelong learners and their attitudes and spirit should be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Singapore's economy may be facing challenges currently, but at this point in time, it is not experiencing a downturn.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, there is unequal growth amongst all the sectors, with several sectors still seeing growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In view of this context, the 2016 Budget aims to ensure that Singapore is able to withstand current uncertainties and drive the nation's economy towards a new phase of development for future growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Budget also builds on the successes of the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Finance Minister has emphasised the importance of the "Spirit of Partnership" that will drive Singapore's growth and help to transform the economy through innovation and industry, and build a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Workers, business owners, the people and the Government must also work together to build a brighter future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also a focus on increasing awareness to ensure that Singaporeans can adapt and gain access to new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Generally, this Budget shows a commitment to support businesses and industries because they are facing pressures Page: 74 currently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: China and other nations are becoming more competitive and we are also facing the issue of an ageing population and the presence of disruptive technology, which will challenge the way firms conduct their businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, I hope that our Malay/Muslim Chamber of Commerce and Industry will receive benefits from the LEAD+ programme to build on their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope, in future, the chamber of commerce can play a more important role to help Malay/Muslim firms enhance their contributions in the global value chain, become more productive and seize opportunities overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The third thrust is helping our people cope with the changing demography and economy, by learning new skills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is important because, during my Meet-the-People sessions and the recent dialogue sessions at MENDAKI Social Enterprise Network Singapore (SENSE), I found that many people within our community are aware of SkillsFuture but are still unsure how to apply and which courses they should take.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must increase efforts to inform the community about the transformation of the economy in the future, the skills that are needed and also how to take advantage of the national SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the increasingly challenging job market has also motivated many of our Malay workers to upskill while many also lost their jobs in certain sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To me, this is important because their children are also Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a small group of elderly who needs help, who may not fulfil all the criteria for Silver Support and should not be left out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): This Budget calls for partnership among all parties: labour, employer and the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am confident that our workers will be more flexible and resilient under difficult circumstances and be prepared to make adjustments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just as employers and the Government adjust to adapt and grow, all Singaporeans, too, can do so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Just this morning, I caught up with 24 Barclays' staff who are professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), both young and not so young, who are going to be retrenched in the next few months.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, in the past weeks during my weekly house visits, many Boon Lay residents, including PMEs, I spoke to are troubled by the outlook in their companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They lament that there is a sharp slowdown in orders and the amount of work to be done.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Unions and union leaders, too, are concerned as some are seeing companies fold while some are negotiating retrenchment settlements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The mood is, generally, one of uncertainty and doubt.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Ministry of Manpower's (MOM) unemployment statistics are clear.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Worse still, it is coming at a point when Singapore is embarking on economic transformation and restructuring, having a relatively flat-line productivity the past few years, an ageing workforce, a tight labour market and slower employment growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Not every industry or sector is hurt and bleeding, but some sectors are already bearing the brunt of low oil prices, currency fluctuations, market uncertainties, recalibration, consolidation and a generally weaker global demand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Unless we do something resolutely and proactively, we may have to face the worst before it gets better.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some used to say that globalisation destroyed many blue-collar jobs but, these days, technology is threatening the PMEs, otherwise known as the middle class or sandwiched class.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I am particularly concerned about how we can support our people through this rough patch of change and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would also like to thank hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim who earlier reiterated the call which I made in this House over the past few years to further examine and relook underemployment as well as unemployment insurance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Government can spend tons of resources and come up with a buffet of programmes but at the end of the day, it takes two hands to clap but more than just two hands to make a resounding applause.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers and businesses across various sectors and industries must believe in the same cause and embrace change before change embraces them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our workers and unions need to stay future-ready so as to navigate, weather through and rise above the storm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Government needs to provide the systems and supporting structures to facilitate, encourage and catalyse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Page: 77 Society, too, must be receptive to changes, abandon old paradigms and adopt major mental model shifts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In these uncertain times and as we navigate through the peaks and troughs, we need to develop what I call "3R" employers and a "3R" workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are employers who are revolutionary, responsible and ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers and businesses need to be revolutionary in incubating and executing ideas to embrace change, technology and innovation to achieve breakthroughs, enhance and develop new capabilities to stay ahead of the game.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: An example would be the use of drones to access hard to reach areas instead of risking human life and yet achieve time, cost and manpower savings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers must be responsible and go beyond that to be progressive in human resource practices and harnessing our human capital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is imperative for them to establish good and sound employment and industrial relations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In unionised companies, they must foster strong union management relations through trust and openness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Responsible such that when they restructure and need to lay off workers, they do it responsibly and in accordance with accepted codes and tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A good example is not laying off workers just before a festive period, such as Chinese New Year, Hari Raya or Deepavali.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Another would be the payment of retrenchment benefits when there is an industry practice to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Hiring such that they focus on developing a strong Singaporean Core, they must eradicate all forms of discrimination or biasness, especially with regard to age and the attitude towards both mature and older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Ready to redesign work processes and recreate good quality jobs to attract and retain the people and navigate the new labour and employment landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Ready to overcome the new norms, challenges and competition that lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is a workforce which is relevant, resilient and ready; not just the workforce but also our unions and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Relevant amid the rapidly changing employment, economic and global landscape of change and development.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Relevant to the needs of the company, profession and industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Relevant in the new economy of future jobs, future skills and future careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Relevance can be achieved through a spirit of lifelong learning and continuing education.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Unions and the Labour Movement must stay relevant to workers of yesterday, today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This can be achieved through our unions stretching the scope of representation and expanding our membership base to PMEs so that we can look after their interests and welfare.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, we need all employers to support us on this front.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We also need to expand our reach and build bridges with professional associations, such as our current 32 U-Associate partners, to build a stronger value proposition to PMEs, helping them progress in their careers and profession and creating a network of excellence and building our U-circle of friends.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We are also exploring ways to be the voice of professional freelancers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is especially crucial during this period of uncertainty and rough patches in certain sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our workers must stay resilient to ride through the global transformation of work, economic restructuring and industry transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Resilient also to weather through greater uncertainty in terms of employment and to move into new jobs and new sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need both new mindsets and new skillsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We cannot just be ready for now but ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I recently had a dialogue with a group of 40 PMEs to ask them what they define as being future-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The answers actually vary, depending on their life stages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the young PMEs, future-ready means being equipped to progress, develop and move up in their careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the not-so-young PMEs, they consider job stability and security, that is, employment and employability, as crucial tenets of being future-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, we need to be ready to Do More, Grow More and Be More!

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I say this because many employers are unaware of CSP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The current criteria also do not address those PMEs who are under 40 years of age and have lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, the wage support can be more generous during this rough patch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Take to task, with more robust measures, those who treat the Fair Consideration Framework job advertising requirement in the jobs bank as mere lip service and window dressing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, we can also go beyond Professional Conversion Programmes to any tailored targeted programmes with flexibility of interventions which can help minimise skills mismatch, jobs mismatch and expectation mismatch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, set up a support network for these unemployed and retrenched PMEs so that they do not fall into a deadly spiral of despair and depression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The programme is supported by a team of career activists who are volunteer PMEs who have faced job losses and who have been through the school of hard knocks and have now succeeded.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have achieved small but steady successes but, more importantly, this support network has helped to boost the self-esteem and morale of the dejected and pessimistic, making them more positive and career-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To conclude, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion and look forward to specific details of the policies and programmes by the respective Ministries, especially MOM, during the COS, to help my fellow workers especially the PMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last year, we had lower revenue contribution from the traditional three main sources – corporate and personal income taxes and Goods and Service Tax (GST) – due to slower economic growth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The revenue contributions from these three sources are expected to be similar or less in 2016.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the dark clouds hovering over the global economy is a stark reminder to spend within our means and save for rainy days ahead.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our open economy is vulnerable to external shocks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the Minister had cautioned, we will meet strong headwinds.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I agree with the Minister that we are coming from a position of strength and should not be overly pessimistic, I am quite concerned.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although our public finances are healthy, our social development expenditure has been growing at a faster rate than revenue growth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With a maturing economy and ageing population, expenses will increase and our fiscal position will be tighter.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whatever schemes we push out, such as the Silver Support scheme, has to be sustainable over time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How shall we sustain our ever-increasing social expenditures?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The way forward is to increase our revenue pie through pursuing economic growth which I have touched on in the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In comparison, South Korea, Japan and China's investments in R&D are 4.3% in 2014, 4% in 2016, budgeted, and 2.05% in 2014 of GDP respectively.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Apple alone spent US$8.1 billion in 2015 and Samsung spent US$13.8 billion in 2014.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I fully support this enormous investment in R&D, I would like to urge the Government to consider investing even more in science and technology R&D.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because we have seen how technological development in robotics, automation, artificial intelligence and ICT are already disrupting business models around the world.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To reap the benefits of this new Industrial Revolution 4.0, not only do we need to utilise and harness its power, we also have to develop, create and own the patents and IP rights in these segments, too, as profits will accrue to the owners.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not easy for our local enterprises to do these on their own due to their smaller sizes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where some of our local enterprises have achieved nascent success, larger and more established foreign competitors would naturally be interested in acquiring them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need Government support, both in funding and in collaboration with local and foreign researchers and universities, as well as foreign firms and for a longer period of time so that these Page: 80 local enterprises could grow to a size that can establish them as significant international players in their own right with a Singapore brand.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But here lies another question: is it possible for us, with a rapidly ageing population and a workforce better known for reliability and efficiency, to become creative and innovative?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What we need to do, and quite urgently, is to change our attitude and mindset.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Creative ventures and setting up businesses require guts because you are putting your own money, time, resources and reputation on the line.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have been trying to encourage risk-taking among our researchers and enterprises for years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As they say, if you want to take on projects in unchartered grounds, "Do not ask for permission, ask for forgiveness afterwards." Is our society ready to forgive a little more easily and make it easier for those who dare, to pick themselves up when they fall and try again?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We await the day when we have people comparing how many times they have failed and are still trying, instead of which company they are working with.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Supporting our people to overcome challenges and seize opportunities is our investment in SkillsFuture − equipping our people with the right skill sets to work in our new restructured economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: SkillsFuture is a fantastic scheme which encourages individual Singaporeans to take ownership for their own upgrading and career development.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A number of my residents have expressed concern over their abilities to relearn and retrain for different job functions or industries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Jim Ratliff worked for 14 years in the mines of eastern Kentucky, drilling holes and blasting dynamite to expose the coal that has powered Appalachian life for more than a century.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, he rolls into an office at 8.00 am, settles into a small metal desk and does something which, until last year, was completely foreign to him: computer coding.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The coal market began to collapse in 2011 and forced five major producers into bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This had hit the miners of Appalachia very hard.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The miners had to find alternative jobs and a number of them turned to computer programming, one of the few growth sectors they could identify.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They prove that with the right support and attitude, it is never too late to relearn, retrain and restart a new career.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I declare that I have interests in the hotel and food and beverage industries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fact remains that Singaporeans are not keen on jobs in these sectors and employers have difficulty recruiting enough staff.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During a recent coffee shop visit, a stall owner reflected that he is unable to secure cooks for his zi char, which is a cooked food stall.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans that he interviewed wanted shorter working hours and long holiday periods.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Separately, I was told a parent wrote in to the human resource department of a hotel to request that her daughter not to have to work the night shift.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are businesses that hire both local and foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This year's Budget comes at a time when the mood in Singapore is rather sombre.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When we walk the streets and talk to our workers across all industries, the things that are uppermost on people's mind are as follows.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One, will I still have a job by the end of this year?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If I do, will I have any pay raise, if I am fortunate enough?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If I lose my job at the end of this year, will there be another job looking for me?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Times have changed, and times have changed very quickly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It was not so long ago that people were choosing their jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But the mood has turned around very quickly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The next question that both businesses and our people ask is this: is the current economic slowdown a cyclical or a structural issue?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Recently, during the festive period, I had the fortune of driving down Orchard Road.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I always make it a point, when I drive down Orchard Road, to look at the taxi queues.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I try to make a mental comparison of the length of the taxi queues with those of last year's or the preceding months.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I try to make a mental count of the number of big bags that the people in the taxi queue are carrying.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I noticed that the queues are shorter and the bags are fewer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, the question in front of us is: is this a slowdown where, sooner or later, the same business model will allow us to pick up steam again and life will be back to normal?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The taxi queues might have gotten shorter and the bags fewer because people are more careful with their spending now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And the taxi queues could also have gotten shorter because Uber is competing with the taxis now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The number of bags may have gotten fewer because people are buying less.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But a friend told me that he tested the online shopping delivery time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That suggests that it is not just a cyclical slowdown but there is perhaps a more fundamental shift in the consumer pattern – from physical offline shopping to online shopping.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If that is the case, the question is how should we respond to this?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will come back to this in a short while.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some workers have commented that this year's Budget did not seem to speak too much about training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There was a lot of news about the $4-plus billion that we are going to spend to restructure our economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, some workers asked me: has the Finance Minister forgotten them?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Page: 82 If I may borrow a quote from Minister Lim Swee Say.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And as Minister Lim Swee Say would say, "Only when we have skills of the future, plus the jobs of the future, will our workers have careers of the future".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I do not see this year's Budget in isolation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I think we should see this year's Budget as an ongoing continuous effort to restructure our economy and upskill our workers so that we can all have careers of the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many workers have given us feedback that they are very appreciative of the Ministry of Finance's (MOF's) effort to expand and extend SEC, the Workfare Scheme, the Silver Support Scheme and the Professional Conversion Programme.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, we are very thankful that we still have the means to do all these schemes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
