text: But I would certainly agree with the hon Member Assoc Prof Randolph Tan who spoke earlier that we need to ask ourselves what is our definition of success for these schemes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the Labour Movement, the definition of success for all these schemes is not in the continuation or the continuous expansion and extension of these schemes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The true mark of success for all these schemes is not the schemes themselves, but for us to work upstream to make sure that as few workers as possible are reliant on these schemes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This suggests that we have to go upstream to do many more things and not see the expansion of these schemes as a mark of success.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, at this point in time, we are at the critical juncture of our economic transformation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How do we restructure our industries to create the jobs of the future?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How do we ramp up the capacity to upskill our workers so as to equip them with the skills of the future?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Government has not shied away from spending resources to upskill our workers or to help our industries restructure.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it is incumbent upon all of us to realise that all these monies come from the taxpayers; and it is incumbent upon all of us to realise that whoever takes any of these monies, either for personal upgrading or for corporate restructuring, has a responsibility to society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our responsibility is to use this money wisely to really achieve the goals that we set out to achieve, rather than to waste or fritter them away.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That would be the greatest injustice that we could do to ourselves, our companies and, of course, our country.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To do this, as hon Members Patrick Tay and Desmond Choo have shared, we encourage businesses to relook business processes, expand the markets to go beyond Singapore, and re-examine work processes to see how to raise productivity gains.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The workers must similarly embrace a lifelong learning culture to make sure that we are ready not just for today, but for tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The example that I shared just now, about people moving from offline to online, does not mean that jobs are destroyed and no new jobs are created.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, although the retailer who used to have a physical Page: 83 shopping outlet might be displaced, on the other hand, there are new jobs that are being created at the e-commerce, data management and logistics management fronts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, the problem is not the total number of jobs available in the economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The real question is how do we help the person who is displaced at the retail line get into another job that has been created?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It will be too far-fetched, for most of the time, to expect someone who is displaced at the retail scene to be able to go into the e-commerce or data management space with minimum training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In order for us to avoid structural unemployment, many people need to literally move one step to the right.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The person displaced from the physical retail space might have to take on another adjacent job and someone else might have to take on another job and, slowly, step by step, upgrade themselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For every one job that is being displaced and one job that is being created, we need to train more than that one person to move from A to B.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It will be a very involved process and the Labour Movement will definitely want to work with employers and the Government to make sure that we minimise the occurrences of structural unemployment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The faster our structural changes go, the more we need to do this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because when growth slows down, the space for manoeuvre that we have becomes tighter.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, growth, in itself, provides us the space to overcome some of these challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When we do not grow fast enough, it will become even more difficult for us to help those who need the help most, that is, those who are displaced structurally.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And the jobs will not come back even after this cyclical downturn because consumers' habits and production patterns have changed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we will need to do much more to overcome this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, as the hon Member Desmond Choo has highlighted, we need to go upstream.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Go upstream into the schools, the polytechnics and ITEs to provide career guidance and counselling so that we minimise the chance of every fresh graduate being put into a wrong course or selecting a wrong course because they do not have the correct information.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to have career guidance and counselling right from the school and onwards to beyond the time they spend in school.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Besides going upstream, we need to do more for the midstream through continuous upgrading.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Labour Movement will want to partner the Post-Secondary Education Institutions (PSEIs) and Institutes of Higher Learning to stretch the SkillsFuture credits that are available to all our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: With the Government's subsidies, it can allow our workers to undertake more than a few upgrading courses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, we still have much to do to ramp up the number of courses that are current and relevant to the workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not just about encouraging workers to take up any course.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is about encouraging workers to take up courses that are relevant to them; that allow them to have a better chance of obtaining a better job and a better career downstream.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And our workers are clever enough to know what are the jobs that may be available and what are the courses that they want to take.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The third thing that we need to do better in tackling possible structural unemployment is to second-skill or prepare our workers at the age of 40 for the second "lift-off".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They have a very concerted programme to make sure that before the worker reaches 60 years old or 50 plus, they are equipped and counselled on the next lap of their career.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It has to start Page: 84 at the age of 40-plus, to prepare for the next step in their career.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we can do these three things well – upstream, midstream and downstream – then we have a much better chance of tackling any possible structural unemployment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: After Dr Goh Keng Swee's time, we have had a rough rule of thumb that has worked very well for us.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For every dollar we earn in our lifetime, we save one-third of it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If you earn $100, the employers put in $20 and we put in $20.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means that there is $40 in CPF out of the total of $120, hence, one-third.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Where did Dr Goh get that magic number of saving at least one-third?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That is because most of us work two-thirds of our life and then spend one-third in retirement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we start working at the age of 20 and retire at 60, we work 40 years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And if we live until 80, that means that we need to prepare for 20 years of our life in retirement with 40 years of earning.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, the rough rule of thumb, without taking in the interest rate and escalation in medical cost, would require us to save at least one-third.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is a choice that we must allow people to make: some people would like to save more and retire earlier, whereas some would want to work longer and prefer to save less.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our job is not to dictate the choices that our people make.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our job is to facilitate their choices with the options available.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is a very involved process, in defining the capabilities required and the job specifications, to facilitate this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we must look into this because our people are working longer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is the total pay package that is important.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our job is to make sure that our workers command a respectable total pay packet that allows them to save up enough for their retirement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Retirement savings have to start from Day One.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The formula that I just shared, starts with the assumption that at the age of 20, when we start working, we save one-third conscientiously.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When we can get more and more people to be self-sufficient without having to depend on the Silver Support Scheme in future, then we have truly succeeded.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can then reserve the finite resources that we have for those who are truly in need because even with the best of our abilities, there will be some in society who will not be able to save enough for their retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our job is to make sure that as few as possible need to rely on the Silver Support Scheme in time to come, and that we can focus our finite resources on those very few.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Page: 85 This will require us to work very hard to look at job redesign and prepare our workers for the eventuality.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And it is never too early to talk about preparing for retirement and saving up for retirement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The third challenge that the Labour Movement is most concerned with is the issue of productivity gains.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have read many statistics that our average productivity is quite low.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But let us go beyond that average number.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not true that we do not have high productivity sectors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is also not true that the average number defines the productivity of the entire sector.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the current volatile environment, many people would think that the oil and gas industry is suffering and is in the doldrums.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it is not true that the entire oil and gas industry is suffering.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are companies in the specialty chemical sector that are earning more because they are able to hold up the prices while their feedstock prices are low.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are companies in other sectors, despite what you say about these sectors, that have above average productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have to do much more if we truly care about the salaries of workers in these sectors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because without real productivity growth, no matter what rules we come up with, it will uplift the salaries of the lowest earners in our economy artificially.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we owe it to them to try our very best to lift those numbers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is why the Budget this year goes beyond a broad policy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to go sectorally to examine where the laggards are in our productivity drive and how best we can help them to uplift the productivity in their respective sectors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not as easy as just giving out grants to encourage people to change their work processes to achieve higher productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If giving out money is the KPI, then perhaps MTI and MOF will not be sweating so hard because it is easy to give out money.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To achieve real productivity growth, we need to go sector by sector and, sometimes, company by company.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It requires the TACs to work very closely with the civil servants, workers and so forth, to identify areas which they can improve, in each and every process that they are involved in.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We either do this or we pretend that some broad macro measures will miraculously lift the productivity of all.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I have visited enough companies to know that no two companies are the same.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: No two companies can even blindly adopt processes that have been proven elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They have to localise and contextualise them; and they have to win over the workers – retrain them, according to their capabilities to adapt and adopt those new strategies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On this front, the Labour Movement is committed to work with MTI, MOM, MOE and MOF to give our best shot for all our companies to do this well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not a short-term challenge but a long-term one.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And very often, when we talk about productivity, we have a lot of new ideas about how new hotels can be differently designed, new production processes can be differently designed, and so forth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would urge all of us to look beyond all these because the turnover is too slow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we only focus on the new ones, it will take us very long before we change the entire stock.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will give an example of the hotel industry, which is very challenging when it comes to lifting the productivity of, say, the housekeeping services.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For all the new hotels that we designed, yes, we can do something different.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But our focus must go beyond that because, at any one point in time, the vast majority of the hotels are from the existing stock.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we need to pay attention not just to the Page: 86 new stock that are coming in, but also the vast majority of the old stock that we have inherited and must continue to work with.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not something that we can do easily.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would suggest that we relook at some of our processes seriously to catalyse some of these.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the area of productivity, very often, we talk about the training of man and the buying of new machines − what we called the first two "M"s − the man and the machine.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have to re-examine − and I hope that the Government will take the lead in this − how we do our contracts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Explore whether there are opportunities to aggregate contracts, both in terms of time and space, for us to achieve greater economies of scale and the scale to redesign some of the jobs for our lowest-wage earners.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are the things that we have to do step by step to raise the productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At the end of this, once again, as Mr Lim Swee Say has put it most eloquently, "Economic growth equals manpower growth plus productivity growth".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If manpower growth is zero, then our only variable is productivity growth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If productivity growth is low or zero, then economic growth is low or zero.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is a very simple equation and we should bear it in mind.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the last part of my comments in English, let me state the Labour Movement's stance on the Singapore Core.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We recognise and accept that for Singapore to be regionally and globally competitive, we need a diverse team − a team of talents from cross-sector and cross-cultural backgrounds and have international exposure.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So what does it mean to develop a real Singapore Core?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It means giving all Singaporeans the best shot to rise up the hierarchy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are not asking for affirmative action that just because we are Singaporeans, we will get ahead compared to the rest.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We want to work with all MNCs to give our workers a fair chance, a fair shot.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And NTUC is committed to working with companies to give our workers chances to be groomed, not just deepen their professional competencies but to equip them with the cross-sectoral competencies, so that they have the best shot to rise up the hierarchy and reach the C-suite positions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It will be such a waste that, after EDB and MTI have worked so hard and we have all these good jobs in Singapore, our people are unable to take on these jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And to take on these jobs, we must prepare our people way in advance − 10 or 20 years in advance − for them to be groomed systematically through diverse paths, to be exposed beyond the country, to see the world as their oyster and not just Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Only then will we be able to take on the very best jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But these two Singaporeans did not grow up just in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They were exposed to the opportunities across the globe before returning to Singapore to take on leadership positions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to make sure that we adopt this inclusive and globally-oriented approach when we define the Singapore Core.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Singapore Core cannot be defined from an exclusive and Page: 87 inward-looking perspective.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will work with MOM and MTI to continue to strengthen companies which want to support us in this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I think Minister Lim Swee Say will announce more about such measures in the coming week.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: NTUC will also be doing what we can to help our younger generation get the necessary exposure when they are young, before their family commitments tie them down.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to prevent PMETs in their 40s from being displaced in 10 years' time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have to start with PMETs who are in their 20s and 30s now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Otherwise, we cannot blame the competition if, one day, our people lose out.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, the challenge is upon us, just as it is upon any other country.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need not fear the competition because there is competition.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, the greater the competition, the more intense the competition, the more we are able to pull ourselves apart from the competition if we organise ourselves well and get our act together.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As I always say, the circumstances will not define us; our responses to the circumstances will define us.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is no reason that our tripartite formula that has served us so well will not be able to help us overcome this challenge ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it requires us to have a shared understanding that this is not just a cyclical slowdown.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are more fundamental structural forces at work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It requires us to have a shared understanding that for every dollar that we take from the Budget, we have a responsibility to do the most that we can, be it businesses or individuals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, last week, former Member of Parliament Mr Yeo Guat Kwang and I met some SME bosses to discuss future challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Yeo Guat Kwang truly lived up to his reputation as "Yeo Guat Kwang" – he compiled all the difficulties faced by SMEs and summarised them into a list of 12 "headaches".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is what he calls the four "threes".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: With these 12 challenges, can this year's Budget really help SMEs?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is our wish for our SMEs to succeed because all large multinational corporations (MNCs) started out as SMEs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Without today's SMEs, we will not have the Singapore MNCs of tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the1960s and 1970s, we developed a number of Singapore MNCs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How do we grow a new generation of Singapore MNCs?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How do we support the SMEs of today so that they will flourish and continue to employ 70% of workers in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am neither a doctor nor the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Perhaps the Minister for Finance has some remedies but I have learnt a thing or two from Minister Gan Kim Yong.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I may not be able to solve all the problems of SMEs and I am not saying that I can do better than SMEs because, ultimately, a lot of problems must be solved by SMEs themselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: SMEs have to address many near-term issues and the NTUC and Government want to do our part to help them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Gan is the Minister for Health, and he takes care of his health in three ways.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Page: 88 So, let us talk about taking less sugar and less salt.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: SMEs agree with, and are appreciative of, the measures implemented by the Government.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, they face a big challenge: they do not have enough manpower and time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even though the Government has implemented so many good policies, they wonder: "How can we benefit from them?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Do I have the time to understand all these measures?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Or is it a case of there seemed to be many options but none is within reach?" In this aspect, we are heartened by the Finance Minister's announcements.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If the Government can streamline these procedures and consolidate various measures and workers can be sent for proper training and there is partnership with SMEs, then I believe SMEs will benefit tremendously and be very grateful.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To be honest, SME bosses are very busy and every day is a challenge.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, as Government officials, we cannot just wait for them to apply for these schemes or come forward to understand these programmes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For NTUC, we will be proactive in helping to promote these programmes for SMEs to benefit from them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we can all do that, even if it is just an ordinary policy, we will see good results.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the other hand, if we do not convey the message to SMEs during the most crucial period, even the best policies will come to nought.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So we really hope to work together with the TACs of SMEs and the Government to address these problems.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, the Minister for Finance gave a lot of "candies" but we all know that we should take sugar in moderation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we take too much sugar and it becomes a habit, then obesity problems may arise and it does nothing to solve our problems.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As Mr Thomas Chua mentioned, the Government has taken one step forward.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we hope that companies and unions will work together and move forward together for a better future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Actually, SMEs have combed the entire Singapore but Singapore will always be a small market.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We all know that if an SME makes $10 out of every Singaporean, it will only be a millionaire.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But if you go overseas, for example, to big cities in China and India, you only need to make $1 out of every customer and you will become a billionaire.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore is a small country and a small market, but it does not mean that we cannot venture overseas and conquer other markets.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, it is easier said than done and requires cooperation from IE Singapore and other economic agencies to help our SMEs expand out of the domestic market and venture abroad.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Only when they go international to conquer a bigger market will our SMEs become MNCs of the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hopefully, the Government, unions and businesses can move together hand in hand.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In this area, NTUC will do our part.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are very interested in the bosses of SMEs, big or small.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, at the recent training session organised by the Bosses' Network, company bosses get to upgrade their skills and open their minds which help them achieve breakthroughs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When bosses achieve breakthroughs, workers will follow likewise.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If bosses cannot make a breakthrough, then there is no need to even talk about productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In this aspect, NTUC will continue to organise programmes for company bosses to learn from one another and share best practices with the rest of the SMEs in Singapore in the shortest time possible.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Only when they upgrade their human resource management skills can our workers have a better future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As for us, the success of an SME means success for our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If the bosses' businesses cannot succeed, our workers will not have a better tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, to us, the success of businesses and improvements to our workers' lives are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They are, in fact, the same Page: 89 issue.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We want to address immediate cyclical head-winds, but the more important task remains in taking measures that will help us fundamentally restructure the economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Towards this goal, the Finance Minister declared, "We will target resources towards enabling firms to build deeper capabilities, develop their people, scale up and internationalise".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The businesses which I talked to welcomed the new economic initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While waiting for further details, many already have suggestions on how we could become more competitive.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They look forward to giving their views to the Committee of the Future Economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For now, I would like to share my thoughts on three of the new programmes.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As a three-in-one package, it provides capability grants, tax allowance and concessionary loans to help SMEs undertake comprehensive remodelling of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For instance, SMEs could undertake automation projects, re-engineer workflows, acquire new technologies and train its workers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: However, some SMEs might find the capital cap of $1 million limiting.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I hope the Ministry would consider expanding the cap if the usage of the scheme is high, which, in itself, is a very encouraging sign.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: If we look at the global market for industrial robots, four key points stand out: one, on a worldwide basis, robot sales have doubled in the past five years; two, the top five markets, namely, China, Japan, America, South Korea and Germany, account for 70% of the world demand; three, Asia is the fastest growing market for robots; and four, China is the largest buyer by volume.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: On a per capita basis, South Korea and Japan are leading the world in having the most robots per 10,000 people, ahead of the traditional industrial power houses such as Germany, Italy, Sweden, Denmark, US, Spain, Finland and Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Hitherto, most robotic solutions have been applied to the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: More and more robots are being deployed in the services sectors, giving hope that we can substantially reinvent our services sector which has been lagging in labour productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Consider, for instance, applications in the hospitality sector: robot bartenders which can mix up to 50 types of drinks, robot concierge providing travel tips to hotel guests, self-guided vacuum cleaners combing common areas, and autonomous guided vehicles delivering room service to Page: 90 hotel guests.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Our hospitals are already using robots to pack medications, move supplies between rooms and transporting patients on motorised beds.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Surgeons are using robots to assist in complicated and delicate surgeries.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In Japan, Showa University has developed a robot dental patient, a robot which mimics human responses: it can talk, blink, roll its eyes, sneeze, shake its head, cough, move its tongue and becomes tired from keeping its mouth open for too long.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It would even choke and show gag reflexes if the trainee dentist becomes too rough.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This life-like robot provides a realistic simulated environment for training and learning.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Others are still trying to figure out what to do.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But all sectors will benefit from having their own industry-level collaboration platforms.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The good news is that we are not starting from zero.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Changi General Hospital's newly opened Centre for Healthcare Assistive and Robotics Technology (CHART) can be a good reference model.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: CHART brings together healthcare professionals, academia, industry players and research institutions to develop the hospital applications which can be shared with other hospitals in Singapore and beyond.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In establishing such centres, I would go further to argue that we should not be contented at being a mere consumer of smart solutions.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We should instead aspire to create our own applications and products that are commercialisable and exportable.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In this way there is a chance that we can build up an ecosystem, a new industry based on our consumption expenditure and R&D investments.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The growing robotic industry will offer us real opportunities or applications for business and healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This leads me to the third point: how do we develop the 20-plus Industry Transformation Roadmaps that give us not just a sustained path for productivity gain but also lead to us to becoming Expert Centres for Best Practices?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It is part of the Government's plan to provide $4 billion to support industry research projects to drive and deepen industries' innovation capability.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The industries I talked to warmly welcomed the renewed emphasis on industry-led research projects.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Furthermore, they also wished to see a better integration of NRF funding with the Industry Transformation Roadmaps, eliminating the perception that our research institutes and our industries have not forged a common vision for the future and are working separately from each other.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The private sector contributed $23.7 billion, which is 99.5%.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The public sector, comprising the Government, universities, polytechnics and research institutes merely accounted for less than 0.5%.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Page: 91 From the above, it is clear that allocating more R&D funding to industry-led research collaborations would greatly multiply the economic spinoffs to our economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In each of these verticals, there is substantial expertise residing in our public sector and "their industries".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) is a respected agency internationally for its world-class planning capability.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: BCA's Green Mark and Sustainability standards are being adopted in other countries.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The Centre for Liveable City is a global thought-leader in urban planning and solutions.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA), coordinating huge investments in building up an elaborate public transport network, has experience that is valuable to other cities.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: IDA architects the state-of-the-art infrastructure to make Singapore a world leading smart city.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: EDB draws in clean and green technologies research needed to grow a smart city.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Each of these agencies has something unique and valuable to contribute to an overall competitive cluster.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The solutions we devise here require a high degree of interagency coordination and seamless public private partnerships.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Together, we are solving very real, day-to-day problems with budget, resource and space constraints.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In this way, we can grow our competencies into new clusters of growth, bringing along our large local enterprises and SMEs to create solutions for a fast urbanising Asia.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In my interactions with the Singapore Furniture Industry Council (SFIC), I have seen how an effective TAC has helped the entire industry to upgrade, internationalise and acquire new design capabilities.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: SFIC could do so because it has successive generations of strong leaderships.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: SFIC's annual International Furniture Fair Singapore is very well-attended.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It also generates for SFIC the financial resources needed to sustain a full-time professional secretariat.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Page: 92 (In Mandarin):   In the 2016 Budget, the Finance Minister repeatedly highlighted the importance of long-term economic restructuring.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Only with a strong economy can we raise the income of workers and invest in social development, healthcare, infrastructure and defence to ensure peace and stability for our nation.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Yet, as Singapore embarks on its 51st year of nation-building, we are faced with a world that is totally different from the one in the early days of our nation-building.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Many developing countries in Asia have caught up with us.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: China has surpassed Japan in 2010 to become the world's second largest economy, and is forecast to surpass the US in about 10 years' time.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: External competition, an ageing domestic population, low fertility rate and limited space – all these have put a limit to our development.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Right now, there is a greater sense of urgency to accomplish the many things that we need to do, for our next generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Ultimately, whether economic restructuring succeeds or not will depend on how our businesses and workers are involved.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I hope we will face the competition with courage, resilience, determination and creativity to overcome constraints and competition.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Our competitiveness is built through roughing it out in the international marketplace.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: If we rely on a walking stick and depend on protection, we will not be able to endure the storms that come our way and will never be able to take flight.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Conversely, if we are able to build upon the pioneering spirit of our nation and work together, with TACs actively participating in industry upgrading programmes, company bosses striving to learn the best practices of world industry players, workers investing in lifelong learning to master new skills, and with the technical and R&D support of our tertiary and research institutions, there is hope that we will be able to strengthen our competitiveness, create our own innovative products and services, and earn our place in the international market.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, at SG51, Singapore faces a vastly different, developed and connected world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Some inspire; some impress; some make me worried.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: When I was in Sanya City, Hainan, last week, I saw a seafront belt of 12 hotels under construction.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Each of these mega-hotel complexes has a private beach, iconic architecture and differentiated theme.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Each would have been a billion-dollar project if located on Sentosa.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Seeing them makes me wonder: are we as imaginative?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How are we to maintain our tourism share?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: To the competition around us, do we keep up or give up?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: China is gargantuan in every aspect of its economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The rise of China has enormous ramifications for us and the region.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Last year, Shanghai Mayor Yang Xiong and I spoke in the Twin Cities seminar entitled, "科技创新驱动合作商机", translated as "Opportunities and cooperation driven by science, technology and innovation." The topic suggested by our Shanghai counterparts clearly showed that Shanghai was like us, at the stage of development where science and technology matter most.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Firms will invest where they can find high-quality workforce and talents.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: On the day the Finance Minister announced the 2016 Budget, The Business Times headline read: "Singapore's continued relevance – that's the big question".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Singapore economy has started to experience significant headwinds that have made the business environment less favourable and the short-term outlook less optimistic.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much of this can be put down to external factors, such as the slowing Chinese economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it has made the operating environment more challenging for local businesses, even as they come under pressure to restructure and raise their productivity.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even as we seek to provide such near-term assistance to local SMEs, however, I would urge that thought be given to enhancing the broader ecosystem that would sustain entrepreneurship and ground-up innovation in the long haul.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In parallel, we have seen that productivity growth has been modest and uneven in the past few years despite intensive efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Raising overall productivity will necessarily involve rewarding the strong and allowing the weak to exit the scene.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Policies that inadvertently keep such "zombie" businesses alive will only hold back productivity growth and technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To tackle the twin challenges of encouraging entrepreneurship and increasing productivity through innovation, we need to consider how we can protect the interest of the entrepreneur even as we allow businesses to fail where warranted.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is especially important in an economic downturn, when even good businesses can fail due to circumstances beyond their control, such as a major customer defaulting or going bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, a holistic set of measures needs to be put in place to support businesses through such events.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 94 I would like to outline three specific aspects where support for entrepreneurs can be enhanced: one, developing the business idea; two, launching the business; and three, mitigating the impact of failure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The key first step lies in developing the business idea to ensure that would-be entrepreneurs have sound, robust business models in place before launching their ideas.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One piece could be around education, equipping them with the skills needed to develop a thorough business plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will involve educating them on business fundamentals, such as market sizing, business plan development, operations and so forth.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important that we go beyond theory and focus on the hands-on, in-depth sessions to strengthen proposals and preempt future problems.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps this could be made a part of the SkillsFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, we have seen the establishment of a number of "accelerators" which are designed to help startups succeed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, these tend to be focused on startups in sectors that are perceived to be "sexy", such as media and Internet businesses, or in financial technologies (fintech), for which a new dedicated one-stop office has just been announced.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we might see as more everyday businesses can also benefit from such support, be they from retail, F&B or basic services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is especially important as it is these everyday businesses that will, ultimately, make up the bulk of the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even with a sound business plan, many things can go wrong when launching a new business.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Startup firms in Singapore can easily be crippled by high costs, and we could consider building more proactive "test bed" facilities to allow room for experimentation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore's F&B industry has a strong international reputation, with many brands successfully going global.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, consider the daunting challenge facing a would-be restauranteur today.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Securing a space is a challenge, as most high-traffic malls are run by Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and will not take a risk on unproven concepts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even if they were able to obtain a space, they might have to sign a two-year lease, with significant penalties for early termination.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This greatly increases the risk facing any potential start-up F&B operator.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another example of potentially prohibitive costs is legal services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not feasible if you are raising a seed round of only $40,000 to $50,000 of funding.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The third area where more could be done is mitigating the impact of failure for would-be entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I should make clear that it should not be the objective of Government policies to completely eliminate the risk faced by new ventures.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We certainly do not want to give the impression that small businesses can do whatever they like and the Government will bail them out.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, what I am advocating is to have more focused efforts to ensure that those who heed the call and take the plunge into the world of business do not risk permanent damage to their reputations and their future income potential should the venture fail to pan out.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 95 In this area, I would like to focus on three issues: one, criminal liability resulting from business failure; two, insolvency; and three, society's tolerance for business failure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chua was a director of a property construction and development company who came to see me for help.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: His company, which employed more than 100 foreign workers at its peak, had run into severe financial problems due to the downturn in the property sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are considered criminal charges under the Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we can all understand that the Act was enacted to prevent fraudulent or malicious failure to pay salaries, the punishment seems harsh in cases where a business runs into cashflow problems due to a general downturn in the sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even a sound business can be thrown into default if one major customer fails to make payment on time.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hence, we need to administer the Act with great discretion and compassion.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I note that the insolvency regime is currently undergoing a timely revamp.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is warmly welcomed and as the region enters challenging economic times, we need to further strengthen policies and schemes to give our local businesses time to turn things around, rather than risk turning a short-term cashflow hiccup into a death-spiral that ultimately kills the company and harshly penalises the business owner.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would highlight the possibility of promoting so-called "schemes of arrangement" in adverse times, as these can help business owner-managers turn around their insolvent businesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us help make schemes of arrangement more widely available.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would it be possible for the Government to create a forum for facilitating the resolution of creditor disputes in the event of insolvencies involving outstanding amounts below a certain cap?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would function in a manner similar to a small claims tribunal or other mechanisms to lower the transaction costs for all parties while ensuring fair outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, every business has a few key contracts that allow it to continue trading.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could be contracts relating to supply of raw materials or lease agreements.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of these contracts may contain a provision where, if the business enters into a scheme of arrangement, the contract may be terminated.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us keep these contracts, ranging from supply contracts to lease arrangements, alive during the duration of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This allows a company with a fundamentally sound business with misaligned cash flow the breathing room to allow it to operate and trade back into success, creating a more stable business environment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 96 Another critical aspect of rehabilitating an insolvent company is to give access to financing.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As with the working capital loan support initiative, the Government can consider covering part of the risk of such loans.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will serve to increase access to such loans, provided safeguards to ensure debt levels remain manageable.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Good businesses will sometimes fail due to bad luck or circumstance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we are to encourage entrepreneurship in our country, we need to develop greater tolerance for business failure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Businessmen should not have to face criminal charges and possible debarment from hiring foreign workers if their plight was due to genuine business difficulty, not any malicious intent to defraud workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Criminalisation of such situations turns a short-term problem into a potentially lifelong handicap which may severely restrict future employment or business opportunities for the affected individuals, even if they had tried their best to do everything right.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Of course, this is not to pretend that all business failures are equally noble; many will be due to incompetence, insufficient planning or outright fraud.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But productivity and innovation require some risk-taking and, without risk takers, there would be no progress.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China, one of the main drivers of global growth in the last few years, is slowing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: High commodity prices, which fuelled growth in many parts of the developing world, including Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and South America, are also dropping.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is anticipated that many industries that had developed to support the commodity price boom, including mining, offshore exploration and shipbuilding and rig-building, will slow.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even alternative energy, which always becomes more economically viable when energy prices are high, may also become less attractive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Financial institutions, which have extended credit to these sectors, may also face a problem of rising non-performing loans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Local businesses are still adapting to manpower constraints from the tightening controls on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this context, an expansionary fiscal Budget is to be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If Government spending is able to pick up some of the slack from the slowdown in private sector expenditure, this will, in theory, help to stimulate the economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Also, it is good that the expenditure is being focused on those sectors that are most in need and most likely to spend.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The expenditure covers a wide range of support for SMEs to modernise and survive in the tougher climate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the Automation Support Package, financing and tax incentives to support scale-ups and support for internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the context of helping transform our economy and helping businesses cope and adapt, I believe these are to be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given the tough climate, I have no quarrel with these as they stand at the moment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only caution I would sound is that we should not institutionalise subsidy to industries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many developed countries, in response to pressure, have subsidised a wide range of sectors, including agriculture and manufacturing, under the pretext of supporting infant industries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These subsidies can prove very difficult to remove.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is because the cost of a subsidy is distributed across all of society, while the benefit is concentrated on just a few people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, the people who benefit from it would have a strong vested interest in resisting the removal of the subsidy, while the people paying the price are usually too large a group to be specifically concerned.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Systematically expanding the system of subsidies, will add to the long-term fiscal burden a country faces and add to the strain that future generations must pay if allowed to expand imprudently.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has stayed clear of this because most Government grants or incentives have very specific parameters and we try our best not to make them recurring even though, at times, they get renewed at Budgets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, as we expand this list of grants and support, we must be cautious not to fall into the trap some other countries have fallen into of having institutional subsidies for various sectors of the economies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, in the event the Government wishes to be more creative or adventurous in extending support to SMEs, another option might be to provide low-cost financing, rather than grants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are some Budget measures that follow this principle including the SME Working Capital Loan, as well as the SME Mezzanine Growth Fund.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in principle, I would support financing as opposed to grant because this way, companies take the benefit of financing when they need it to get over a tough patch, but the expectation is that they will pay it back in future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may also give the Government more ability to finance and support a greater range of activities as earlier successful finance recipients pay back what they have received.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of this is due to increases in revenue from expanding the definition of Net Investment Income.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is also good that much of this is going towards social spending.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As our population ages, the reality is that the workforce will shrink relative to the non-working population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The working people may face multiple strains of supporting young children and others who are unable to work on account of age or illness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To the extent that the Government is able to socialise some of these costs, the burdens on this working group would be less.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My only concern is that as these support schemes get increasingly institutionalised and the base of people receiving support rises relative to the working population, there is likely to be significant additional strain on the Government Budget.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is my hope that we will continue to Page: 98 finance these schemes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only way I can see this being sustainable, apart from increasing taxes or finding other sources of income, would be to continue growing the economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The biggest challenge we face will be to continue to be creative in finding new drivers of growth, so that we can support what is likely to be a falling working population and larger base of dependants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Mr Deputy Speaker, at the opening session of this Parliament, I spoke about the importance of sending children to preschool.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the facts that I believe that had contributed to this were concerns about the costs of pre-school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time, I mentioned the many schemes that the Government already had to help defray the cost of preschool education, including the availability of Centre-based Financial Assistance Scheme for Childcare (CFAC) and the Kindergarten Fee Assistance Scheme (KiFAS) grants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With these grants, the cost of childcare and kindergarten education can be significantly defrayed for those with lower incomes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, even with those measures, there are concerns about the cost of bringing up children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, I welcome the measures in the Budget to further assist with the costs of bringing up young children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This account can be used for the child's healthcare and childcare needs and this can be of help to them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, if they put an additional $3,000 into their CDA account, this will be matched dollar-for-dollar by the Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, not all parents fully utilise this account and some do not use it at all.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I encourage all parents who have concerns about meeting the cost of childcare to maximise the CDA grants available if necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With these new schemes in place, I would strongly encourage all parents to enrol their children in preschool education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you know of neighbours and family members who have not done so, please encourage them to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe that with the help and financial assistance available, all families should be able to send their children to preschool so that they will be adequately prepared for primary school.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, I wish to talk about Singapore's engines of growth.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Finance Minister began his speech by sharing some history of the first Budget speech by Mr Lim Kim San in 1965.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For over 100 years before our Independence, Singapore has made use of its good location to act as a trade hub, connecting Southeast Asia to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We became a major ship building and oil refinery centre.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We reclaimed swamp lands in Jurong to create the first industrial estate and attracted many MNCs to set up factories here, creating jobs for many of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We moved towards electronic trading of shares and removed estate duties.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And we gave attractive incentives to foreign financial institutions to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The increase in the number of players pushed our local banks to also up their own game, providing better service to all.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sure Marina Bay Sands, with its spaceship rooftop, is one of the most iconic in the world.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: People see a photograph of the Sands SkyPark and know this is in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I wonder what is next.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are we going to be like a pack of cards with just four aces?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are we going to be faced with slower growth?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can our children grow up in a Singapore where they will be able to follow the rainbow and pursue their dreams?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New schemes were introduced to promote the use of automation and aim to help our SMEs "scale up".

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I cannot crystal ball and say what our next engine of growth will be.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But if we look back at the four previous engines of growth – trade hub status, manufacturing centre of the world, regional finance centre and tourism – a common thread runs through them.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each of these has to do with Singapore opening itself to the rest of the world, and this we can never stop.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whether for companies or people, Singapore must continue to be a beacon for the best and brightest to set up their base here and to call Singapore home.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot afford to turn xenophobic or to be inward-looking because if we do, Singapore and Singaporeans will be the worse for it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It will not be an easy year ahead for Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is also very clear that once again, the Government is in the driver's seat of the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While this has worked for us for the last 50 years, we need to evaluate if this is sustainable or effective for the next 50, as we live in an increasingly competitive and volatile world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At some point, the people and private enterprises need to steer the economy while the Government is playing a supporting role by ensuring that policies are business-friendly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the US, its largest and most innovative corporations are private enterprises like Google, Intel, Microsoft and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Japan has large conglomerates like Mitsui and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT), while Korea has chaebols, like Samsung, LG, Hyundai and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These companies are all important driving forces in their respective domestic economies and are also huge global players.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, the driving force of the economy has always been the Government.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From attracting foreign MNCs to creating jobs in the early days to developing strong Government-linked companies, like SIA, PSA, DBS Bank and ST Engineering, to expand overseas in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the year 2000, Dr Tony Tan chaired a Technopreneurship 21 Ministerial Committee to help nurture local high-tech enterprises.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It was tasked to study entrepreneurship in several major cities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Committee members were told by some in the US that the US government has no role in developing entrepreneurship, but Singapore went ahead anyway to put all the policies and support in place to nurture entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At that time, the foreign observers commented that Singapore was probably one of the few countries in the world that had put in so much effort to promote entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Subsequently, the Singapore Government's effort to promote entrepreneurship has been cited as a successful model by Mr Josh Lerner, who is the author of the book, "Boulevard of Broken Dreams: Why Public Efforts to Boost Entrepreneurship and Venture Capital Have Failed – and What to Do about It".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Today, Singapore is consistently ranked as one of the easiest places in the world to do business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Despite all these measures which create an entrepreneurship-friendly framework and a growing awareness of the need to drive productivity among SMEs, the actual state of private enterprise is lacking.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While there has been an increase in the number of young startups, our productivity growth is dismal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When the Minister for Finance, Mr Heng Swee Keat, singled out the major innovations in Singapore’s history, most, if not all, of the innovations were led by the Government, be it in NEWater technology or innovations in our social policies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are very few private sector-generated global innovations we can be proud of besides the Soundblaster by Creative Technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even then, technological change has superseded this innovation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If we scratch beneath the veneer of good news, some CEOs in the private sector questioned if the Government really understands the way the private sector thinks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Page: 101 Take the PIC scheme as an example.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In 2014 the taxman had to claw back $7 million worth of improper claims.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: PIC has been successful in promoting awareness of the productivity movement but less effective in promoting innovativeness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It was introduced in 2011 to provide support to employers to hire older Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is supposed to expire this year but it has been extended to 2019.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does SEC really influence employers to employ more workers above the age of 55?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of the five employers I have asked over the last one week, ranging from SMEs to MNCs, all of them conceded that SEC did not influence their decision to hire older workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Given the current tight labour market, they will employ workers above 55 years old as long as they qualify for the job, regardless of SEC.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, all the five employers, as expected, welcomed SEC as it improves their bottom line.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Rather than just merely extend SEC for another three years, my suggestion is to increase the employers' CPF contributions rate for workers who are between 55 and 60 years old to 17%, that is, the same as workers who are below 55.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just increase the employers' contribution rate for the workers between 55 and 60 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: By doing so, more elderly workers will be encouraged to stay or return to employment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Without better understanding, the Government's efforts cannot effectively transform the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Our business promotion policies will not be effective in driving the desired outcome.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, the Government may be doing too much to protect and cushion private enterprises from developing resilience and true excellence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: William Kerr, an assistant professor at Harvard Business School, argues that "subsidising individuals can have a perverse effect of encouraging entry or keeping alive lower ability entrepreneurs".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In coming up with policies and programmes geared towards promoting enterprise, those from the private sector could be involved to a greater extent in the development stages.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Coming from the target audience, they would know better if the programme would be useful and how it would be taken up or abused.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This would hopefully result in programmes which are more realistic, effective and targeted.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Private sector involvement does not have to end at discussion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similar reciprocal arrangements, where public officers are given the opportunity to better understand the private sector, would also help in formulating more effective policies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After their private sector stints, they can help to Page: 102 formulate better policies and incentives to encourage enterprises to improve productivity, innovation and expand regionally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The healthy exchange of staff between the public and private sectors will deepen understanding between the two sectors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Certainly, there are constraints and it is easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, well-thought-out and administered policies and programmes generated from a solid base of knowledge will likely result in less abuse, and make them less of a hand-out nature.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They should result in spurring on our SMEs and private enterprises to aggressively compete in the local and global marketplace, because they want to, and not because the Government wants them to do so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For the sake of future-proofing our economy, it may be worth a try.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2016 has stayed on course to fulfil the Government's mission to build both a future-ready economy and a caring and resilient Singapore beyond SG50.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
