text: Analysts have acknowledged that it is a far-sighted Budget, with resources committed to support businesses to scale up automation, create high-value jobs and internationalise.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SkillsFuture, a big piece to secure Singapore's place in the new economy, is another key feature.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Work is underway to develop more than 20 Sectoral Manpower Plans to identify the skills required in each sector and to develop a Singapore core.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the individual level, the first tranche of training dollars was already credited to Singaporeans to encourage lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The people's voice through the Our Singapore Conversations can still be heard in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Anxieties over high healthcare and financial worries of the ageing are addressed with several key moves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our national safety net is now visibly stronger by the additional pieces in the form of higher Public Assistance quantum – the Pioneer Generation package, Silver Support and MediShield Life for all.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a significant task that not many Singaporeans fully appreciate but is nonetheless critical for their future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On concerns – as we confront the brave new world, I cannot help but still be alarmed at the speed and the disruption of change in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the logistics industry, for instance, both overseas and in Singapore, where large warehouses have been major employers of workers, robots now replace warehouse workers in jobs such as picking and packaging.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fully automated production processes from design to delivery, with very little manpower needs, is not far from reality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even our radio journalists in the local radio stations have had their jobs re-scoped.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I was working with a lady, Lu-Ann from 938LIVE, and she now video-records her interviews with us, Members of Parliament, and presents reports in voice, video and other online writings as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yes, as they say, embrace the digital economy or be left behind.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Groups at risk – there is indeed cause for concern for businesses and people who are at risk of being left behind in the future economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They include our small- to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), our Professionals, Managers, Executives and Technicians (PMETs) and the lesser-skilled and unskilled employees amongst us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are, after all, our own and are here to stay.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: By sheer size and presence, they cannot be ignored, and they have to drive our growth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Granted, many of them have moved up the league and are a lot more conscious and open to the need to upgrade, but even more of them are stuck.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Remodel their business; fend off disruptive technology; move from value-adding to value-creation; use big data, use cloud computing, get into the Internet of Things – these are calls that are easier said than done for many of them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many SMEs are still concerned about the here and now – rental and manpower challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the retail industry, brick and mortar stores are fast and furiously replaced by online stores.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the travel industry, tour operators continue to fold as travellers make their bookings online.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Shake-outs are inevitable, but how can we reduce the numbers and how do we support those who finally exit?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The PMETS – at the individual level, there are still PMETs who are unsure of their place in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many were not formerly exposed to the changes that are taking place.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The days when PMETs who lost their jobs turned easily to the real estate, financial planning, insurance and even taxi-driving, are over.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Low-skilled and unskilled – it is a known fact that unskilled or low-skilled jobs will disappear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In my effort to find jobs for my low-skilled, lowly-paid elderly residents in the Central District as a Mayor, I was informed that even makers of the 手工包, or handmade buns, are replaced by machines in South China, for instance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Do we tell them go digital, or go home, although we all know that there is nowhere else to go for many of them because this is where home is?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on segmentation by ability, attitude and altitude.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The first suggestion I have has to do with segmentation or adopting a less of a cookie-cutter approach when working with the groups of vulnerable SMEs, partners and individuals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My colleague, Assoc Prof Randolph Tan, said in Parliament yesterday that this is a matter of the head, and not the heart.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, because so many of our enterprises and people are involved, I would urge that one more layer of intervention be considered.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Other than industry segmentation and partnering with trade associations, another dimension of segmentation must be considered.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must be even less cookie-cutter in our approach.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the stars who possess all three "A"s – ability, attitude and altitude – the Government's key engagement strategy should be to facilitate and to open doors, so they can scale and soar.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These stars may or may not be leading trade associations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They may not toe the line or fall in place nicely with the rest of the industry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They could be the Ubers in their own industry, disrupting current business models.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to find a way to identity them so they could reach their peak.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If they do not wish to be led by their trade associations, give them the creative licence and space to soar on their own.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second group – those with the Attitude and Ability but lack the vision at the moment and are at risk of being displaced, quickly guide and direct them to schemes and grants that can help them land firm and scale.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As for those with a willing Attitude, but lack the Ability, then, training comes into play.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For those who have the Ability but lack the willingness to change the Attitude, invest in counselling them, nudge them into action before giving up on them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And then for those who have neither the Ability, Attitude nor the potential for Altitude, help them develop an exit strategy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They should not have been in the business in the first place.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe SkillsFuture is one of the best answers to prepare our businesses and people for our future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is, however, an urgency to move the whole nation more quickly into the SkillsFuture mindset and action.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SkillsFuture must be more than active ageing training programmes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It must be more than meeting only the current sectoral manpower needs of businesses, although that is important.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While the Council works on the bigger pieces such as the Sectoral Manpower Plans, we need to convince the man in the street that Singapore's future jobs and the funding of our social safety nets depends on how future-proof each one of us is.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to transform the mindsets and skillsets of as many Singaporeans as possible before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, beyond intellectual rationalisation, we need to develop a SkillsFuture Communication Matrix for communication strategies to reach Singaporeans from different backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to outreach with more everyday applications to show the importance and impact of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A Hokkien-speaking aunty running a fashion accessory shop in one of the markets in my division, told me recently when we were discussing about re-modelling and reducing the cost of business, she said "MP, we are already buying stock from the Internet" in Hokkien.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This morning, I heard Love 97.2 radio deejay, Chen Jianbin, sharing that he now has to find ways for the audience to not just listen to his jokes, or 听他的笑话 , but also "see him making jokes" or 看他的笑话.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these are applications, our SkillsFuture is already happening and we need to get the message out to the streets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, from the thousands of choices in the SkillsFuture galore of courses, we need to be able to appoint coordinators, SkillsFuture Ambassadors who can identify, help curate and communicate the list of competencies that will enhance the Future-Readiness Quotient of businesses and especially people on the streets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, we need to encourage and incentivise as many Singaporeans as possible from young to each own their personal Individual Future-Proof Development Plan with a Future-Ready Toolkit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no end to what one can learn, regardless of age and language.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to spread the message of the new economy more urgently to the man in the streets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And, finally, let me move on to the subject of partnership.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And indeed, in a landscape that is featured by structural changes, disruptive technologies that can displace jobs easily and manpower constraints, the former top-down problem-solving approach by the Government can no longer suffice.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While I truly appreciate the importance of partnership, I fear that unless we move towards a more enlightened form of partnership, the outcomes of the Budget may not be as effective as desired.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are two things I would like to highlight.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First is the application of the enlightened form of partnership in the business arena.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst it makes sense to engage Trade or Clan Associations to take the lead in selected industries, we must not be overly rigid with this strategy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the Social Service sector, where Minister Heng has kindly created the Business and IPC Partnership Scheme (BIPS) to incentivise businesses to donate services in kind to IPCs and charities, I would caution against behaviour that may be counterproductive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Volunteering is, after all, about giving something back and not getting something back.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Already, business consultants have started to issue advice to businesses to start reviewing their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) strategies or plans, so that they can enjoy greater tax deductions under this new scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is also a worry that if we are not careful, the BIPS would cannibalise what charities are currently receiving in much-needed cash donations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who used to donate in cash may now decide that service or volunteering is more pocket-friendly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To this end, I would recommend a more targeted approach to direct corporations and donors to the known pain areas or the growth areas in the social service sector, areas such as: (a) Redesigning jobs for the elderly, the lower-skilled or even the unskilled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: (b) Helping children with rare diseases and their families.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of the young parents are really under a lot of stress and need a lot of help.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: (c) Others old and young who are severely disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: (e) Those who are isolated elderly residents in many of our estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: (f) Need for pro bono accounting, audit and legal services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: (g) Fundraising and marketing and even e-learning modules or curricular development for these special schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For outfits that serve the very severely disabled, their needs are way beyond $50,000.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, in summary, my suggestions are, first, on the triple "A" − the need to identify those with the ability, attitude and altitude − and help these potential trailblazers to trailblaze and soar; second, to make SkillsFuture a more pervasive phenomenon to the man-in-the-street; and third, for more enlightened partnerships.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a considered Budget that I know is the outcome of much of the Minister's style of listening to the ground.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a balanced and sensible Budget that will play a large part in securing the future of our country and our people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I would like to speak on four issues: first, the need for vigilance and heightened security in Singapore; second, the importance of providing flexible work arrangements for employees, especially for working mothers; third, reviewing existing property cooling measures for Singaporeans; and lastly, growing our total fertility rate (TFR) organically by promoting the process of adoption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before delving into those four topics, I would like to share a few broad views about this Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the second major announcement in this House post-GE 2015, following the President's Address earlier in January.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Budget displays a confident, clear and deliberate charting of fiscal policy for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That the Government, the Minister for Finance, is able to plan so methodically what Singapore's people and economy need is itself a major advantage, which so many other economies in the globe, unfortunately, do not possess.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that these fiscal policies have the financial fuel, that is, the money they require to be implemented and implemented well, that is indeed a rarity regionally, possibly even globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must never take such an eloquent and hard-earned fiscal position for granted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should preserve tough-minded prudence in our Budget and fiscal planning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the need for vigilance and heightened security in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is, indeed, illustrative of the climate of heightened security that we are presently experiencing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore no longer faces the same conventional threats that she faced some 10, 20 years ago.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, we now face threats from non-state actors like ISIS, who spread fear and discord through domestic terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also face the self-radicalisation of individuals through social media and the Internet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has made the threat of terrorism more insidious than other threats that we have faced in the past.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that the best way to address these threats effectively is to have both hard and soft measures in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the one hand, we need to have the wherewithal of a good military and Home Team to detect and deter any threats beyond our shores, and to ensure that we have a safe and secure Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other, we need to win the hearts and minds of Singaporeans so that should the threat of terrorism materialise here, we will be ready to stand united as a nation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The aim of terrorists is often to inflict maximum fear and to divide society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given Singapore's multi-ethnic, multiracial and multi-religious make-up, it is particularly important that any potential instance of domestic terrorism does not sow discord or distrust between our different communities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To achieve this, consistent efforts must be taken to build strong bonds between the different ethnic communities, and the strengthening of our multiracial national fabric must be made a priority.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, our ability to deal with the threat of terrorism effectively will depend on how we choose to respond as a country in the aftermath of an attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans, the Government and local authorities must work hand-in-hand to keep Singapore safe, and to prepare ourselves for the possibility of an attack happening here.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we get our security right, that base plate right, then we can talk about the economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This leads me to the second part of my speech: providing flexible work arrangements (FWAs) for employees, especially for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, the Government has worked closely with the tripartite partners, through the Tripartite Committee (TriCom) on Work-Life Strategy, to promote the adoption of FWAs in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And it is heartening to know that we are starting to see the results of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I see this as a positive indication that employers are starting to recognise the value of providing flexibility to their employees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I would like to highlight the importance of these FWAs for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the labour force participation rate for women continues to increase every year, employers need to understand and appreciate the importance of adopting good workplace practices that help working mothers to balance family and work commitments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, mothers with newborns need help to adjust back to working life after their maternity leave, and it may take time for them to strike the right balance between their responsibilities at work and at home.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, in the interim, employers need to be compassionate to these working mothers as they learn to cope with work and added family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides reducing time spent at work or their workload, flexibility can also be applied in terms of working time, for example, allowing for staggered hours and shorter work weeks, and work location, for example, allowing working mothers to telecommute.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By doing so, more mothers can return to the workforce and increase their family income without compromising on their family life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In his speech during the Debate on the President's Address, Mr Desmond Choo proposed that the Government consider providing working mothers with the legislated right for an additional eight weeks of FWAs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will give mothers more time at home to bond with their newborn and would also allow them to breastfeed for at least six months, which is the recommended period according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, under this proposal, employers will not be financially disadvantaged as they would not have to pay them during the eight-week period of unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, some employers may prefer to give these working mothers the eight weeks of unpaid leave because it makes it easier for them to forecast manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These measures can go a long way towards helping working mothers integrate their work with their personal and family life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is my hope that employers will continue to show compassion and understanding to their employees, especially working mothers, and will work towards exploring innovative ways to provide FWAs for their employees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, the need for a timely review of existing property cooling measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the Government has been successful in stabilising the property market through the introduction of the Additional Buyers Stamp Duty (ABSD) and the Total Debt Service Ratio (TDSR), the lacklustre property market that we see today is rather different from the overheated property market back in 2012 and 2013, when these measures were first introduced.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In light of this change in circumstances, I believe that it is time for the Government to seriously consider reviewing and easing some of the existing property cooling measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I understand and appreciate that the Government will want to be cautious and will be keen to adopt a calibrated approach in reviewing the property cooling measures that are currently in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, by retaining the TDSR, a Singaporean is only going to be allowed a credit line that is within his means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This should allay any concerns that easing the property cooling measures will cause a surge in Singaporeans purchasing second or third properties when they may not be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, if a Singaporean is able to afford a second or third property through the TDSR regime, why should he be taxed with an ABSD?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, by retaining the ABSD for foreigners, we ensure that the foreigners will not enter the Singaporean property market in an overly speculative way.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The benefits of this model are that it discourages foreigners from engaging in an overly speculative way as foreigners are only allowed to buy new property, and are only able to sell that property back to domestic buyers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This discourages speculation by foreigners because they will not buy property at a price that they would not be able to sell it back to a local for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, adapting the Australian model to Singapore could help to deter speculative or overly speculative behaviour by foreigners in the market while the property market starts to pick up after the review of the existing property cooling measures, which review should contemplate the suggested removal of ABSDs for Singaporean buyers, in my view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So far, Madam, I have raised Defence – the need for heightened vigilance; Manpower – the need to tap on the immense potential of our working mothers; and Homes – the need to safeguard against overly speculative behaviour of foreigners in our property market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But to do all this, we need to grow our TFR, so that we will have a Singaporean core who will be able to staff and push for key initiatives for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This leads me to the next point – inculcating a culture of adoption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, our TFR has been much lower than it has needed to be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Singapore's population continues to age, the effects of having such a low TFR will continue to affect our economy in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I would like to speak about how we can promote the loving, nurturing and voluntary alternative of adoption to pregnant mothers who might be thinking about terminating their pregnancies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, it is mandatory for all women, regardless of nationality, educational status and number of children, seeking to terminate their pregnancy in Singapore to undergo pre-abortion counselling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is my hope that these pre-abortion counselling sessions can be an avenue to provide pregnant mothers with further information about adoption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By understanding the process and the benefits of adoption better, pregnant mothers will be able to make an informed decision when considering an abortion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The promotion of adoption could also have the happy result of increasing our TFR organically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have heard stories of Singaporean couples trying for a baby for many years and are open to adopting a child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have heard also of stories of Singaporean couples who have children who are also open to adopting a child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the option of adoption were to be publicised more extensively, then these couples would be able adopt and raise the child as one of their own.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More than that, adoption does not only help couples who are unable to conceive, as there are many couples who already have birth children of their own who are open to adopting another child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, there are many wholesome, loving and beautiful traits in adoption, not just for the family seeking to adopt, but also for the adopted child who can grow and be nurtured in a loving family environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope due consideration can be given to proposals that I have raised in my speech when the Ministries are planning and rolling out their programmes in the coming year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that with good fiscal, economic and social policies in place, we will be well placed to chart our future together as a nation – Government partnering Singaporeans; Singaporeans partnering Government.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   Mdm Speaker, may I first of all extend my salutations to you and to the respected Members of this House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Before I begin my speech, I would like to read the words from a poem during the Sangam period by great Tamil poet, philosopher and humanist Avvaiyar.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: She said, "ஒப்புர வொழுகு", which means that "one should change one's goals and oneself to adapt to the changing world".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Her work called Aathichoodi contains 108 single-lined quotations.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I read the words "ஒப்புர வொழுகு" in line 10 earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget debate stands on the footing of this principle that was written thousands of years ago.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Based on this principle, we should focus on the importance of education, resilience and innovation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Committee on the Future Economy, Ministries and agencies have their work cut out for them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that we should "muster resources, to innovate, scale up and internationalise".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is a call which we and the stakeholders and constituents whom we may represent must heed as members of Singapore's business, professions, Government and society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The call for productivity is not new nor are well-founded fears that we live in decidedly challenging times.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We are accustomed to our inherent limitations as a small, low-lying island State.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We are also aware of heightened security threats.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza reminded us just moments ago – natural disasters of historic proportions in Asia and the re-emergence of geopolitical turmoil in Eastern Europe and the Middle East highlight the need for collective action.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is a very significant acknowledgment and I would say it is a relatively new acknowledgment as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, I would like to perhaps depart slightly from the learned hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza who earlier said that before we can have the economy, the first thing we have to get right is security.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would add that, unfortunately for Singapore, we do not have the luxury of seeing them separately; both need to be met at the same time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Our base plate places three things on equal par.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, of course, the economy; second, security; and third, I would say, compassion for our people.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is something that gives us pause for thought as we decide to increase our expenditure even further.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Other Members yesterday have highlighted the plight of those of us who may be inadvertently left behind, or perhaps "sandwiched".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think we have to think carefully as we go forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is time for our economic strategy, which we have exported for a very long time as the "Singapore Model" to be transformed, as Minister Heng puts it, to be re-calibrated, forged afresh in light of the new and fresh projected developments and changes we now face.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In response to the transformative spirit of Minister Heng's speech, I would like to focus on two aspects: the reference to innovation and the one to resilience as imperatives for Singaporeans, going forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I agree they are crucial, but would like to note that these two ideas or principles are not precise science; there is an art about them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In an increasingly fast-changing and interconnected world, fostering resilience to withstand unexpected shocks is becoming more important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The effects of financial crisis still linger, as do prospects of further financial seismic shifts to come.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I want to consider what resilience means and why it must be instilled in the education process from an early age and at all levels.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the discipline of psychology, resilience is defined as "that ineffable quality that allows some people to be knocked down by life and to come back stronger than ever".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than letting failure overcome them and drain their resolve, they find a way to rise up from their woes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It requires flexibility to thrive and to be kept alive.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Productivity and resilience have some things in common.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Box-ticking exercises; rehashing old routines; staying in the office past 10.00 pm just for the sake of appearance, for example, are not resilience and they will not yield productivity.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In short, resilience means we have to have grit.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It means having Paralympics gold medalist Yip Pin Xiu's courage to never give up.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It means having mountain climber and pro bono medical surgeon Dr Kumaran Rasappan's verve to scale new heights.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And to me, resilience means being a lifetime supporter of Liverpool Football Club.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has to be able to brace for shocks and stresses as a nation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They can take and have taken several forms – transboundary haze pollution, infrastructural failure, civil disturbances, cyber-attacks and economic crises.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Building resilience – the ability to bounce back quickly and effectively – is an urgent social and economic issue and one that unites many countries and cities all throughout the world.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I support the Budget speech's emphasis on resilience.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few suggestions though and these pertain to education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having an OBS campus at Coney Island is all well and good, but why do we not send our youth beyond Singapore or beyond Singapore's Sisters' Islands?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Send them to other countries in the Asia Pacific to cut their teeth.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng has noted in his speech that "we are in the center of the Asian growth story: China, India and ASEAN are expected to grow" exponentially.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would say more about this in my cut for the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in time to come, but I think this also is a clarion call for other agencies, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), and societal organisations in our country.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Surely, the Singapore International Foundation has a role to play towards ensuring that our youth are toughened up through real-life challenges, so they are strong by OBS, but they have to be intellectually rigorous as well and they have to think out of the box.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I commend going beyond adventure training, and having adventures safe in the knowledge that this spirit of adventure will build character for our young and will create future leaders of business, science, government and society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans, particularly our youth, need to be given a chance to show how rigorous they can be, intellectually and physically.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would add though, that when we have a new space, we should take a step back before ploughing forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I point here first to hon Member Mr Leon Perera who spoke about why benchmarking is important for SMEs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having a district of their own is very important, but what benchmark do we say to show which businesses could thrive, which may fail, and what we can do for them?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He makes good points worthy of our consideration, as does hon Member Ms Denise Phua who very succinctly talked about ability, agility and altitude.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, can I just say on the point of altitude – as lawmakers and policymakers in the House, it is often a suggestion from people in Singapore, including SMEs and businesses, that we may fly at a high altitude.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We are not quite on the same ground level to receive their concerns.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps this should be borne in mind as we plough forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Focusing on this exciting new idea of a Jurong Innovation District, it looks set to be Singapore's Silicon Valley, a Mecca for talented entrepreneurs looking to make their mark.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I add that as it is in Silicon Valley, research and planning is just one part of the enterprise.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In Silicon Valley, there is, increasingly, a concentrated business cycle that requires all the companies there to be nimble, calculated and quick in their judgement and execution.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is a very fast turnaround in Silicon Valley.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Can I just say a few words by Stanford University Economics Professor Yossi Feinberg?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He says this, "The best entrepreneurs prove the value of being able to set clear, long-term objectives and weigh up risk effectively against these objectives.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: For this reason, beneath the skin of the typical entrepreneur is often a stressed individual under intense pressure to pluck the right choices from a plethora of information.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Just like the rest of us, these people have no innate intellectual ability that allows them to glide through work or life." I would fully agree with the sentiment.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Jurong Innovation District aims to give our entrepreneurs, our Silicon Valley professionals, some guidance.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think this guidance is very, very important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: To truly support and equip innovators, we cannot just provide seed funding or pair them up with venture capitalists alone, as much as they would like that.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must focus on ensuring education and skills development by giving them the room to find inspiration in the company of like-minded individuals.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: All of this should begin in secondary school and junior college or, perhaps, even at a younger level.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But they must obviously continue through polytechnic and tertiary or university education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would say that while ICT is an important sector to begin, it must look beyond the ICT sector.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having a clear business model with a route to profitability is the norm for most successful new enterprises and business ventures.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This should be developed and strengthened from the get-go.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A can-do attitude is a trait that is observed obviously in all entrepreneurs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But it is just a beginning or a seedling of innovation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot, by itself, give rise to innovative projects and products.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As we create new agencies, bodies and spaces, let us remember that we must also actualise our current and traditional nodes of education and skills development – our higher level education and tertiary institutions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My fellow Nominated Member, Ms Chia Yong Yong, has put forward a compelling suggestion for greater synergy between research institutes and business.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Remarkable projects are being beta-tested at every level in Singapore and more should be known about this.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: These projects come from a variety of disciplines as diverse as architecture, engineering, business, political science and law.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If I may, I would suggest to the Ministry and to the Minister, as we look at SG Innovate as a point or a node for ourselves, to look at other entities such as the Royal Society of Science and the British Academy of Humanities and Social Sciences.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I look at these as examples because they are not universities per se.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are research institutes that traverse all universities in the UK.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I note, for example, that the hon Member Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef is one such example of a Young Outstanding Singaporean, who represented Singapore at the World Congress.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My point is that we have had innovators for a long time, it is not new to Singapore, and these innovators who are in our midst must be engaged with.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that "everyone has a role, and together, we are weaving a rich tapestry – each thread a different colour and texture, but woven together to give strength and resilience to our economy and our society".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I would caution against assuming the tapestry is ordained or static.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The artisan's craft of weaving rich texture and producing a masterpiece cannot be overshadowed by our administration's focus on the mapping of professional or business standards to produce a good short-term product.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It must have the long term in view, always.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must understand that tapestry will have its fair share of artistic blocks, changing perspectives, agendas and unanticipated outcomes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Many Members have spoken about the importance of a Singaporean Core everywhere − in business and in society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: To remain relevant, our art must been seen as a batik.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot be seen as something from another country.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must adapt it; it can never be perfect.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As I began with a Tamil poem, let me end with a few words from a poem we might recognise.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are indeed fortunate that we can afford such an increase due to increases in both Operating Revenue and higher Net Investment Returns Contributions (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government provide more details of the projects to be launched this year with the fiscal expansion and how many of them are likely to benefit our local SMEs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government will look into launching proportional higher number of projects that can be undertaken by SMEs which employ about 70% of Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am looking forward to the changes the Industry Transformation Programme can bring to our business landscape.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It aims to offer a more targeted and sector-focused approach to restructure our companies and drive their growth through productivity gains and innovation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I certainly hope that our SMEs will be proactive in their approach to these new measures and work with the Government agencies to take their business to the next level.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many companies are so focused on their day-to-day operations or meeting deadlines that they fail to take advantage of the benefits of the various schemes the Government has launched due to their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also challenging for them to make the short-term adjustments which are inconvenient but necessary for them to progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The present economic environment presents a good opportunity for many companies to leverage on the low commodity prices and work on projects with reduced costs of production.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, while their businesses benefit, they risk having lower revenues, too, in view of aggravated downward pressure due to lower material prices while faced with high capital outlay made in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, we have to be careful when we measure productivity based on revenue or by its face value.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies may have to work doubly hard to obtain the same revenue.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, our enterprises have to move to secure higher value jobs to compensate for the downward pressure of costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, companies still have to tackle significant business costs, like rent which can be reduced further.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, JTC can set the lead to bring down the cost component as it is a major player in the market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Great efforts by Government agencies with strong support from Singaporeans continue to be warranted to attract and bring in quality investment that can give Singaporeans the five "C"s – namely, comparative advantages, competitive edges, competencies, capabilities and capacities that can generate quality and well-paying jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This measure is welcomed by workers as they can receive WIS more quickly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Raising the income ceiling and simplifying the qualifying criteria will provide financial support for workers, and helping more workers to keep their jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amid the current economic uncertainties, these measures are very timely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through working, persons with disabilities also hope to have a career, live a meaningful life and contribute to the family and the country.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Next, on the subject of levy increases for S Pass holders in every sector and work permit holders in the construction and services sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I can understand the rationale behind this decision, I feel that we must be cautious towards over-reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The impact on business costs is substantial and comes during a time when businesses are facing more difficult and challenging conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel strongly that we should rethink and keep in view the levy increases for all the businesses for this year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Higher levies just add onto the business cost burden without necessarily resulting in the desired productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This brings me to the next subject of improvements in productivity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are various Government assistance schemes to help our companies work towards gains in productivity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are cases when a company just does not know how to go about improving its productivity, let alone access the appropriate schemes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, different sectors have different problems, and within each sector, companies serve different niches which present their own unique problems.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appeal to the Government to provide expertise to our local enterprises to help improve their productivity as part of an entire ecosystem overhaul.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will be a much more proactive approach and will underscore how seriously we view the problem of low productivity gains and our collective determination to overcome this challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another issue which we have to address urgently is the growing number of PMETs who have been retrenched.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Government to explore incentivising employers instead to keep the jobs for all these experienced PMETs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, this programme does not guarantee the same pay for the workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With business cycles getting shorter, skills can become obsolete very quickly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SkillsFuture will come in very useful, not just for our PMETs, but all Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SkillsFuture will keep our workforce updated and versatile and well-equipped to meet the evolving demands of the job market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The quality of our workforce will play an essential role in attracting investments to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, of course, the Government must continue to work hard to bring in good quality investments which will provide good jobs with attractive salaries or wages for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we could possibly equip Singaporeans with skill mastery, multi-skill sets as well as lifelong skills learning in meeting the dynamism and rapid changing economic challenges, it may be necessary for all of us to rethink of our pursuits in life.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Child Development Account (CDA) First Step grant, the KidSTART initiative and the Fresh Start Housing Scheme are thus useful and helpful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we would probably not see any significant increase in the number of babies next year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For our fertility rate to improve, we would need to invest more in building up our infant care and childcare infrastructure and system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is relatively easy to hire foreign domestic workers to look after babies, there is also a demand for good infant care.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Finding such services in convenient locations and with well-trained staff is not easy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I was a child, I recall that it was quite common to find homemakers who are also nannies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, there are far fewer women doing this work.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The main reason is that women are better educated and have better opportunities in their careers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parents have shared with me that sometimes, both husband and wife need to work late or travel overseas, and it would be ideal if they can leave their young children in their usual infant or childcare centres beyond the current operating hours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nannies, compared to centres, are usually more flexible.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government look into possible solutions for this problem?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Twenty-four-hour care services will also be helpful for workers who work shift work.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Alternatively, some parents leave their children in the care of their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not consider this to be monetising something which many grandparents do for the young in their families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather, the money would help to ease the burden of the young parents in raising a family.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this, I conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It calls upon the partnership of all Singaporeans to work together in new ways to transform our economy and build a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As our economy transforms, we will have to transform ourselves.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: During this period, the vulnerable group needs the most help.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This group includes low-wage workers, women workers and mid-career individuals who take on new jobs, and more needs to be done to ensure that they are taken care of.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Retirement adequacy continues to be a challenge for the low-wage workers, and more so for the women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Statistically speaking, women are expected to live longer than men.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This means more retirement savings is needed so that we can age gracefully with peace of mind and with dignity and vitality.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For the older or senior women in Singapore today, many have not worked in the formal economy or have suffered from a gender wage gap in their earlier working years.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For the women workers, it is important that they are given fair opportunities at the workplace, while continuing to care for their families at home.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The family unit is the basic building block of a thriving nation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our families give us support and keep us grounded, and women continue to play a larger role in the families.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, striking a balance is not easy and more needs to be done for the women workers to ensure equal opportunities in placement and career progression.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Women should be given stronger support to be able to pursue our different definitions of success.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Women should not be fearful of "sacrificing their careers" for a family if they are given the right to request for flexible work arrangements (FWAs) or given equal opportunities when back to work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Against the backdrop of a slowing economy, will this vulnerable group be faced with more challenges?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, more support can be given to not just companies but also individuals as many often suffer pay cuts when they change career paths, voluntarily or not.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While she can look forward to better career progression, as the sole breadwinner of the family, it is challenging having to cope with daily expenses for the family and, at the same time, upgrade herself to make sure there is retirement adequacy towards her silver age.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A concerted tripartite effort can create a stronger support network for this group of people.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A hands-on approach from the agency to offer not just training grants but also psychological support and guidance can help acclimatise workers quicker in different workplace environments.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share another example of how psychological support, guidance and help by all parties – union, management, family and friends, and society at large – had helped an accountant in his 50s to have successfully completed PCP many years back.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He did well in his academic programme which included a hospital attachment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, after commencing work, he was not able to cope and adapt in a fast-paced ward environment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There was a constant struggle to the extent that he was in a state of depression and did not know who to turn to until he met up with the union.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He needed a pillar of support to lean on and a listening ear to hear his struggles.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With much discussion with the management, he was then given another opportunity to show his ability in a smaller ward that was less demanding, in terms of workload.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He was then able to cope and subsequently shone to take on higher responsibility.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He is a living example of how age is not a barrier and resilience is the key to success.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Now, he has been successful to the extent that he was further given the opportunity to take up advanced diploma in nursing and he was glad that he stayed on in this meaningful career to care for the patients.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   Like this accountant, there are many workers who face changes in their workplaces.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some endure because of their passion, some may return to their previous industries when opportunities are made available, and some may give up.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They have made the first step to learn a new skill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They can only succeed with the help and cooperation of all stakeholders, such as the workers, workers' union and the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Every worker's story can be a success story.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For this, it is necessary to have the support of the tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, I would like to now switch over to English.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would be talking about inculcating the culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The economy will continue to transform itself and our jobs will constantly evolve.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our education system has brought us this far, but in the era of rapid changes, we need to have a certain level of nimbleness and agility.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to inculcate a culture of lifelong learning so that we can be future-ready with future skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: So, how can we be the catalyst of this mindset change?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does our ecosystem allow our people to be independent; to plan for our career; to adapt to changes; to take on new skills every few years; and to constantly learn, unlearn and relearn?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What better way can one do this then tapping on the slew of grants offered under the SkillsFuture initiatives, beginning with the SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this, workers especially those who wish to take up courses on their own to upgrade or even switch industries can use this to pay for their courses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are others who may not be forthcoming to attend courses or learning as a whole due to long hours of work and the need to work overtime almost daily.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For such workers, bite-sized programmes can be another approach to keeping them relevant to the needs of the current skills as well as future skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be open and accept that individuals are different and therefore we need to employ different strokes for different folks.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The initiatives announced at this year's Budget to help and support the SMEs is much welcomed.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This will help many SMEs to transform to grow together with our economy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, such measures, while prolonging the survival of some enterprises, may lull workers working in such enterprises from understanding the need to upgrade them to be future-ready with future skills as they get complacent in their current job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, how can we ensure that workers in these enterprises are upskilled through the slew of programmes and initiatives offered by WDA, especially the SkillsFuture initiative, so that SMEs can continue to have an effective Singapore core in their workforce?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we advise and guide such enterprises?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we render early help and better assist the workers working in such enterprises?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many middle-income earners, commonly known as the sandwich class, whom I have interacted with, had expected tax rebate this year.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Of the many with families, there are singles that support the aged parents and, in some cases, those who support the siblings who are physically challenged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, we can have a richer discussion on the Budget and my speech will seek to provide some suggestions on the contours of such a discussion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As with almost all Budget announcements made over the last few years in particular, it is usually followed by a discussion in some quarters, especially in commentaries and forum pages, about whether the Government is turning populist, if welfare is taking root in Singapore, or a combination of similar themes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Very seldom are fears of welfare accompanied by a look at the overall fiscal state of affairs and both in the short and long term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The additional details in this Budget about the Silver Support package exemplify a recognition by the Government that there are many Singaporeans – more than 140,000 of them, in fact – who are not adequately equipped for retirement and live precarious lives, perhaps, not only physically, but more significantly, even mentally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To put things in some perspective, the State collects $2.2 billion a year in gaming revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our vulnerable elderly deserve to retire with dignity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This must be a central social objective of the Singapore system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No discussion of financial prudence can escape the important behavioural question of ensuring our society retains a positive work ethic with permanent schemes like Silver Support and Workfare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this question should be posed with a sense of not just perspective, but also proportion, in view of the demographic transition in Singapore and the structural changes that come with economic transformation, both of which will become more apparent in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How can we better approach a discussion on the Budget going forward?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same way, the Ministry of Defense (MINDEF) human resource planners can project with sufficient granularity the number of men that will serve National Service (NS) in about 20 years' time, and as a consequence, determine the force size and structure to a reasonable degree, a richer public debate on permanent schemes like Silver Support can take shape if we assess the sustainability of such schemes with a long-term perspective in mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would help the public better understand the overall costs and sustainability of such schemes rather than leave it to conjecture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a more coherent and holistic public debate on the pros and cons of potentially expanding Workfare can also take place if the public is presented with tools to better understand how much such permanent initiatives are likely to cost years down the road.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans have in the past suggested tweaking Workfare to raise the cash component.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, an important consideration in the context of fiscal prudence, and understanding such permanent schemes better could be, for example, an exercise that compares raising the WIS payout amounts as compared against the initiative announced in this year's budget which increases the income eligibility threshold from $1,900 to $2,000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many additional Singaporeans would benefit by this threshold rise and is there scope to further raise the payouts under WIS, and if so, what would be the specific impact on the Budget, and would it be wise?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such enquiries will make the public better appreciate the trade-offs and operationalise the meaning of fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second trend that often repeats itself prior to the Budget debate is the wishes of specific industries or industry leaders who call for more reliefs or taxpayer support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What we do not see much of is the debate about whether some companies have grown to expect the equivalence of constant assistance or "welfare" from the State, without the same scrutiny extended to permanent schemes for the needy or less well-off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like permanent schemes that help individual Singaporeans, a fuller public discussion on fiscal prudence should also extend to companies and industries, and enquire whether Budget initiatives indeed achieve the policy outcomes that they were intended for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is relevant, as even the Government has acknowledged that some companies have used their PIC credits to buy equipment they do not need.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fiscal sustainability would also require accounting for the extent of such leakage and unintended consequences as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The lessons learnt from the shortcomings of the PIC scheme should be transferred to the Budget's announcement of the three-year $400 million Automation Support Package, specifically with regard to grants, which assist in the roll-out of new automation projects and investment allowances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would ensure that the technologies introduced actually improve productivity as envisaged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the cap can be progressively lowered or even removed completely for companies that do not meet the policy objectives of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would also be important for any exercise in fiscal prudence to distinguish and incentivise activities that actually create something tangible that have a real trickle-down effect as opposed to economic initiatives that just "rotate around the high-finance microcosm enriching the 1% as they buy and sell existing assets to one another, bidding up their value, while failing to invest in research, products, jobs or innovation" – an apt descriptive which I read in a recent TIME magazine article that reviewed a new US primetime television show, titled "Billions".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An inclusive Singapore must be underwritten by Singapore-based companies that support the employment prospects of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would also, I hazard, have the parallel effect of engendering a more inclusive citizenry that is rooted to Singapore's long-term success.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a Budget that tells us that change is on the horizon and we must take this journey of change together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would have been a speech about a few main issues from the above cuts, but I scrapped that speech and decided instead to focus on something more fundamental and what the President had asked us to do in his Address to us in January this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And that is to "engage and partner with Singaporeans in nation building", the fifth of the five key aims this Government aims to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I see this Budget debate as one of the last few chapters of this "Budget" journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do feel that we perhaps need to take a few steps back and add a few more chapters in this journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget is one huge item in our agenda that affects everyone in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is something that everyone has a stake in and everyone should have a voice in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly believe that we should use this opportunity to engage and partner Singaporeans in nation building.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is our best opportunity to do so in each financial year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In less than a month, the Budget Statement was announced and many have asked if we can effectively digest all the feedback from the public within a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the question here is whether we can make this journey less rushed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not advocating for us to delay the Budget Statement but rather, I hope we can start the process earlier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, we start the consultation in November rather than February, and this consultation is similar to what we are already doing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It gathers general ideas from the public about what they want to see in the Budget and members of the public provide this feedback without knowing what the Government has in mind or the general direction it is heading.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We then take two months to digest all the feedback, which is from December until January.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In February, we release a draft Budget Statement similar to what we released on March 24.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We then have another round of public consultation about that Budget Statement for a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This second round of public consultation is a good opportunity for Members of this House to obtain feedback from the ground and work towards incorporating them into the final Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And the feedback obtained from this consultation will likely be more specific, since members of the public now know what the Government has in mind based on their previous feedback and it is now about finetuning the ideas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This final Budget Statement is then read towards the end of March, after digesting the feedback from the second round of public consultation for a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But will people feel more engaged, more empowered and will this strengthen our partnership with fellow Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The answer is, without a doubt, also yes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to change the narrative and I accept that it is changing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has gone from the Government organising sessions to tell people what the new policies are, to sessions now asking for feedback before we draft the new policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I think we can, we should and we must go one step further.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The destination is important but I feel the journey is even more crucial.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Communication has to be two ways and after we obtain feedback from the public, we should incorporate as many of them as possible into policies, show people the draft policies and then get feedback again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will show that public consultation is not just an exercise for us to put a tick in the box but that we are truly listening, and that their views and feedback are being looked into, worked on, perhaps even expanded and then incorporated into the final product.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do not get me wrong; this Budget 2016 is a good Budget for Singapore and Singaporeans but it can be better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel there are more ideas out there that can be explored.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no doubt that there has been a lot of public feedback about this Budget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure we have all seen the feedback about the Budget Statement both online and in the print media and on the ground, during our house visits and during our coffee shop visits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As always, there is praise and there are criticisms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There will always be negative feedback, but these may also be ideas we have not thought of, and they may be worth exploring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are concerns about whether the cap on the tax relief will hit working mothers hardest, is 1% but I met that 1% on Sunday.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To engage people, we need to listen more than we speak.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I quoted, "The most basic of all human needs is the need to understand and be understood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
