text: The best way to understand people is to listen to them." And how we are not there just to explain policies to people and to throw them facts and figures, but we are there to truly listen and understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I held my town hall last Saturday and spent close to two hours just listening to the feedback from residents about the Budget and many other issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They spoke of their hopes, their aspirations and their dreams for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For me, it was a powerful session and there are ideas and suggestions there that we need work on and perhaps incorporate into the next Budget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget is about partnerships and about starting our journey together for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I agree with Minister Heng that there is no doubt that we need to grow our economy and invest collectively for the long term – in our people, our home and our security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And with a population that is engaged, empowered, inspired and mobilised, this journey will be even more amazing, the Singapore story even more powerful and this red dot will shine even brighter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Always well-planned, always structured, always comprehensive addressing the issues of the day; current, prudent and practical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The question I then asked myself is, how do we ensure that we grab all the opportunities that are available, whether from the Budget or from any other platforms to empower ourselves, to uplift ourselves, our families, our companies and businesses and of course our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The question is also, Madam, are we as hungry as we should be?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Once, a young man approached Socrates and asked how he could achieve success and even greater success?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Socrates took the young man out to the sea and they walked on until the water level reached the shoulders of the young man.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Socrates then grabbed the young man's head and pushed it under the water.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The young man struggled but Socrates was a big man and, of course, stronger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Then slowly he lightened the grasp on the young man's head and allowed him to surface, gasping for air.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Socrates then said to him, "When you want something so bad, as you had wanted air a moment ago, you would naturally achieve success." Every Budget, every National Day Rally, many would ask, "What goodies are we getting?" Is this the appropriate question we should be asking?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The late Minister Mentor said in an interview with the National Geographic Magazine: "Singaporeans are not as hard driving and high striving as they ought to be." Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong himself said at one of the National Day Rally speeches, "Singaporeans are not as hungry as the Vietnamese." Our forefathers worked really hard, showcasing sheer grit and discipline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But are we hungry enough to carry on?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We can build all the best facilities for training sportsmen for example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Discipline, dedication, sheer grit, sweat, blood, tears and toil does.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough to utilise these as appropriate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For those involved in business, can we think out of the box to make this relevant?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If the box is small enough, are we brave enough to enlarge it?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And even with that, if it is still restrictive, do we dare, are we hungry enough to break that box, but do not break any laws of the nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough to also perhaps pre-book our lot at the Jurong Innovation District?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The stronger our desire for achievement and the hungrier we are, chances are we will strive hard to get whatever we want.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we keep our motivation wave riding high?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we ready to not peg grades to our self-worth?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we ready for education beyond textbooks and the four walls of our classroom that can enrich us, and widen our mindsets and empower us?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our communities, the world, the Internet, virtual learning and simulation are all our newer platforms for learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In all these, we can instil discipline in the approach and gauge the desired outcome in order to reap the maximum benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough for jobs, coming in at the appropriate level and working ourselves up?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough to maintain or even further our competitiveness, knowing the rest of Southeast Asia, China and India are up and coming?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will enable SMEs to explore new businesses and models, and help restructuring and even streamline their company's investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will reduce their worry about any incidental tax costs that can be incurred.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For those venturing overseas, the Double Tax Deduction (DTD) for the Internationalisation Scheme is an option to help jump start initiatives as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough to better what others know and even to do better than they have done?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Such broad-based schemes will be replaced by more targeted ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This may throw off some companies and pose challenges for some SMEs at first, but I would urge businesses, especially the smaller ones, to view this with a broader perspective, plan early and assess financial commitments and capabilities appropriately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we hungry enough to further the frontiers of research, in the various disciplines?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The flexibility to claim writing-down allowances on the acquisition costs of intellectual property (IP) over a longer time frame can help relevant companies and institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we become a research hub, we must continue to encourage companies to bring in more IPs to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we come out of our comfort zone and choose to be extraordinary?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Get the greatness and the mastery that we want?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Parents have been presented with a blank canvas in their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How ready are we to be creative and expressive with this canvas?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we ride the tide of change and transformation and be willing to take the beating as we strive?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we take ownership of our learning and growth?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have met many young people who have interacted with me and said, "I do not really know what my interests are, nor my passion", or "I do not know what I am good at".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Well, knowing ourselves and understanding what we like is really a function of two things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The second point is really about internalisation and adequate introspectionary reflection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, if you can put the two together and work on it a bit, you will realise your strengths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We can choose to sit in a café or by the beach and watch the world go by or wait for inspirations to strike us or we can get up and do something about it, and tame that hunger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: On a cautionary note, as we enhance our drive and get more hungry, remember to think of others and appreciate people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we grow and develop ourselves, people like our parents and grandparents and the less abled are growing older and need to be treated with respect, patience, and love, even as they become slower than they used to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we pursue to fulfil our hunger, let us not trample over others or venture into non ethical territories.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We always want a clean, upright, caring, nurturing and stimulating environment with a long-term goal of building resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the end, it is about being balanced, well-equilibrated, successful and happy in our lives together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   The Malay community has attained so much success and achievement including in the new fields, and if we look closely, those who succeed, as well as their families, they possess certain traits that lead to their success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But there are a few who are still stuck in challenging situations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In my experience in interacting with and assisting them, there are a number of issues that need to be dealt with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They only go to nearby places such as mosques and Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS).

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Geylang Serai, for instance, I worked with these institutions so that they can refer cases to me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that those in this group would speak to us so that we can help them and formulate an action plan that will assist them for the sake of their future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They have to be open-minded enough to see the bigger picture and look far ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If others can achieve success, they can do it too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But they have to develop a mindset that is inspired, motivated and have a strong desire to achieve something.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Attend courses such as the "Spending Wisely" course which is held near your place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If you need personal counselling, we can do it too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The mindset where you "work hard first and enjoy later" is the right way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is the source of financial problems for certain families, spending beyond their means, buying things on instalment plans and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are those who still have credit card issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are those in this group who prefer not to undergo health screening or early screening.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If they are diagnosed with an illness, they find it hard to accept and sometimes refuse treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Sometimes, this is due to financial reasons, but in other cases, it is because of their mindset.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some have just reached the age of 40 years and think that they are already old and they are less motivated to take care of their health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do what is necessary for your future and your families' future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Despite these issues, many of our Malay/Muslims have managed to turn their lives around and are more positive and self-reliant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I find that those who are able to overcome these five factors are able to progress with the available assistance schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We are now facing a new world with new challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We need a new mindset; to be more proactive, to be more global and to be more reliable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Every individual in our Malay/Muslim community, together with other communities, must undergo this transformation together as one for the sake of our future and the future of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): With ourselves being described as a wonderful tapestry, interwoven and interlaced, a piece of batik art, but let me add my piece.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Different pieces of vegetables, fruits, nuts, raisins cut up into small pieces but, at the same time, always maintaining the character, the flavour, the taste, the colour and whatever they have individually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But they coexist in that salad bowl; happily together, loosely held by a salad dressing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Not mayonnaise, but a vinaigrette dressing or a lemon dressing would be much healthier for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And, co-existing in that salad bowl, sharing that common space, limited as it may be, but together cohesive, and when you take a spoonful of this salad, and put it into your mouth, the flavour is wonderful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That is how we must be like – the salad bowl where we are all together in it, together for the future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, the plight of the middle-income group; second, innovation and the culture of inquisitiveness; and lastly, Malay SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me express my appreciation to Minister Heng Swee Keat for the delivery of Budget 2016.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am highly impressed by the clarity and simplicity with which the nation's strategic goals were presented.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I must say, I have some concerns which I would like to highlight.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Through my involvement in community issues over the last 13 years, I have become impassioned over the welfare and well-being of the sandwiched class, or as they say, the middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There were rigorous discussions on the middle-income group during the run-up to last year's Budget Statement delivered by then-Finance Minister, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I get the impression and sincerely hope that this is because existing initiatives are making substantial headways in alleviating the plight of the middle income.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore progresses amidst the global and at times uncertain economic backdrop, our economy will have to adapt and adjust.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Both local and multinational corporations (MNCs) would be continuously re-inventing and restructuring themselves while trying to cope with the changing economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As new economies replace old ones, the possibilities of jobs redundancy and obsolescence are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I sincerely believe our progress equation will have to include these unwanted elements.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a systemic constraint that we are confronted with, which we have to manage.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I also appreciate the Government's effort in trying to circumvent this by introducing proactive and constructive measures on our workers through re-training and skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With the middle-income group constituting a major proportion of our workforce, it is imperative that we place safeguards to ensure robustness in the times of adverse economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As recent as last month, the Singapore Economic Society discussed the idea of cushioning workers in the event of involuntary unemployment.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Other Members of Parliament had also expressed similar proposals on workers' safety net in the past.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps it is timely that we should revisit this with the purpose to ensure the worker's and his or her family's well-being, should the unwanted event occur.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me express my appreciation to Minister Heng Swee Keat for the delivery of Budget 2016.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Although it is very interesting and comprehensive, I would like, however, to register some concerns.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Throughout my involvement in dealing with community issues over the last 13 years, I have been very concerned with the welfare and well-being of middle-class Singaporeans or the group often termed as the sandwich class.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I concur that the Government has already identified and discussed this issue at length, and has already provided various assistance schemes for the middle-class in the 2015 Budget.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore progresses amidst an uncertain global and economic environment, our economy will have to adapt.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Both local companies and MNCs will continue to re-invent and restructure their businesses and operations, while they also try to cope with a rapidly changing economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As the new economy replaces the old economy, several jobs will very possibly become redundant and obsolete.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that our progress equation will have to include these unwanted elements.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We have to accept that this is the systemic constraint that confronts us and we have to manage it well.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to express my appreciation to the Government for working hard to overcome this issue by introducing proactive and constructive measures, through the skills upgrading and retraining schemes made available to our workers.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With the middle-income group making up a large proportion of our labour force, it is important that we provide this protective and safety net to ensure that we stay strong during the times when the economy is bad.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, just last month, the Singapore Economic Society discussed ideas about measures that can be implemented to help minimise the impact on our workers if they are retrenched.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is an idea that we can explore and discuss further.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Other past MPs have also expressed similar proposals to provide such a social safety net.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The time may have come for us to re-examine this idea with the aim of ensuring that the welfare and well-being of workers and their families are cared for, in case anything unfortunate happens.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): I shall touch on innovation and culture of inquisitiveness.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I have been involved in innovation and R&D since I started my career in 1986.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The value creation and the unique value proposition that these companies offered through innovation kept them ahead of their competitors.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was also a primary factor which enabled these successful companies to be able to tread through difficult times.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation was clearly one of the key drivers towards success and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I heartily laud Budget 2016's key thrust in placing innovation as one of the strategic pieces.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am convinced that this is the right element for enterprises to embark on if they are to forge into the future successfully.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, going forward, I support wholeheartedly towards this initiative which will enable us to transform our economy and bring us into the future that we desire.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, innovation is neither a product nor it is a material item.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is an intangible capability and competence which need to be nurtured with time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: For innovation to be successfully and sustainably applied, it has to be deep-rooted in the way we do things and the way we run our business.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation calls for the intelligent application of knowledge which ultimately creates value.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And it is this purpose of continuous value creation that elevates enterprises from one level to the next, thus transforming themselves.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Having worked for large MNCs in my many years of employment, I frequently met and dealt with local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, I must admit that my impression on most local enterprises that I met was not encouraging if I were to assess them on their involvement in R&D.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Somehow, investing in R&D and innovation activities is not an important and top-of-the-list item on their agenda.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, it is apparent and noticeable that they are unable to provide that special value which is needed to differentiate them from their global competitors.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If we want innovators to create and create value, we have to start by creating innovators and nurture them.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And to achieve this, we have to start from young.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I mean we have to start as early as primary schools.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am of the opinion that it would have been too late if we start later than this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to share with you my personal experience on how I ended up being involved in the R&D domain.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: When I was a young boy, I used to sit next to my father on weekends while he would start dismantling parts of his Vespa motor scooter.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: He would then hand me pieces and items of the motor scooter engine – screws, bolts, piston ring, piston, engine blade, brake clutches, spark plug, you name it, and he would then ask me to start cleaning them on a pan filled with kerosene.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A bit dangerous though, but I did it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Though the odour from the kerosene can be challenging, I enjoyed it and felt intrigued.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What ran through my mind was – how can all these small parts, when put together, be able to make the motor scooter run, whereby each part itself is almost useless, just a mere piece of metal.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And that was the time where I started to develop a sense of inquisitiveness.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is this inquisitive attribute which I gained and later on in life propelled me to become an R&D engineer upon my graduation after completing university education.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: R&D and innovation is still my passion to this day.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We have to start as early as possible if we want our young to have that inquisitive attribute and to make it second nature.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it is an important prerequisite if one is to be an innovator.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the relevant Ministries will pick up the suggestions and steer the way.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Our SMEs play an important role in our economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Industry Transformation Programme is apt and timely to bring us into the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The slew of support schemes and incentives offered by the Budget 2016 are again laudable.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to highlight that there are gaps with varying degrees of capabilities and competencies among our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is against this backdrop that I would like to raise my concerns.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I wish I have all the statistics to share and understand where the Malay SMEs are.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Even if we have it, it would still be a cause of concern.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They are young and aspiring entrepreneurs whose aim is to expand and become a global enterprise one day.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The outcome of their work, without a doubt, justifies the standing they are accorded with.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, one of the main themes for this year's Budget is the Spirit of Partnership.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In his speech, Minister Heng Swee Keat emphasised the importance of this factor in transforming our nation's economy and in strengthening Singapore towards being an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I agree and concur that emphasis and focus should be given to this Spirit of Partnership because, in our present lives that are full of trials and tribulations, efforts that require cooperation or collaborations between different groups and entities, are the best way to cope with an uncertain living environment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the Malay saying goes, "Whether the burden is light or heavy, we will carry it together".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The value of the Spirit of Partnership is the main theme of my speech for this year's Budget debates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is to be expected, especially with the gloomy overall economic outlook in the near future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If something unfortunate happens to our SMEs, the whole of Singapore will be affected.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the winding down of an SME will result in job losses for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I feel that the main objective is to gain a collective benefit and not for only certain groups.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The collective benefit is gained by Singaporeans through the jobs made available when small and medium enterprises continue to grow and progress.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This collective benefit is a main factor in achieving an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For this Budget, one of the main emphasis is the effort to increase systems automation and encourage mergers and acquisitions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government has provided grants to support SMEs to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In terms of economy of business, any increase in automation will be viewed as something positive because it is closely linked to an increase in productivity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the next question will be, what will be the impact of automation on the economy of employment?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Economic experts have different views on the impact of automation on jobs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The moderate view is that, while automation will make jobs disappear, at the same time, it will create new jobs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A study by George Graetz from the Uppsala University and Guy Michaels from the London School of Economics in 2015 showed some evidence that automation will result in job loss to low-skilled workers and to certain moderately skilled workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchments and job losses cannot be avoided when mergers and acquisitions occur.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this decade, mergers and acquisitions occurred rapidly in many industries, like banking, logistics, manufacturing and others.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The main aim of the Government in supporting the increase in automation, and encouraging mergers and acquisitions, is that Singaporeans can reap the collective benefits, and that it will not only benefit certain groups.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many hope that the Government will pay close attention and monitor it closely, so that this aim of reaping collective benefits can be realised.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We certainly do not want a situation where automation and technological development result in certain segments of society feeling that they are left behind, and sink amidst the tide of modernity and progress, resulting in negative feelings, as the saying goes, "being discarded after they are no longer useful." If this happens, it will weaken our efforts to build an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This simple scheme can give an indication that the help provided is short-term in nature, but at the same time, it can give some relief and financial assistance while these individuals strive to look for new jobs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The people welcome the SkillsFuture scheme, especially amongst the low-skilled and low-wage community members, who wish to upskill so that they will not sink amidst the tide of technological development and automation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, their intent to upskill will be affected due to cost issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the basis of inclusiveness and caring for one another, I hope that the Government can seriously consider the suggestions mentioned as part of the Spirit of Partnership between the Government and the people to help Singaporeans cope with the challenges that will emerge in our nation's pursuit of progress.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In his speech, the Finance Minister said that we will like Singapore to be a great place to raise a family, where we bring out the best in every Singaporean, and a society that takes care of those who have special needs, and who are less well off.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Minister once again emphasised the Spirit of Partnership between individuals, society and the Government in order to achieve this objective.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The KidSTART scheme aims to help the early development of children's physical, cognitive and social skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As mentioned, these schemes provide support for Singaporean children in order to give them the best start possible in life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do understand that the Government provides these schemes only to children who are born to married couples in an effort to strengthen the institution of the family.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a family and household counsellor, I agree with this approach.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But I also feel that we should assess this from another angle.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, these children should not be treated differently because of something that their parents did.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government's approach in this issue should be changed so that when these children grow up, they will not feel marginalised, left out and angry, because society seems to blame them for something that their parents did.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the Government's support towards the development of every Singaporean child, regardless of their status, will be welcomed by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In order to build one's resilience, we need to have a holistic approach, whereby every aspect of the human brain, that is, Intelligence Quotient (IQ), Emotional Quotient (EQ) and Spiritual Quotient (SQ), must be developed and nurtured.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: SQ first came to the attention of academics, especially in the field of psychology, early last decade.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: According to academics, SQ is closely linked to awareness towards the meaning of life, being responsible in life and the need for humility in life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: By possessing SQ, it will point an individual towards having a personal vision and work towards it, with the objective that every benefit gained is not meant just for him, but also for society and the world in general; in other words, achieve collective good.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In short, he turns himself into a blessing for all.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that a combination of these three quotients will not only result in resilience, but it will also build other positive human traits.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Here, I would like to repeat a suggestion that I gave previously in this House, that is, the reintroduction of Religious Knowledge subjects in secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I feel that schools are the best place to develop a holistic person that should combine IQ, EQ and SQ.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I had the opportunity to examine how these three schools nurture good values and good traits.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The advantage that Mission schools and madrasahs have over public schools is that they also focus on developing SQ.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Following that, I said that it is better to undertake early preventive measures so that this situation, where a child is born out of wedlock, can be lessened or prevented.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am confident that this can be achieved through the development of the Intellectual, Emotional and Spiritual Quotients in each person.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A partnership, which combines the Intellectual, Emotional and Spiritual Quotients, can result in individuals who are highly resilient and gives priority to the collective need.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These are the Singaporeans that we need in our effort towards building an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The final issue that I will touch on is the Government's move to encourage Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and other ground-up initiatives, by providing more support.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do understand that the main role of the SSO is to coordinate and increase cooperation between voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) within their respective jurisdictions, so that the local communities can receive the maximum benefit.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is done by monitoring the demography and needs of the local community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, monitoring is done to see if there is a duplication of services, whether the service provided currently is sufficient and so on.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The partnership between the SSO and programme organisers, be it corporate entities or interested individuals, can help to fill in the service gaps within a certain area.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This partnership not only benefits the needy, but it also helps organisations that provide assistance or that wish to implement community programmes, and hence creating a win-win situation for everyone.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Before I end my speech, I would like to state that the Spirit of Partnership is an important aspect of personal development, as well as the development of society and the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Spirit of Partnership aims to combine resources and manpower so that it can give the best and maximum benefits possible to every member of society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But we must be careful so that this partnership does not lead to unwanted side effects and resulting in a segment of society feeling marginalised and neglected, because that will run against our country's mission to build an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak on three areas today: why our economic restructuring is so important; pitfalls and opportunities; and how we must continue keeping our social system progressive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, as circumstances change, jumping to a new branch on another tree, continuing to climb, climbing higher, and climbing better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a good approach, not just in the Year of the Monkey, but throughout life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And our startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) provide opportunities too − the skills that come with running a business and the chance to build a successful enterprise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, a thriving society with its jobs and enterprise, all these help our young Singaporeans to rise and grow, while adding dynamism and value to our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also know that a strong economy gives us the means to support fiscal redistribution and the many social programmes that underpin an inclusive society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also ensures we can maintain a credible defence deterrence through a strong Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), as well as a Home Team that is ready and equipped to face the challenges of this century.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All these keep us relevant to the world and ensure that our voice can be heard, even though we are small.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In summary, Mdm Speaker, we must not forget that a strong economy secures our Independence, sovereignty and security, and is also key to building a fair and just society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there are still lessons we can learn from the experience of other developed countries, the challenges they faced, the lessons they have learnt.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In February 2013, the Harvard Business School published its 2012 survey on US competitiveness led by Prof Michael Porter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is useful to look at the observations and what we can learn that are applicable to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One observation by the Harvard study was on the importance of shared resources, for example, workers having relevant skills in the labour market; workers moving in between employers, between sectors, but having that base of skills; supply chain networks; and physical, technical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, the authors of the Harvard study found that there was a shortfall of investment by businesses in shared resources.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Investment would have helped all companies in the long term.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But at the level of individual companies in the US, it did not always make short-term business sense.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Building up this local pool of talent also helps our SMEs because the more skills and talent are in the pool, the more there are who can forge on, start their own enterprises, and help fellow Singaporeans to grow and rise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Different industries, different ways, but it must always be an on-going effort.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when companies invest in workers, upskilled workers, it uplifts the entire sector of skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It helps other companies in the sector, it helps the workers, it helps Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mariana Mazzucato at Sussex University, who studies the economics of innovation, has proposed many ways to do this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, loan repayments that are adjusted based on profits of the enterprise, or allowing the state to retain equity, just as private venture capital firms do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It does not have to be a controlling stake, but the equity could be preferred stocks with priority in receiving dividends.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Harvard study, Mdm Speaker, also observed that some American corporations were driven by short-term performance indicators – short-term shareholders driving short-term corporate behaviour.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This led to extractive optimisation in the short term, rather than longer-term investments which add value and create sustainable innovation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The lesson for Singapore, Mdm Speaker, is that even as we boost our productivity, we must continue pursuing both kinds of innovation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is part of competition – enhancing existing situations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But they can also easily be undercut by cheaper labour, cheaper economies and lower costs elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Other innovations create new value and new markets, pathbreakers, game-changers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They complement each other and help bring each other to greater heights, and it has to be continuous – a never-ending process of innovation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each chapter having to be better than the previous one because that is how we write the story of tomorrow's enterprises.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: GDP growth is not pursued for its own sake.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have spoken earlier about how a strong economy is key to Singapore remaining independent and a pre-condition for a fair and just society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is crucial that our socioeconomic system remains progressive – supporting social mobility and making sure every child has a fair start in life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Helping children who start with less, without pulling down those who were blessed enough to start with more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, Mdm Speaker, when a child from a disadvantaged background does well, it uplifts the rest of the family.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A few years ago, Economics Nobel Laureate James Mirrlees led a team which reviewed the UK tax system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One key point was the system must be considered as a whole when deciding whether taxation is progressive or regressive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another very important part of redistribution, another very important progressive policy, Mdm Speaker, is our subsidies for first-time buyers of HDB homes because that first opportunity to get early access to home ownership is deeply important – that early opportunity to have an asset which can appreciate and accumulate value throughout life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, we must continue helping young couples have affordable home ownership early in life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But Madam, progressive redistribution alone is not enough to build a strong, cohesive society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Tax relief and tax deductions help recognise behaviours which benefits the community, while keeping the system progressive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must continue encouraging personal and corporate charity as they add something special to our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It acknowledges that meaningful charity is not just about cash or tangible assets.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It empowers people to give in ways other than cash.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These charitable deeds, Mdm Speaker, are an important part of our social fabric.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Of course, some may argue that fiscal transfer achieves the same numerical outcome.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps on the balance sheet, the numbers might look the same, but there is a fundamental difference, because volunteerism and charity are transformative.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It transforms the recipient, it transforms the donor and it transforms our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Volunteering and voluntary giving uplift our spirits in a way that taxation and tax transfers can never do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And these are important externalities which transform the inner life of the people we serve, as well as the inner life of those who step forward to serve.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On another point related to this, Mdm Speaker, the Community Networks for Seniors are another big step forward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many hands, and many channels of assistance – VWOs, volunteers, schools and businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when it is complicated for the end-user to get access to help, the overall system can actually become regressive on the ground because of that complexity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When the application process is complicated, when there is red tape and when there is bureaucracy, it becomes harder for those who are less well-informed, less IT-literate, or from more disadvantaged background, to seek help or to find out what avenues of assistance are available.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We are moving towards online e-government, but for residents who do not have a computer or a smartphone or who do not happen to be literate in English, e-government channels, instead of an open-door, can be a digital barrier.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One important insight in that report is the concept of bandwidth constraints.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What it means is the idea that psychological stress and hardship can place a cost on people's mental resources.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some economists call it a "cognitive tax" or "bandwidth tax".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You have so much to worry and think about that it is harder to apply, harder to go about your daily life and harder to find your way, especially if there is bureaucracy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must continue looking into how to make the journey simpler, improving access to helping hands.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many steps have been made earlier, even though we can do more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, Mdm Speaker, for our Pioneer Generation ambassadors, who in many constituencies, have been helping pioneers understand policy better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: May we always innovate and coordinate well at all levels: achieving economic prosperity, supporting a system that is progressive in its progress, and helping all our people to lead a full and happy life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of their 40 cleaners now working for the new company had not only their salaries reset to $1,000, but also all other employment benefits as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also came across many workers during NTUC's employment seminars lamenting why their salaries were not increasing every year or why their employers were not giving them their 13-month bonus.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are many Singaporeans who are working in the low-income sectors who are facing stagnating wages and have resigned to the fact that their situation cannot change.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In some countries, any wages below two-thirds of the median income are considered as low wages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, I would like to call for the Government to set a target for a higher percentage wage increase for workers at the 20th percentile compared to the 50th percentile to reduce the income gap.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would help us have a more objective assessment of the effectiveness of measures taken to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to think out-of-the box and have a concerted effort to create better jobs and improve skills so that these workers can enjoy a higher percentage real wage increase.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, it will create a level playing field for all service providers and service buyers to remain competitive while, at the same time, boost the income for the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, it will send a strong signal for other employers to follow as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement also welcomes this year's Budget to support industry transformation but for this to happen in the clean, green and safe sectors, we need changes in the four "M"s – Man, Machines, Mindset and Methods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This, perhaps, can make any wage increase in these sectors more sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Progressive Wage Model (PWM) is not the only key to help our workers earn better pay through higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond PWM, SkillsFuture also promises a hope for a better future for our workers – the Man.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, SkillsFuture outreach efforts towards low-wage workers must be customised and targeted to suit the profile of low-wage workers who are mainly matured with limited education.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an area that the Government can work on with its tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, the respective sectors need to ensure there are current jobs to match the higher skills the workers have acquired through SkillsFuture training where workers must be comfortable in using technology.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can be achieved through job redesign in the clean, green and safe sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Increasingly, more service providers would like to adopt greater technology to reduce manpower requirement and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their workers are also being trained to operate this equipment, but service buyers must be receptive to different ways of service providers delivering their service using technology.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A change in mindset is required to ensure productivity can be achieved in a more sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Earlier, I suggested job redesign to match SkillsFuture training to enhance productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For this to happen, service buyers must have a cooperative mindset to work more closely with the service providers during the procurement process to explore different possibilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This involves giving service providers more time to suggest a solution to meet service buyers' needs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an area which I feel that the Government Ministries and statutory boards can lead by example to create success stories for others to adopt.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A mindset change is also required amongst service buyers in buying services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They need to have a performance-based mindset by doing more to adopt performance-based contracts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite best sourcing efforts, many contracts continue to be headcount based, and, hence, there is little incentive for service providers to explore other means of improving productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, headcount-based contracts will be very expensive and unproductive, given that labour supply will be tighter in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For industry transformation to happen, it also requires an accompanying change in methods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The latest manpower report has highlighted clearly that labour supply will continue to be tight.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on the old method, unless there is a change in the method, there might not be enough people to be deployed to provide the services required.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Concerted efforts must be made to explore the potential of aggregating demand for services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are also other methods that could be explored to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also want to make a call for procurement processes to be more worker centric.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Being more worker-centric in procuring services means that service buyers need to pay more attention to or specify the employment benefits to be accorded to the outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would help the workers have better wages and benefits and would definitely motivate them to be more productive at work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure if the statutory boards, as I said earlier, had a worker-centric mindset, the workers would have enjoyed the current higher salaries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This also ensures that outsourced workers do not always find themselves as the disadvantaged lot every two to three years when their salaries get reset again.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may be the next breakthrough in our policies for the outsourced sectors to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next aspect of "method" we have to tackle, Mdm Speaker, is the issue of unfair contracts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ultimately, such contracts will impact the workers as the service providers will find ways to cut corners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It could also be challenging for service providers to embark on productivity efforts given that their operating margins are very low.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless a variation in contract price is allowed, it is usually the low-wage workers that will suffer from stagnating wages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have written a blog on this and I am happy to note that MOF will play its part to encourage fair contract clauses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, with the Government taking the lead to promote reasonable and fair contracts, it would play an instrumental role to shape the behaviour and practices in procuring outsourced services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If stakeholders in the industry can change their "mindset" and '"methods", the transformation needed for "man" and "machines" would follow as a consequence.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers, through SkillsFuture, can now be better trained to leverage on technology, making investments in training and machines less risky and with greater promise for higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in order to enjoy better pay, Malay workers, particularly those in the lower income group, should focus their efforts to upskill themselves through Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) training.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Malay workers who are working in the outsourced sectors, such as cleaning, security and landscape, can receive better pay based on the skills that they obtain after undergoing the WSQ courses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will help workers to obtain better wages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, in conclusion, I believe that unless we take bolder steps to negotiate the glaring disparities between our low-wage workers and the majority of the Singaporean workforce in matters like wages and employment benefits, low-wage workers will continue to feel marginalised and the income gap will continue to widen.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a nation, the onus is on us to ensure that when they look ahead, they see beyond the status quo.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They should see positive change for themselves, their jobs and, more importantly, their families.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that Mdm Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like past Budgets, it is one where we get some disappointed sighs from those who do not stand to benefit while others heaved a sigh of relief as the much-needed safety support is provided.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Minister Heng noted that, in 2016, there are cyclical headwinds and challenges that exist, but there are also opportunities if we adapt and grow in preparation to capture those future opportunities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With this context, we clearly understand there cannot be generous packages annually.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the years ahead, we will inevitably encounter some years similar to 2016 where economic outlook is not at its best and yet we need the tenacity to weather the storm together as a nation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Central to this is the question, "How can we find a balance between state support and involvement of community to enhance our social safety net?" As Singaporeans, we share a common wish deep in our hearts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We want Singapore to reach SG100 and beyond for many generations to come and in a much better position than today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is apparent that to provide for such rising needs, we may reach a stage where there is an over-dependence on the Government for social programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To sustain an appropriate level of state support for social programmes, more revenue streams must be created, and this may increase the burden on our future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Being aware of what the potential outcome may be, it is prudent for us to take the necessary steps today to avert such an outcome.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe we can do so by defining our new chapter together and creating options to strike a right balance between state support and partnerships with the community at large.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To begin, we must recognise that a social safety net must be present for some groups of individuals and those with lower likelihood of being able to be self-sufficient without external assistance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Typically, some of these groups are our seniors, the lower-income workers, people with disabilities (PwDs) and our younger families.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let us take a closer look at each challenge and what could be done to address it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First is the complexity of the public support system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: An example is the support for our seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It was good that PGP covers all seniors who were 65 and above at the point of policy implementation regardless of their household income.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Post-PGP, MediShield Life was introduced, and it provides further protection for those who do not have insurance coverage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Herein is a possibility of the successive generation of seniors not being able to support themselves at an earlier age, if income disparity and social support are not properly managed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This brings about the urgency for us to review and begin engaging them while they are still active income earners.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we begin charting the directions for the future, I feel that we need to take strategic and proactive approaches rather than time-based subventions specific for each generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And second is increasing funding and cross-subsidisation from public.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To reduce the burden on subsequent generations, we must begin the planning right now and choosing the right paths for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the same note of strategic and proactive approach, below are some suggestions of how we can involve our future seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, there is a need for earlier community involvement and collaboration with today's middle-aged group as they plan for both their family and retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, the people involved have to be aware and prepared with passive income and financial planning for old age beyond today's primary twin pillars – their property and CPF.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, options have to be made available for them to balance the level of dependence and financial support on their family, bearing in mind the smaller family units and increasing trend of singles over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These approaches, if taken in tandem, could be alternatives or will at least maintain cross-subsidisation at reasonable amounts or levels.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, groups that do not qualify for any state support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For this group, I feel that some of their needs can be looked into through funding at different aspects instead of direct subsidies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One of the options is to supplement it by fostering care in our society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In doing so, we can broaden the support base for some groups that fall outside public support due to their household income or property value.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Knowing that state support will always be required, how then do we partner and involve the community at large to enhance our social safety net?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a country, we need to ensure fostering care in society becomes an ingrained culture and paying it forward is a social value that Singaporeans are associated with.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, partnerships also require willing parties to step forward and the willingness to smoothen the creases together along the journey.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some of the schemes that are encouraged include corporate social responsibility (CSR) as well as promoting the scale-up of ground activities and community networks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To take the Budget's focus on partnerships a step further, I propose some areas for future considerations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, introduce the social culture and inculcate values at a young age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, some schools do conduct projects under the Community Engagement Programmes (CEP).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, there is a lack of emphasis on values learnt from these projects.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe that these projects should go hand-in-hand with training and such emphasis begins from home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Parents should be given opportunities to be a part of the CEP experience with their children and not be restricted to giving back only through CSR organised events.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Family role models and precious time spent as a family would be more effective benefits emerging from such programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, there is a growing trend of self-organised groups for different causes that benefits the society at large.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We applaud these efforts and should assist them in scaling up.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It would be helpful to have platforms made available where the different self-organised groups can leverage resources, shorten their learning curve and enable volunteers to extend their contribution to other new areas which may interest them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, many groups on the ground who receive help from community networks today are not registered or belong to any IPCs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This does not mean that corporations who are willing to support community networks cannot do so.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, I advocate that IPCs and VWOs extend their support and work closely with local communities in conjunction with these corporations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, social enterprises that assist in similar ways should be given consideration and concession under the framework.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This way, more individuals and vulnerable families can benefit from the system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With close community involvement, tangible benefits can be achieved and more individuals with varying circumstances may also receive assistance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Unless we begin planning early, the right balance between state support and community involvement will not emerge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To ensure that social support will be sustainable, it needs like a balloon to have more than one party adding their lung capacity to keep it afloat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Budget, to me, is more than the announcements of basic subsidies and handouts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should view it over a longer horizon and chart directions for Singapore both socially and economically.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, there is urgency for us to act in the interest of our future generations and prevent any undesirable outcome.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving forward, I hope the Government and the public can jointly view subsidies and funding support packages or programmes more holistically and taking longer term perspectives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This way, we can continue our prudent spending approach with an aim to improve wealth distribution throughout our society and funding timely investments for the subsequent generations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Budget 2016 is a new chapter for this term of Government and one that provides for Singaporeans for our current needs, and also prepares us for the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through my conversations with residents and many ordinary Singaporeans, many have serious concerns that their future is uncertain and they have question marks looming over several aspects of their future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chief among these concerns is whether they can retire comfortably.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many young Singaporeans today are already looking ahead and have set expectations of their expected lifestyles in years to come, which also raises the issue of whether they see their future beyond their working lifetime, whether it is here in Singapore or somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To give Singaporeans a sense of security about the future, we need to stabilise their future expectations for them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have built mechanisms such as the CPF.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But unlike ordinary savings, its use is rigid and does not do enough to provide stability amidst uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reality is that most Singaporeans use a large part of their CPF for housing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When needed, most of their supposed savings are hard to access and of limited use.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If they need to monetise their assets, these days, downgrading does not provide much benefit because the gains are also limited.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a start, to provide stability in an uncertain future, the CPF itself must be certain.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To the ordinary Singaporean, the goal posts have been shifting and that has created this uncertainty and insecurity among Singaporeans about their future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That has to be a clear definitive and firm end point that all Singaporeans can agree on and work towards.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There has been a lot of recent progress with MediShield Life – a scheme I personally believe provides many benefits to citizens.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these changes have not done enough to provide the assurance of a secure retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even the standard integrated shield plans announced recently cannot guarantee that the premiums will remain at a fixed price after two years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, many are worried about premium hikes in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we need to monitor all our schemes collectively, because each is often governed by individual agencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If most of our schemes are means-tested the same way, then there is a possibility that our policies could end up skewed too much for the lower-income, with little going in the way to help the middle-income groups.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is the sentiment on the ground, and it may be time for the Ministry of Finance (MOF) to study the impact of our schemes holistically.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of my older residents have asked the Government to move away from using household types as a cut-off because it is no longer reflective of income and wealth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, a 5-room flat in Choa Chu Kang today sells for about $450,000 to $488,000, compared to a 3-room flat selling at $550,000 in Upper Cross Street or a 4-room flat selling at $900,000 at the Pinnacle.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, I met Mr Ho, a resident in Choa Chu Kang, who has lived in his 5-room flat for the last 18 years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He had purchased the flat together with his son 18 years ago at $190,000.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That was what he could afford then, and it reflected the wages he had accumulated over his working life.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It does not mean that because the flat is worth $450,000 today, he is rich.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For him, not much can be monetised from his joint-asset because his son and his family still need a home.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Downgrading to a 4-room or 3-room flat will not be practical for him because he has himself, his spouse, together with his son's family and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In all likelihood, Mr Ho needs to find another flat if they downgrade and the total costs could be more than $450,000.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, is it worth it to make that shift?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Ho explained he had purchased a 5-room flat with his son because they wanted to live together in a multi-generational setting.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And I agree with him when he says that this disincentivises seniors who want to live with their children, because they will always lose out on Government benefits and rebates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The use of the lifetime CPF savings approach as an indicator of the Silver Support Scheme was indeed innovative and I was hopeful that it would serve to help many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the variable criteria for each scheme, how many Singaporeans actually do know what they are getting from Budget 2016 and all our Government policies?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, it is important that the Government provides clarity to every citizen on the benefits that they receive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If they have visibility today, it will also help them plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At that point in time, it may also be useful, given their current state of CPF, CPF LIFE, Medisave and MediShield Life, and so forth, whether they are adequately covered for their future, compared to others of similar profile or certain pre-defined retirement benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not a new idea in the sense that it is similar to the annual consolidated statement of accounts that banks, utilities or telecommunication service providers send to their customers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this can be a first step in helping Singaporeans better understand how they are benefiting from the various schemes, so that they can better manage their finances today, and be assured of what they have in place for their future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Finance Minister and the Prime Minister in recent speeches have also spoken about technology developments that can create opportunities for businesses and jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would also mean that work requirements and the environment are likely to change for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I cannot help but think that while our taxi drivers worry about competition from Uber drivers, there is a larger concern ahead, which is the impact of driverless vehicles in the near future.
