speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The trend is already visible, and I think it is just a matter of time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same can be said of many other jobs that would be affected by this digital wave reaching our shores.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also many studies that predict that we are more likely to see some PMET segments lose their relevance due to automation and artificial intelligence, compared to skilled personnel such as engineers, technicians, even plumbers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Job security for Singaporeans cannot be taken for granted and we must be prepared for this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a responsible, far-sighted Government, we must prepare Singaporeans for this possibility, or if you must, eventuality.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will take us years to reinvent our workforce, but it must start today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must get better at re-inventing our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The key to countering unemployment and under-employment is how quickly we can transform our workers to be relevant to a new set of jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The key is not just about training or matching, it is about re-inventing the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For the educated group, we must also start looking at the depth of our skills developments and focus on mastery in areas that are not so easily replaced by artificial intelligence or robots.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   This year's Budget represents a turning point, in terms of not only dealing with current needs, but also in reaffirming the paths that should be taken to preserve our prosperity, both socially and economically.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some may perceive this Budget as one that provides a lot of help to businesses, but the fact remains that a significant investment is made towards the needy, as well other investments in young Singaporeans, for example, the new Outward Bound School (OBS) campus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Looking at the economic challenges now, it is not surprising to see many Singaporeans feeling worried and concerned about, among others, job opportunities and job security, while for businessmen, it is about the challenging business prospects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, if there is something meaningful and important that can be derived from this Budget, it is that it gives hope that despite the dark clouds, there is a ray of hope and a huge opportunity for everyone, provided that we are ready to undergo a transformation, and the Government will always provide support.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although several sectors are affected, there are many other sectors that offer many opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many companies and entrepreneurs have seized this opportunity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the fall in oil prices may have affected the oil and maritime sectors, but it is something positive for the aviation industry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is also the same for industries like the halal food exports, where its global market continues to expand, and should be exploited by our local businessmen.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Technological development has created many business and career opportunities, and hence, our people must be prepared to take advantage of it through a mindset change and by obtaining relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that the foundation built through a culture of lifelong learning for a knowledge economy will help Singaporeans undergo this transformation, supported by industries and the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Infocomm technology (ICT) is one field that is developing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It promises many business opportunities and careers like cyber security, analytics and application development, with high salaries, because it requires a lot of expertise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, apart from ICT, technology is also required in many other careers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, the banking sector uses a lot of technology and needs capable talent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This digital wave is becoming more prevalent and will change how we work in many sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, the Malay community must be ready for this change.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the way we shop or hail a taxi has also changed in this digital era through applications like Uber.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that the Government can help by showing us the way and direction that will help the community to tread potential pathways, as well as motivate our youths in terms of giving career guidance, academic counselling and the training that is required.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It should be done using better approaches and giving better information.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Madam, just as our forefathers rallied together for a common cause and vision to build Singapore into a developed economy over 50 years, we will need our current and future generations of Singaporeans to also find meaning in doing the same for our Singapore tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For that to happen, they will have to continue to see their future in Singapore so that they can build it to be the home that they want it to be.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They must feel that the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow is attainable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That the rainbow is real and is not a mirage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every Budget is a balancing act, striking a balance between generosity and prudence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But this year's Budget has to balance another set of factors – helping Singaporean firms and families weather the economic storms ahead, while setting our long-term course for the right direction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is definitely not an easy thing to do and I thank the Minister for largely accomplishing it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the short term, companies, especially SMEs, will be facing quite a lot of pain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, rental and wages remain high.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides helping with wage credits and loans, is there more that we can do to help our companies weather the storm?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to keep re-looking into the high rental cost issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, very often, I hear feedback because a lot of industrial buildings and shopping malls have been bought by REITS.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of my residents told me that whenever the lease is up for renewal, if they make money, the rental will surely go up and this is one of the main concerns of those who are in businesses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, I have also seen many business owners who have not made any progress in reducing their reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Instead of relooking into their work processes, they ask their Members of Parliament (MPs) to appeal to delay the time they have to send their foreign workers back.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I have a resident who came to see me and he told me, "MP, do you know that foreign workers are like a drug.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The moment you give it to us, it is difficult to wean it off.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You want to take it away from us; it is difficult for us to survive".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure my fellow colleagues also meet similar residents in their Meet-the-People Sessions asking for more help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One of our founding leaders Mr Lim Kim San was a perfect example of this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After World War II, when Singapore's economy was still ravaged by war, he came up with a machine to produce sago pearls cheaply and made his first million.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He did not wait around for the Government to give any research grants or Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) for machinery purchase!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will hurt our economic growth and specifically the wages of locals.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I suspect both Government and businesses will have to work harder on this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To sum up, we need to strike a balance between helping companies and preventing a passive and reliant attitude.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is an old saying, "Give a man fish and you feed him for a day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Teach him to fish and you feed him for a lifetime." In the short term, Singaporean firms might rightly expect some fish from Government to keep their workers fed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But ultimately, the whole country will run out of fish if they do not develop bigger, smarter and faster fishing ships to get better fishes from international waters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That is why I fully support the idea of automation and internationalisation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is not going to be easy but whichever companies embrace these longer-term plans will emerge stronger and survive better in this very competitive business climate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to raise three specific points with regards to the economy: red tape, trade associations and retrenchment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am delighted to see the Government provide a business grants portal so that companies can apply for grants easily.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the portal, Government can also look into harmonising the different types of grants and simplifying rules, so that companies do not have to resort to consultants just to navigate the grants, and have their grants creamed off by these middle-men.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Over the last few months, I have met quite a lot of my residents who come to my Meet-the-People-Sessions for help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And why did they come to seek help?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Actually, they were approached by consultants, or, for some, they appoint the consultant and the consultant promised them that there is some money to get from Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the end, when their PIC application was not successful, you know what the consultant did?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ask them to go and see their MP.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I am sure companies, especially SMEs, will need a lot of help as automation is much more complicated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope SPRING Singapore can play the role of facilitators or consultants, without creaming off their grants of course.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Civil servants, trade associations and businesses should have more trust in each other and have common vision of transforming our businesses, with more automation and bringing our businesses to the world stage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   This year's Budget is to help local businesses especially SMEs to transform and adapt to the new economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However the economic outlook in the next few years is worrying.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can further explore how to help SMEs to overcome the present difficulties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, local businesses should not develop a mindset of relying on the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They should be like our pioneer entrepreneurs who were self-reliant and made breakthroughs without the help from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore companies now cannot be "kiasu" or "kiasi".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I applaud the Government for simplifying the application process for grants and subsidies as well as strengthening the cooperation with trade associations to help more SMEs increase their efficiency.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the Government should encourage trade associations to organise more overseas study trips to look for new ideas and opportunities, helping our companies to go overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay):   I would now like to highlight the issue of retrenchment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With this deferment, we should ensure that Singaporeans do not lose their jobs, so please do not allow our people to be retrenched, like what happened recently, or more may lose their jobs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to urge the Government to ensure that companies give priority to Singaporeans and not sacrifice them in order to save foreign workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This includes reducing those who earn higher income, while retaining those with lower salaries to fulfil the quota.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that the Government can provide comprehensive assistance to retrenched workers, assistance from the point of training until they gain employment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, the other major thrust of this Budget is families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the Government for not overlooking the plight of the needy in our midst and of young couples who are starting families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The CDA First Step Grant, KidSTART and Fresh Start Housing Scheme will greatly help needy families with young children to ensure no child is left behind as our nation progresses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge more people to complement this effort by volunteering their time and expertise, to befriend and encourage such families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   After the announcement of the Budget Statement, I went to the coffee shop on Sunday as usual to have breakfast and chat with my residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One resident pulled me aside and said to me, "MP, I have something to tell you.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Before, I worked very hard to be able to afford this flat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, I am retired and have no income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why does the Government not give me any money?" After a while, another resident came to tell me, "MP, I live in a HDB flat, but it is an Executive Apartment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I pinched and scraped in order to buy this flat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now I have retired and have no income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why does the Government not give me money?" Again, after a while, another resident came to me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She said she has a friend who lives in a bungalow.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Her friend worked two jobs to buy this bungalow, which is rather run-down, not the modern type.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, he has no job, no income, why is it that the Government does not give him any money?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What they are referring to is the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What worries me is that none of these residents mentioned whether their children gave them money or not.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Traditionally, we have the responsibility to maintain our parents – so-called "raised children to provide for old age".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will not delegate the responsibility of looking after our parents to the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The purpose of this Scheme is to help those at the lowest 20% to 30% income percentile.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If everyone asks for the Government for subsidies, then Government will not be able to help those who are truly needy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this "He has, why I do not have?" mindset will not become a characteristic of Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, another change that I have heard a lot at the ground is the capping of tax reliefs, which will primarily affect high-income mothers with two or more children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She has three children and was considering a fourth, but with this change, she no longer feels the same incentive and support from the Government to do so.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The cap appears to contradict the Government's effort to encourage procreation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, may I know what has changed to prompt this change in policy?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And talking about procreation, based on the feedback from my young residents who are young parents, I doubt that all these financial incentives are going to give you the desired outcome.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the young parents told me that they are discouraged to give birth to more children by the increasing costs of childcare and increasing costs of milk powder.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I asked them, "Under what circumstances will you give more children?" They told me, "You give my children free education from childcare all the way to University.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You subsidise the milk powder." Many do not want to commit resources, both time and money, to the next generation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With trust and unity, we can surely weather the storms ahead, and chart a new course towards broader and brighter horizons.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.11 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will first start with the Budget proposal to enhance the Revitalisation of Shops (ROS) scheme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In November 2007, the Government introduced the ROS to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of HDB shops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also stated that this covers over 50% of our town and neighbourhood centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The scheme covers upgrading of common areas, promotional activities and rent-free periods for tenants to renovate their shops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Assuming the effective period of expenditure was from 2008 to 2014, this amounts to an average of $1.2 million per year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Minister can share with the House some details about how the ROS scheme has improved the businesses of HDB shops in the past nine years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It could be due to their relative poor location compared to shops in a different location in the same estate, or it could even be due to oversupply of shop spaces in the same estate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For such shops, I hope the Minister can look into how the ROS can better assist them, or to consider how parts of the town centre where these shops are located could be redeveloped.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we provide assistance to our existing HDB shops, let us also not forget about building adequate new shops in our newer HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents of then-newly built HDB estates like Sengkang and Punggol experienced a lack of basic amenities and shops when they first moved in.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The design of most of the void decks was also not conducive for constructing shops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One reason for this is the philosophy of building amenities like convenience shops and coffeeshops only when there is a critical mass demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I feel that this philosophy should be tweaked to build amenities ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is so that pioneering residents are not deprived of amenities when they move in.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You may ask how can businesses thrive when demand has not reached critical mass.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is where the Government can step in to provide reduced rents until critical mass is reached.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another way we can improve new HDB estates is to build town centres consisting of low-rise HDB shop houses to a competitive retail mix to meet the wider needs of residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that in recent years, the approach has been to build a shopping mall that acts as an integrated hub for the estate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, in my view, a town centre like the ones in mature estates, such as Bedok and Tampines, are better suited to meet the needs of residents and to create a sense of community and identity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A shopping mall can still be built but only as a complement to the town centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A shopping mall must not compromise the businesses of the retail shops in the town centre but complement and enhance the business in the neighbourhood shops by helping to draw people to the town centre and making the town centre a lively place where residents of the town and even residents of nearby estates will want to visit and spend their time, thereby bringing business and vibrancy to the town.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad to note that the URA Masterplan states that the Bidadari Estate will have a wide range of amenities like a bus interchange, neighbourhood police centre, places of worship and healthcare facilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I certainly hope that amenities, such as mini-marts, provision shops, convenience shops, and coffee shops can be built ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also hope that town centres with low-rise HDB shop houses can be incorporated in the plans for not just new HDB estates like Bidadari but also other new estates as well as when older estates are redeveloped.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will end this part of my speech with an anecdote.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hawker centres at different parts of Bedok, such as Block 85, Bedok North at Fengshan Single Member Constituency (SMC) and Block 511, Bedok North at Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), see many customers who are from relatively new estates like Punggol or Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spoken to quite a few of these customers during my visits to these markets over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One common reason given is the lack of good dining places in Punggol or Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How often do you actually see people from Bedok going to Punggol or Sengkang to have dinner?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be various reasons for this but certainly, in my view, poor town planning is one of the reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, from this year's Budget, it is evident that companies are facing difficulties and uncertainties in the business environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although the Government has announced measures to benefit employers and employees, for Singaporeans who are already unemployed or are facing impending unemployment, their difficulties warrant even more help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially so when the unemployed is the main breadwinner of the family.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides supporting their own family, they may also need to service their housing loan and look after their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means that we are unable to utilise our human resources effectively to fully develop our economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, our employment statistics does not reflect this underemployment situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not know which category these "underemployed" people fall under in our employment statistics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also do not know whether our published employment statistics reflect this situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Underemployment will cause under-utilisation of the working population's productive capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question is, how do we prevent this from happening?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, how do we fully utilise the working population's productive capacity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, these measures are primarily targeted at existing workers or workers undergoing training for career conversion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It not only requires the cooperation between employers and employees, but also takes some time before the effect kicks in.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For unemployed or retrenched workers, in the absence of a stable income, their entire family's financial situation may be adversely affected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may alleviate any financial difficulty and lighten his financial burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): I would like to spend the final part of my speech on what the Budget has provided for our children and young people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is found in section C of the Budget which is entitled "Building a Caring and Resilient Society".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under this section, there are various sub-headers, including "Caring for our young".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a departure from the previous practice of dollar for dollar matching which placed lower income families at a distinct disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that my Workers' Party (WP) colleagues have spoken up on this in the previous Parliament and indeed other Singaporeans too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new CDA grant with its $3,000 is certainly a good first step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think this would be good because we should not focus on the parents, but the welfare and benefit of their Singaporean children and the value they will bring to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, under the section "Caring for our young", there is also the sub-heading "Building Resilience in our Youth".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is stated that the new OBS will be built to help our young people develop a sense of adventure, resilience and be ready to challenge themselves to be their best.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that the new OBS will be able to provide many opportunities for our young people to enhance their sense of adventure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A one-off participation in the OBS programme alone may not be enough to build resilience or a sense of adventure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are other activities that our young people can be encouraged to participate to build resilience or nurture a sense of adventure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we can encourage our young people to join co-curricular activities (CCAs) like certain uniformed groups, sports or outdoor activities clubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Spending six years in the National Cadet Corps (Sea) opened my eyes to adventure and teamwork.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I struggled when I had to canoe round Singapore in three days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I could not disappoint my buddy in the same canoe and, together with our friends in other canoes, we learnt to cheer and encourage each other and finished as one big team.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Resilience training involved much more than a round-island Singapore canoe expedition or a one-off OBS programme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to re-look at the way we educate our children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not be happy with an education system that encourages our children to succeed by being "exams smart" alone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The system should encourage more of our young people to explore different "adventures", for example, taking time off studies or work to excel in sports or hobbies, like some of our national athletes; o	r even taking time off to see the world and broaden your horizon, like what many young people in Europe do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And our young people should not fear losing out by graduating later or starting work later.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have had Singaporeans who took time off to climb mountains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also have to find a way to teach our children not to be afraid of failure but to learn to cope with failure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must be latitude in the education system to allow this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our children are afraid to fail, they are less likely to be adventurous.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are also less likely to appreciate innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can forget about Singapore having the next Sim Wong Hoo, not to mention Steve Jobs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a schoolboy with questionable motor skills, I was not very good at sports like rugby or football.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather fortuitously, I discovered the joy of distance running, and never stopped running since.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What has running got to do with resilience or fortitude?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You can run many miles to prepare for a marathon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like marathon runners, all of us have our own race in life to run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Finance Minister spoke about "spending more and spending right".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are fortunate that we are able to spend more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What is just as important is that we are committed to spending right.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Right, because this Budget upholds the fundamentals that have made Singapore special.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget embodies the principles that make us special.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It continues the work to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It strengthens the fabric of our multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It invests in our people, so that everyone has the best chance to do well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It delivers on our promise to our people that we will be able to take care of those who have less.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That we will help those who fall behind get back up on their feet.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That we will give our children a better future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That we will help our seniors age with dignity, assured of proper healthcare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I would first talk about how our Industry Transformation Program helps our economy today, and builds our economy of the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I will talk about how our Budget helps Singaporeans through restructuring, and the slowing economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Last, I will share about how our community programmes build shared experiences among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most SMEs I spoke to are very supportive of the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most SMEs acknowledge that increasing productivity and restructuring are critical and urgent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But to make further progress, they face three challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, they are too small to implement major productivity efforts within their own companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, our SMEs generally find it difficult to understand and tap onto the many Government incentives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, our Government can do more to improve on internal Government processes, to benefit our companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, the Industry Transformation Programme is a strong start to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, the programme strengthens our trade associations and chambers as the voice of their industries, so that they can best represent diverse views, and be strong partners to the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the business grant portal improves SMEs' access to Government assistance, so that SMEs can focus on getting the help they need, rather than on figuring out who to get help from.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the National Trade Platform helps our trade sector cut through unnecessary red tape.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is an excellent example of how the Government can actively spark productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It addresses many of the concerns of high-technology start-ups, some of which I raised during the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because when it comes to innovation, what matters is not just the ideas but the circulation and popularisation of the ideas as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It creates an innovative sandbox to test-bed and integrate technologies in areas where Singapore can boldly invent the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And some people I talked to are excited to see that we are using robotics not just to build our economy but also to improve Singaporeans' lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What more can we do to improve the transformation programme?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I want to touch on four ideas, and I hope they can be considered.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, I hope SG Innovation can work hand-in-glove with the JID, so that the ideas born in the former have a fair chance to be realised in the latter.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As Singapore invents the future in areas of urban planning, digital health, smart nations, and advanced manufacturing, we can and we must bring our startups along on this journey.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But once we achieve a few quick wins, I hope we can extend to more sectors, even to those without strong trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Given how critical and urgent our restructuring efforts are, the Government must come in and provide strong leadership.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the National Trade Platform is a step in the right direction for the Government to drive productivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As we come up with the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) for different sectors, we should pinpoint the inefficiencies and come up with solutions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What matters is not whether the inefficiency comes from the industry or from the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What matters is that the Government and industry come together to solve these inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As someone familiar with both business and economic development, it is clear to me that the Industry Transformation Programme is groundbreaking.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is ground-breaking because we are realigning and networking ourselves in an unprecedented way to support our economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In this new way forward, our economic agencies will have to work much closer with our non-economic Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our research sector will have to work much closer with our companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our Government will have to work much closer with our industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, the civil service will also develop a deeper knowledge in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Over time, the knowledge gained can help us best evolve Government regulations and programmes in safety and health, manpower and labour, education and SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This could go far to address concerns from the businesses about excessive regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But all these efforts will not be easy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the Industry Transformation Programme is the difficult way forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But it is also the right way forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must be prepared to give the programme ample time to take effect, and for us to get the formula right.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must be prepared for both success and failure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Yesterday and today, in this Chamber, we heard several ideas on how we must measure how we spend on our economy carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I believe we have to strike a good balance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The risk of over-measurement in the name of accountability is that we will move too slowly and too cautiously.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Especially for the future economy, we must move decisively but be prepared to make quick adjustments when circumstances change or when better methods emerge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with the Finance Minister's view that there is no "rulebook" for us at this stage of development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to add: "time is short; let us get to work".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Another reason why I support this Budget is because it helps Singaporeans through restructuring, and the slowing economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It does so in at least four ways.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many enterprising business leaders I have met understand the importance of skills.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our SkillsFuture movement, coupled with industry collaborations such as TechSkills Accelerators, is closely watched by many, and they have high hopes for it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I hope that more of our companies will hire based on skills, especially workers being re-skilled.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Taking re-skilled workers on board makes good business sense because companies get to hire employees who are committed to success, committed to staying relevant and committed to change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In this slowdown, the rise in most types of workers' levies is tough for businesses to bear, but it helps level the playing field for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It reinforces the message that Singaporeans must form the core of our workforce and our economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having smaller Government construction projects means giving Singaporean main contractors, many of whom are of mid-size and doing private sector work, a fighting chance to win much-needed Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The effect will be felt all the way down to numerous Singaporean sub-contractors and Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is a cost-effective way to pump-prime our economy and to help Singaporeans at the same time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have raised this idea several times during consultation sessions, and I am very heartened to know that the Government is acting immediately on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The sum total of our 2016 Budget policies related to the Singaporean worker is that even as we restructure, even as sectors and companies rise and fall, the Government will make sure that Singaporeans are looked after.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Last of all, I concur with the Government's effort to build shared experiences among Singaporeans: by getting every Singaporean youth to go through Outward Bound School; by getting more people to visit the National Gallery; by encouraging Singaporeans to come together and adopt ground-up initiatives under the Our SG fund; and by encouraging companies to get their employees to do more for our society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: All these will deepen our people's sense of identity and strengthen our unity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget will help us write the next chapter together.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I commend Mr Heng for a good Budget in his first Budget Statement as the Finance Minister.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst it is a prudent Budget, it is a well thought-out one to assist companies to ride out the present challenges and it is a caring one on social spending for the groups that need the most help; the low-wage workers, people with disabilities, the young and the seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I also like the focus this Budget sets out on the way forward to strengthen Singapore's future economy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This global downturn and its possible effect on Singapore's economy in the coming year are constantly on the minds of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many hear, read and follow the global economic updates from the mainstream media or internet whilst others actually experience the market sentiments, the retrenchment of colleagues, neighbours and friends.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Although Minister Heng said that "we must not let pessimism take hold, lest it creates self-fulfilling expectations", I am of the opinion that we cannot not discuss it.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is better to address people's worries where possible and offer solutions to allay concern.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore is one of the world's most open economies and, therefore, can be very adversely affected in any global downturns.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: According to economists then, this portends the real possibility of an impending recession.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Sadly, there is no reprieve in sight due to continuing weak global demand.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Economists are saying that the global risks are mounting.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: China is restructuring its economy from export-led to consumer-led and is projecting slower growth of 6.5% to 7% this year, signalling a continued contraction in the world's Number Two economy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: China's economic slow-down affects many countries, especially Singapore, as China is Singapore's largest trading partner.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The economic outlook in the US remains uncertain.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The rise in US Federal Reserve rates could result in foreign capital outflows from Asia to the US and put downward pressure on the dollar exchange rate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: US companies, much like Chinese companies, are shelving imports.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore's export to the US accounts for almost 8% of our GDP.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As it has been said before, "Whenever the US jumps on the global trampoline, Singapore gets a bump".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The downside risks are clearly more pronounced now.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat said, "I am aware that current business conditions are difficult and uncertain.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of our firms are facing weaker top-line growth, rising manpower costs and tighter financing.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers are anxious as retrenchment has increased, including professionals." May I ask the Minister for Finance whether our Government should start looking at policies to mitigate retrenchment?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Budget feedback exercise conducted by REACH showed (a) worries of an economic downturn, (b) concerns over job security and (c) support for families, as the top three concerns of the participants.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, I would like to touch on the following two topics in addressing the concerns mentioned: one, that are the relevant measures to better protect Singaporeans from redundancy?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: And two, coping with challenges and seizing opportunities?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: So, what are the relevant measures to better protect Singaporeans from redundancy?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans need some assurances that the Government is in control of the global economic downturn and the knock-on effects it has on job stability locally.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a possibility that this economic slowdown may be a slow drift with increasing numbers of redundancies that saps the economic vitality of this country.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, keeping labour force participation high would be one of the means of supporting GDP growth.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In this context, I would like to suggest that we adopt a Singaporean-centric policy to expand job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government can take the lead in the expansion of job scope availability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many areas in almost all Government ministries that are in need of expansion.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, we can look at the expansion of IT professionals in the MOF and many other Ministries, the establishment of stepdown care with more homecare providers in MOH or the recruitment of more early-childhood professionals and the social workers for MSF and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is an opportune time for the Government to earnestly support the various Ministries to expand.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This can help us absorb the excess workers or retrenched workers; but more importantly, this will enable certain departments of various Ministries to thoroughly improve on what was previously not possible due to the shortage of manpower.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The resultant effect will be that people are in employment and the Government Ministries are improved.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Would our Government also consider facilitating the growth of part-time work arrangements?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: If more companies can take this option, we can achieve a dual objective of reducing redundancies, and also of establishing future part-time work option norms.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This latter objective is worthy of consideration because there is a value-add if there is an increased participation of part-time workers in the workforce down the road.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Availability of part-time work will enable those who want to have family work-life balance to continue working as without which, they might have opted otherwise.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government Ministries can perhaps take the lead in establishing such work options in the public sector.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Now may be a good time to take this step as previously, it might not have been possible due to the shortage of manpower.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This Jobs Credit Scheme was implemented for one year and was announced in Budget 2009.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This way, we can ascertain that the assistance is given directly to Singaporeans whom we want to safeguard from retrenchment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We can therefore hope to achieve an upgraded and more productive workforce from this exercise.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is in line with the focus on the "short-term patch and the medium-term opportunity" of Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Middle-aged PMETs are finding it hard to find re-employment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As we approach the one-year mark, it may be useful to do a stock take and gather feedback to see if the measures need to be tweaked in any way to increase the employability of PMETs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The worst affected group of people in any retrenchment would be those in the lower-income bracket.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This group usually lives from hand to mouth and does not have any savings due to their meagre incomes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, any redundancy will put their subsequent daily livelihood in severe jeopardy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Although they are eligible for ComCare, there is a need to empathise more with them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, we can assist and handhold them for skills upgrading courses and better job placements.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a need to sustain them financially while they are having upgrading courses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope our Government can subsidise them on their dependents' needs before they get to be re-employed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is the era of the Internet economy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Information Technology (IT) has transformed the business world.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: IT is here to stay and is developing very fast indeed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Now is the time to ensure that our workforce stays relevant and competitive by being more IT-savvy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, we should take this opportunity now to upgrade more, if not all, of our workforce IT-knowledge and skills to a higher level.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This should apply to even the low-skilled workers in their own capacities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: IT has dramatically accelerated the processes of new business-world creations.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, people spend an increasing percentage of their time in the virtual world in their day-to-day living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: And this has made IT very relevant to the business world where customised information on products and services can be easily accessed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, companies cannot even survive and compete without it.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need increasing numbers of infocomm professionals to address the present shortage in this area.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Equipping our workforce with higher levels of information and communications skills for medium-term opportunities is vital and is the way forward.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Recent surveys have shown that optimism about the economy has fallen right across the board.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many companies have indicated that their immediate focus is to defend their positions at home, making a change from 2015 when the top goal was to enter new markets.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These companies will spend and invest to remain competitive with other companies.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be useful for our Government to design innovative schemes that can encourage companies to upgrade their workers' knowledge of IT.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The intention is to facilitate our firms to keep their workers, packaged with improving their skills especially in IT, for a longer-term economic goal.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not sure, as I do not have the details yet, of the newly announced "Adapt and Grow Initiative" measures and whether this initiative adequately addresses the intentions mentioned.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will also be ideal to have incentive schemes in place, for those who are retrenched, to pick up IT knowledge or to switch to IT jobs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We may need more coaches and staff to persuade and to facilitate them to learn new IT skills and job-matching and placements.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I end by saying that I am in agreement with Mr Heng Swee Keat that we must have the courage to try new ways – think long term, dare to try and be open to change so that we will move in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to commend the Finance Minister for delivering a Budget that is progressive yet balanced, with specific focus on certain key groups, organisations and individuals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a clear sign that the Government is aiming to stay ahead of the curve by recognising that the next technological transformation of our economy is already taking place and will inexorably continue.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also clear that our Government would like our SMEs to be at the heart of this economic development and transformation, with various financing and tax incentive support provided to our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The focus of my speech today will thus be on how our Budget aims to set the foundation towards building a caring and resilient Singaporean society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I was younger, tree-top adventures meant you went out with some friends and you climbed trees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, apparently, you have to pay a fee, put on a safety harness, get your helmet on and attach your pulley to a safety line to ensure you have this tree-top adventure.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My five-year-old daughter took to the course four times and had to be stopped from going on for a fifth time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But my eight-year-old son found certain parts of the course rather challenging, struggled at points and, at one point, even froze some 10 to 15 feet above the ground.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through cajoling, through persuasion, through determination, he completed the course, I am happy to say, and came down with a wild look of exhilaration in his eyes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And he said, "Dad, I was scared but I did it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us do it again." This real adventure I had with my children re-emphasised the importance of exploration and experimentation for young children; of situational learning for youth, and the crucial life lessons such as perseverance and resilience are best learnt in experiential settings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident that the brand new Outward Bound campus will be the vital catalyst that will kick-start and accelerate adventure learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak more on this during the COS debate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They only need to qualify for the scheme to get this payout.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, there might be those who have made more than $70,000 contribution to their CPF by age 55, but who presently find themselves in a financially challenging position for one reason or another.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The same could also be said for some seniors who might be living in a 5-room flat or larger, that they do not own, but are struggling financially, without much support from anyone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This point was also raised earlier by the hon Member Mr Zaqy Mohamed and I hope that the Ministry can look into this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A final area I would like to speak on, Sir, is the need to provide more support for the emotional wellness of the sandwiched class.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier, my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Azmoon, used this term to refer to the middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am using this term from a family structural perspective to refer to those individuals that have young or adolescent children and are also caring for ageing and chronically ill dependents, such as parents or even their spouse, at the same time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are quite literally sandwiched between their obligations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should the difficulties they face as providers and caregivers be compounded by the fact that they are from a lower-income strata, then we have all the elements of a perfect storm of stress.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the family is receiving Public Assistance and ComCare aid, Mdm Tan is herself under a lot of stress as she finds herself being pulled in many different directions due to her multiple commitments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has done a good job of putting in place social safety nets such as financial assistance schemes and even MediShield Life to keep financial and medical expenses low.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I feel that we need to see how we can assist these individuals to cope with the emotional and psychological burden of being caregivers simultaneously to two groups of dependents, the young and the aged, who have differing caring needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And all these while also dealing with their personal issues and challenges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that social services have been decentralised from the five CDCs to the Social Service Offices (SSOs) that are now located in their various constituencies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Government to consider providing community-based mental wellness centres that offer solutions to stress-related problems or issues related to mild depression for residents who need such services.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I declare my interests as an entrepreneur in the field of social innovation and I also ask the Deputy Speaker's advanced pardon for any lapses into informality.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is the language of the heart for youths, and I speak to them as much as I speak to the hon Members of this very formal House.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, we celebrated our Jubilee in a big way – as we should.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our dramatic jump from third world to first in 50 years is an outsized achievement we will probably never see again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Already, the future in front of us looks nothing like the past we just left behind.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Random terrorism, climate change and all kinds of breakdowns all seem to be part of our new and very scary normal.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, clearly, the year-long party is over and SG51 is in a different emotional space.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One of the ways we could try to cope with all this rapid change is to fantasise about our past.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But nostalgia, while lovely as a sentiment, is pretty lousy as a strategy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The sobering fact we must all accept is that our world is not our father's world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And we have to find our own way forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Life is just going to be more complex.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Success is no longer straightforward, and disruptive change will come for us all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are asking Singaporeans to just accept the call to arms, to step up and take some risks, be productive, internationalise, collaborate and oh! along the way, please care for the needy, get married, have more kids and do not forget to be resilient.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These are all great aspirations, but in the field of social and emotional work I come from, we know this to be true – the greatest barrier that will stand in the way of all these changes we hope to see are going to be fundamentally human.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At the heart of every frustrating roadblock we will face to our technical solutions is actually a cluster of cultural habits – deeply rooted patterns of behaviour, emotions and narrative that can prove surprisingly resistant to change even in the face of overwhelming logical evidence.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Finance Minister has talked about the need to get precise with solving our economic issues by coming up with bespoke roadmaps for the long-term transformation of specific sectors.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My request is that we also get equally serious and precise in the way we resolve the human cultural habits that stand in the way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We should treat it seriously as we would with any other priority economic initiative.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And treat the observations of cultural analysts as seriously as that of our economic analysts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we track specific cultural metrics – critical behaviours or beliefs – we can get early insights that signal to us whether we are on track or just seriously off-course.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Just telling us "X number of businesses were started in Y years" tells us nothing deep about whether genuine innovation or meaningful entrepreneurship is on a healthy rise.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What would yield deeper insight is to also track over the years, qualitative data about the emotions, beliefs and behaviours Singaporeans hold towards risk, failures, possibilities and uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we want to know why productivity does not really happen in Singapore, we should track our behaviours and attitudes towards the creation and sharing of value.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Not the last resort or just one of many resorts; first resort.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: All too often, companies actually severely underestimate how much strategy's effectiveness hinges on cultural alignment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At any top-down strategy that is at odds with ground-up culture is, at best, hamstringed and, at worst, utterly doomed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Almost every enterprise that has gained peak performance – the Four Seasons, Apple, Southwest Airlines – they all got there by prioritising cultural interventions as their best accelerator for change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Successful cultural intervention is about focusing on just a few critical shifts of specific behaviours, deeply linked with the strategic outcomes that we hope for.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It should take the lead in holding discussions with thought leaders in Singapore's entrepreneurial ecosystem to learn what are the beliefs and behaviours we must encourage or discourage in our youths so that by the time they enter the workforce, they are primed with the habits of innovation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Cultural transformation does not reach a tipping point without winning over a small but crucial crop of influential early adopters.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The early adopters bring in the early majority, the early majority brings in the late majority and the late majority brings in everyone else who is still wondering what on earth is going on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is galling to me that at our innovation conferences here, we are still getting keynote speakers from everywhere but Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This just reinforces the perception of our own people as well as outsiders that Singaporeans are just not as capable of innovative thinking as Westerners.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we look hard enough, we will find that we already have pockets of people who are just as cutting-edge in their approach to their public, private and people sector work but are also excellent at communicating their views.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need to take bigger bets on our own people and shore up our confidence in Singapore's ability to do things different.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There are many cultural roadblocks to transformation, but I will focus on the two that I think have the greatest cost on our economy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are our national habits of fear and scarcity thinking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because fear is such a quick and effective emotional lever that galvanises our survival instinct, it has been the favoured motivational tool of many of our parents, teachers, bosses and even politicians.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And managed well, fear is a perfectly healthy kick-in-the-pants we all need to force us out of complacency into action.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fear compels us to man up, save more, study hard and work long.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And fear, in that sense, is an emotion that does help us take care of our future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But fear loses these powerful, positive effects when it goes beyond a temporary emotion that we feel to a permanent disposition we live in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And when the fear becomes part of our emotional and cultural DNA, we lock ourselves into a habit of self-limiting behaviours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And this is why we need to talk about our "kiasu" culture.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It really disturbs me that year after year on those funny National Day surveys, we still rank "kiasu, kiasi" as among the top few defining traits of what makes us Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We laugh about it but it has been 50 years and the joke is on us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How much longer will we self-identify as a people living under siege?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What human potential and opportunities have we lost over the years living as a nation of people scared to lose out and scared to fail?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How much more opportunities are we prepared to lose?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think "kiasu" culture should be celebrated.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I think we should kill it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because all these behaviours that we are telling Singaporeans are necessary to take us into the future – innovation, productivity, collaboration, generosity to the needy – they are wholly dependent on a person's desire and drive to generate greater worth and real value to share with the world. "Kiasu" culture does not give a damn about generating or sharing worth and value.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The "kiasu" person will even pursue things of questionable worth he himself does not believe in, as long as he sees everyone else is doing so.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Nothing illustrates this best than the toxic arms race between "kiasu" parents.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the "kiasu" entrepreneur is driven by the anxiety to make short gains rather than a mindful desire to win at a long game, so he will only take the risks that everyone is already taking and innovate what everyone else is already innovating.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why entrepreneurship here tends to lack originality and is really just a copy-and-paste work of little worth.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday's bubble tea shop is today's hipster coffee joint and cat café.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We have a ridiculous number of entrepreneurs in F&B and way too little in industries like marine and construction, which have far more opportunity, profit and need for new blood willing to go where nobody else wants to go or dares to go.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we embrace uncertainty, what we experience is the emotions of mindful ambition and wonder.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I suspect our highest innovation and productivity will only come when more of us move beyond the fear of "Die lah, die lah!

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What must I do to survive?" to the mindful ambition of "I have no idea what lies ahead, but I am still here and I am still alive.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What things of great worth do I still get to create for somebody else today?" The other habit that costs us plenty is our scarcity mindset.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is most toxic when it dovetails with the "kiasu" culture.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Scarcity mindset is the belief that there is not enough to go around and the giving of any advantage to someone else is stupid because it comes at the cost of our personal survival or happiness.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You see it in the way we push back on whether columbariums have a place in middle-class neighbourhoods or the anger we feel about immigrants – one more foreigner here means one less MRT seat for me.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen it in the way some non-profits work in silo, believing it is every NGO for himself in the fight for the limited pie of state and donor funding.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And now, you can hear it in the outrage amongst some mothers in the 1% when they discovered, "I cannot claim tax relief on income above $80,000 anymore because we want to support greater social spending." In scarcity thinking, there is no "win-win".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is always a high stakes competition of "win-lose" or "lose-lose".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In scarcity, power or profit cannot be shared, even with the very people who help support the position we enjoy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, nobody wins in this destructive zero-sum game of scarcity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we adults push back hard on why our domestic workers should be given their right to their day of rest since it impedes on my day of rest, then how can we expect anyone to do any better?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Should it surprise us if someday we see many in the next generation grow up refusing to take responsibility for our welfare when we become the powerless ones in our old age?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Why should it anger us when our bosses push back hard on why they should be forced to give us our right to more paid paternity leave when it infringes on their right to make more profit?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Rich or poor, employer or employee, local or foreign, powerful or not, we will all bear the cost of our collective scarcity mindset.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yes, the habit of scarcity is an unavoidable product of our context as a small country of limited resources.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And it is true, small countries do not get to be naive about survival and we have little leeway to fool around with our future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But when we keep pushing out the story of how we are the little red dot surrounded by big, bad wolves that want to eat our lunch, we risk reinforcing the zero-sum mentality as the most significant story for Singapore and our best way forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is counterproductive to our push for more open and giving collaboration as the best way forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, in SG51, what I hope is we can start pushing out a new Singapore story founded upon the opposite of scarcity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And no, it is not abundance, because the paradigm of abundance that there is plenty out there and enough to spare for everybody is not always true.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Resources are limited, especially in a small nation and there will always be tough trade-offs which we will all argue over.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, the most honest alternative to scarcity is actually not abundance, but satisfaction.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is the mindset that says, "Whatever we have, it's enough.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we are satisfied, we are far more willing to give something of ourselves, and from that mindset of satisfaction flows the desire to share decisions, information, recognition, profits and yes, the tax burden for social spending.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Only when we are deeply satisfied as a people will we want to subtract some value from ourselves to multiply the value that can be had by all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think it is a beautiful thing for the Government to advocate deeper, respectful partnerships between stakeholders as the best way forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
