text: With the state acting as the guide, it challenges us stakeholders to take our place as the "heroes of the story" instead.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The outreach to trade associations, Our Singapore Fund, Community of Seniors and Business and the IPC Partnership Scheme will hopefully open our eyes to seeing each other as equal partners in a win-win game on the same quest to solve the same pains.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng talked about how we must change our paradigm and view our greying population and disabled as a source of strength that can shape our society rather than a weakness to be managed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I appeal on behalf of our weak and marginalised that in the design of our social policies, we choose to see them not through the lens of a zero-sum game too.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As we execute our policies like SkillsFuture, Fresh Start Housing Scheme and KidSTART, let us use this chance to set up more win-win situations for our working poor.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How different would our interventions be, if we designed them around a vision for our poor, not as a cost to manage but as a partner, a possible source of strength, who can share the same quest to solve the same pains.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our policies must accord our poor the same dignities and assumptions we accord our privileged.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not expect our middle-class families to raise children well in overcrowded conditions, then let us not expect poor families to do any better in overcrowded rental flats co-shared with a stranger.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We know the divisive effects of favouritism in the family.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Well, a country is like a family writ very large.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Let us do away with any form of structural favouritism in the way we treat our rich versus our poor.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the marital status of parents has always been the eligibility criteria for CDAs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, you can imagine, on that single word "all" hangs the hopes of so many single mums as well as the hearts of us married mothers who are rooting for a win for them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope we can clarify whether "all" includes the children of our unwed mums, because single or married, rich or poor, many of us mums share the same heart.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We want to partner the state in the common mission to bring up our children to become all that they can be, and many of us mums stand as one on this – see us all as equal.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know there is an argument about why not just invest in innocent children rather than invest in the bad parents who make bad choices?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But well, then all of us parents in this room stand equally condemned, for we too have made varying levels of bad choices in our lives that messed up our own families.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The difference is that the more social and financial capital we have, the easier it is for us to recover and learn from our stupidity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Wealth buys us second, third, fourth, fifth and sixth chances.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But for many who are poor, bad choices are more difficult to recover from and good choices are not always available or easy to take.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we show our strong support to the uplifting of parents who made poor choices, we teach not just them but their children, and ours too, the power of grace.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That even when we mess up and the consequences must be paid, as long as there are people rooting for us to find our way home, there is a chance for restoration, and that is what sows the ambition for transformation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You do not have to go to a physical prison to be an offender in society.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Not the riches of Reserves, our fancy buildings or our amazing industries.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those are just outcomes, wonderful results we create through choosing again and again to do things as one people and one Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When threats become real, when the money runs thin, we will see conflict.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And we will want to fight, and I pray we do fight.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But let it be a fight for each other and not against.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A fight to work through differences and partner across the divides.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A fight to move out of a spirit of fear and scarcity into a new spirit of ambition and satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, we had a Budget that many people cheered about because we were celebrating SG50.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, there are several things which stand out in this year's Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: First is the Minister's promise on building a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I applaud the Government's continued efforts to look after the different segments of society which need more help.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will enable a bigger group of workers to supplement their income and CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to regularly review the qualifying income ceiling to ensure that those who would really benefit from the WIS are not excluded because they had worked harder during the past year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is the target group of people whom we are trying to help so that they can eventually get out of the poverty circle.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This would help these lower-income workers to cover increases in cost of living as well as ease their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The improvements to WIS, the increases in public assistance and increases to the Singapore allowances, together with other schemes like the GST Voucher scheme, rebates on Service and Conservancy (S&C) charges and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: All these are a strong signal that the Government is very mindful of the needs of the lower income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This Government should continue to render care and assistance to low-wage workers, seniors and those with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Regarding care for our seniors, I strongly support and welcome the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It continues the Government's approach to care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In my constituency, I have several seniors who have worked hard all their lives and are living in either 5-room flats or private properties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have worked hard to purchase their dream home and today, some of them have no income as they are retired and are advanced in age.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If they do qualify for the Silver Support Scheme based on the other two criteria, why should their housing type exclude them from being eligible for the Silver Support Scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They may not have children who are supporting them so the fact that their housing type excludes them from being eligible for the Silver Support Scheme would be of great disadvantage to them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The fact that they live in 5-room flats or private properties does not mean that they are financially able.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of their properties may be very old walk-up apartments which are not easy to sell.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some may have inherited the property and some may have worked hard and lived in their current property all their lives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is it the intent of the Government to push these seniors, at this stage of their lives, to uproot themselves from their neighbours and a familiar environment just to qualify for Government support and for a better quality of life?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am quite sure that it is not the intent of the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What about seniors who are living on the charity of their relatives who are not their children, but staying in private properties?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These seniors would be excluded from the Silver Support Scheme because, their nephews, nieces or their god-children staying in private properties had, of their kind heart, decided to look after them even though they have no obligation to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Should the Government disqualify these seniors from benefitting from the Silver Support Scheme and then place a heavier financial burden on relatives or even friends who are simply being charitable to them?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How about seniors living in nursing homes or old folk homes; what is the address used by the Government to consider whether they qualify for the benefits of the Silver Support Scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, I urge the Government to reconsider using housing type as a criterion in determining whether seniors should qualify for the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Prime Minister had said that the Singapore Story belongs to all of us.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Let us include this small group of seniors who, for one reason or another, live in properties which do not meet the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The second aspect of the Budget which stands out for me is the push towards transformation of the economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I agree that businesses need to take a good hard look at themselves and ask themselves how can they prepare themselves for the future?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How can their businesses grow, bearing in mind, the uncertain economy?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is the Automation Support Package, support for industries to scale-up and encouraging internationalisation, schemes to develop and deploy new technologies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think these are good schemes to help nudge businesses towards being more innovative and to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One challenge is how to ensure that the benefits of these schemes reach the companies and businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One feedback which I had received regarding the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) was that many businesses did not fully understand the purpose of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a result, there are consultants who helped these companies apply for the PIC, not because it would result in improved productivity, but simply because the Government is giving away monies to businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is an abuse of the intent behind the PIC.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I urged the Government to ensure that the Industry Transformation Programme (ITP) is better explained to the industries or businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: More should be done to prevent abuse of the scheme and to ensure that the funds are properly applied to achieve the purposes of helping companies innovate and improve.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Expand our SME Centres so that we have more staff on board to help reach out to the businesses to explain the many schemes available to assist them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Make it a target that the majority of businesses will think of SME Help Centres or SME Advisory Centres first if they need any advice or help regarding Government schemes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Get the banks, the accounting firms, the lawyers and other professional advisors involved in helping to refer their clients to the SME Advisory Centres or the SME Help Centres to understand more about the types of schemes available to help the businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also glad to hear of the Adapt and Grow initiative to help our people adjust.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government's expansion of the wage support scheme to encourage firms to hire workers affected by retrenchment or business restructuring is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One feedback which I have received from residents who are retrenched or have lost their jobs is that they find it difficult to find another job easily.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of them remain unemployed for several months, and during this time when they are unemployed, it is a huge challenge for them as they have to juggle with bills to pay and other family expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The last thing on their mind is to retrain or reskill because they need to find alternative sources of income to cover their daily expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, the law is that if you have served for a minimum number of years with a company, you are eligible for retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However such payment is not compulsory unless you have an agreement with the company or the union has negotiated an agreement for its workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In this way, the staff retrenched will be able to concentrate on learning new skills for the future job and not have to worry about paying off the family's monthly expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It would make the transition less worrisome if they are able to rely on some short-term retrenchment payment to tide them over for a few months whilst they find another job or undergo retraining.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Perhaps, it is timely for Singapore to consider similar laws, especially since a recent report suggest that higher skilled staff make up the bulk of layoffs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that it is no longer the case that if you are skilled, you can find alternative employment so easily.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker Sir, I stand in support of this Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Not too long ago at the opening of Parliament, the President asked all of the Singaporeans to stand together in solidarity as we embark on the new chapter of nation-building.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The broad vectors in the President's address which were supported by this House have now been put into an action plan in the form of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The two main themes of the Budget is the spirit of partnership and transformation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Today, I would like to share my perspectives on these two themes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many have come to associate the Budget announcements with the handouts of "goodies".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government will also need to continually work towards making life better for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, people should also help themselves and each other.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I would like to share the story of a lady I met at a focus group discussion between several Malay/Muslim women entrepreneurs, Mdm Saadah Jan d/o Rasif Khan.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It was the lowest point in her life as she had gotten into some financial trouble as a result of a failed business venture.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She recalled that her MP, who was Minister Shanmugam, arranged for her to receive financial assistance, among other support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She said receiving financial assistance was a wake-up call for her.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She asked herself, "How did my family get into this state?" and vowed to get out of that situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She was a homemaker but started looking out for work that she could do.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She started by taking orders for roti kirai on Facebook.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She asked her mother to teach her how to make the dish and successfully won the heart of her first customer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She figured that since she was cooking for her family, she could cook for other families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, she started cooking for three other families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Before long, she was cooking for 10 families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One thing led to another, and she found herself with a happy problem of having too many customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her sister then gave her some seed money and she rented a commercial kitchen space which allowed her to grow her business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her journey was not always smooth, she said.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She had to put in a lot of hard work and had many trying moments. including the time she had to sleep at a nearby park so that she could stay close to the kitchen and not have to go home.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, she did not give up and trudged on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She is now a proud owner of a thriving catering business, Dapur Ummi Abdullah.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She also believes in the importance of paying and treating her employees well and in not taking any shortcuts in the business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She said she complies with all business regulations and continues to be prudent by investing the bulk of the profits back into her business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, she said, at the end of the sharing, that she had nothing to complain about and is very happy with her current situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What struck me most about her story was how she took personal responsibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She refused to stay dependent on public assistance and pulled herself out of financial difficulties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And she continues to be responsible towards her employees and her business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that some may need more support and may take more time than others to get out of their financial rut.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But what I think is important and what makes the difference is having the right attitude and that sense of responsibility of self and the country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think this is what striving together means.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is what the spirit of partnership and the spirit of the community should look like.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans should look out for gaps and see where we can play a part to uplift the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On a lighter note, I must say that the artwork of the tapestry in the Budget handouts reminded me of a ketupat, a Malay rice cake.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If you think about it, it is quite a meaningful and a poetic symbol.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One strip of the coconut leaf is limp and not as useful, but several strips of coconut leaves when weaved together forms the lovely ketupat which can hold the rice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just like how when the Government and the people work together, we can and will create something meaningful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I move on to the second theme – transformation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a need to transform and do things differently because the world is changing and we are facing new challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Local businesses and Singaporeans should be supported to go through these changes and be equipped with skills to be future ready.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But I think that this is only one aspect of the equation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is also a need to do more to enhance social mobility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The families will be struggling to deal with day-to-day expenses and challenges and have very little time, money and energy left to focus on upgrading and enrichment for the children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Impact to their children can be great and it may be some time before the families' standard of living is improved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that sustaining social mobility is a great challenge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And I note many existing measures are present to seek to address social mobility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, we have quality education accessible by all, the revised housing policies, skills upgrading through SkillsFuture, initiatives such the Opportunity Fund and KidSTART, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While I welcome these efforts, I feel that we can and should do more.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So far, the Government has taken the right approach in targeting the young and providing continued support for families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I believe there is scope to focus more on helping young people from lower-income families to build social capital.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Social capital is the access to resources and networks that can help one move up the social ladder.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In respect of the coordinated interaction between students, I think there is scope to work with various schools, especially with secondary schools, ITEs and polytechnics to create platforms for regular sharing or peer mentoring.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such sessions should include students with different academic capabilities and family backgrounds and can include sharing on study techniques and reading materials, for example.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Interaction with students from different backgrounds can help develop a student's world view, develop his or her relationships and networks and create access to other resources that his or her family may not have.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These platforms can be created through collaborations between different schools, as well as within students from the same school, where they can share resources or knowledge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The network should specifically target this group and link them up with groups of individuals with relevant expertise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, a young person from a low-income family who may be interested in music can be linked up with local renowned musicians.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such groups of individuals can help with sharing of knowledge and insights, and building relationships and networks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The effort in linking individuals with those with greater expertise and better connections will help build their social capital.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are many existing programmes that provide resources to lower-income families but there needs to be increased effort in creating interactions between groups from various income backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have and should always continue to invest in our people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When our people are empowered and strong, Singapore will be strong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, allow me to end with a few words in Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   For the 2016 Budget announcement, many commented on the Government's efforts to navigate the tide of global change and a challenging economic environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, perhaps among the general public, not everyone pays attention to the details of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The question that is perpetually being asked is, "What will I get this year?" Some may even question why they did not receive any assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think that the Government certainly must help those who need it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, I feel that it is equally important to inculcate the spirit and attitude of taking on the responsibility to help yourself as well as those around you.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Finance Minister spoke about the spirit of partnership; this is in line with the Government's call for Singaporeans to create the next chapter of the Singapore story together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have to be mindful about the changes and competition globally.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must quickly prepare ourselves to obtain the knowledge or skills that can prepare us for any challenges that may come.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to educate our children to have the courage to try and the desire to achieve excellence in their respective fields.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Whether the burden is heavy or light, we will carry it together – I think that this proverb has a lesson for all of us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Malay/Muslim community plays an important role in the nation's development and I am confident that we can work together to enhance Singapore's reputation internationally.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am very aware of time, that I have only 20 minutes, and so I will be very mindful.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First of all, I would like to begin by congratulating Minister Heng for delivering a Budget that seeks to place Singapore in good stead to face our future economic and social challenges.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That was the year when there was the financial crisis, and some of you would have remembered it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The performance, in the form of forum theatre, was about a husband who was also a middle-aged PMET, who was retrenched and because of the retrenchment, was taking out his frustrations on his wife.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Forum theatre is a form of theatre where the protagonist is facing a crisis and after the crisis is being played out, the audience is invited to replace the protagonist to try to find solutions to deal with the problem.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this particular story, both the husband and the wife are the protagonists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In one performance, many people replaced the role of the wife, speaking to the husband about the need to accept the change, all the Government schemes that were available, advising him and encouraging him.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The husband understood all these, but he was still not placated.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: She sat the husband down, held his hand.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The audience and myself were waiting for her to speak.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When I, as the facilitator, asked her why she did what she did, she said, "在这样一种情况底下，人需要一点点的空间，一点点的时间", that is, "In such a difficult situation, people need some space and some time." I share this anecdote to highlight the importance of time and space during a crisis or when you are facing change or a loss.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Restoring damage to renewed use." This quote comes from a US-based theatre company called the Goat Island, which believes that theatre is a small act of repair, repairing the body and the hearts that have been bruised by the experience of crisis, change and loss.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Human beings are not like little bolts which can be melted down and made into nuts if there were not enough nuts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To change a mindset is not about switching into a different mode.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It requires the emotions and the spirits to be engaged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The woman who participated in that performance told us later that that was how she helped her husband who was retrenched during that same financial crisis.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The performance became a demonstration of what is possible.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It became a place for learning and sharing of wisdom by the public.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Here is my response to the Budget, and I would like to ask these two questions: where is Art in the future of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why is Art important in the future of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure that if I searched hard enough, I will be able to find statistics on the arts in Singapore – how our audiences have increased over the years, the number of art works that have multiplied since the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the very fact that I am standing here, asking about the importance of the arts in Singapore, suggests that there is some cause for concern.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The word "culture" is mentioned, but in reference to the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation is a primary objective of the arts and artists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The arts can be innovative in its creative process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We innovate, break old regimes and create new paradigms.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To play means, first of all, you play within the rules of the tried-and-tested methods.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And after a while, one must start playing creatively, go beyond the rules, tear apart those little parts and then you improvise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, only can one start to make new discoveries.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As we strive for change, we must also strive for sustainability.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, how do we deal with economic growth, yet be aware of how it will impact the environment?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The creative mind, coupled with critical thinking, can complement our usually pragmatic and logical approaches to problem solving.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation also happens in the arts through collaboration.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Composers, writers, film-makers and other artists have always collaborated with other disciplines, such as science, technology and education.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such collaborations are vital to the lifeblood of these industries.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This was an experiment that was conducted in 250 BC.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Two equal length sticks were placed upright in the ground 500 miles apart.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, at the exact moment, a person at each location would measure the length of the shadow.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If the earth were flat, both shadows would be of the same length.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But they discovered that the lengths were different, which means that people started to think that maybe the earth was round.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But it took another 1,000 years before we all agreed the earth was round.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A triangulation must occur for us to make sense of this story.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Two people collaborated, setting up the experiment and measuring the shadows.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It took two of them, from two different viewpoints, to visualise the earth as round.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It also took time – roughly a thousand years, a millennium – to finally arrive at a conclusion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It was through a collaboration on such a fundamental issue – whether the earth is flat or round that we are able to gain a more accurate view of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Simply, it means two things – giving and taking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Giving is sharing, offering, so that one can contribute to, and feel invested in the process of nation-building.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Taking is listening, engaging and the ability to accept criticism.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Where criticism is concerned, it is always easier to give than to receive.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And as artists, our works get reviewed and critiqued all the time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: No artist, trust me, wants to read a negative critique of his or her work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But if we see the critic as someone who cares about the arts, our mindset will change.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The critic is no longer an opponent but a collaborator.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we learn not to be offended by difference?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we respond if we were to be offended by difference?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What if one person were to impose his ideas on another person?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what about the many other people who do not have a problem and, in fact, appreciate the artwork or the book?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Should we encourage audiences to write in when they are not offended to balance those who write in who are?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Being fair means being fair to all, not just those who write the angriest letters, shout the loudest slogans or garner the most signatures.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is about letting go of presumptions and judgements in order to create meaningful dialogue.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Collaboration is also a way of demonstrating our resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One hears that word quite often these days.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We must be resilient in case of economic downturns, in case of outbreaks of diseases, in case of terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But resilience is not just about being strong.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is about the ability to adapt and to accept change.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To be resilient, we must first be able to tell our own story.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we know who we are, when we have the confidence to express ourselves, we will know how to manage changes within our means.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The ability to tell our story is the first step towards empowerment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We will then realise that there is no one grand narrative but many micro narratives which collectively define who we are as a nation and as a people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It examines our relationship with the environment we live in.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It examines our relationship with people we live with.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why is art important in the future of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Art can contribute to the resilience and maturity of the populace.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, why are we not talking about art and innovation?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why are we not talking about art and the creative industry?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Living together in a tight space means difficult questions should not be raised for fear that some people might not be ready enough to be engaged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our culture rewards results and success, but art promotes process and the value of failure.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And it is precisely these intrinsic aspects of art that can help empower us to create a diversified, creative and sustainable future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And art can prepare us to engage critically, with wisdom and empathy, like the story of the woman.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Artists break rules, not legal rules, but the rules of the creative process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They want to paint a green sky and a yellow sea.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But as they grow older, they were told, "No, no, no the sky must be blue and the sea cannot be yellow.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Where got such things?" How does one innovate if one does not ask hard questions?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How does one innovate if one has to keep seeking permission to be playful, the permission to transgress, the permission to make mistakes?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When artists create in Singapore, we are told the rule is: create art to foster social harmony and community bonding.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If you do not do that, you are breaking the rules.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what if we want to create art that encourages critical thinking?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What if we want to create art that asks difficult questions?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Can this art be seen as positive, one that promotes social cohesion?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I should reiterate that having open discourse does not mean having no responsibility.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One needs to be accountable for one's words and actions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the day, the laws are still in place.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But having a good debate and a deep exploration of our shared issues will only benefit everyone.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why are we preparing our young only for study and good academic results but not for important and difficult life questions?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, young people want to talk about life's complexities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They want to know that what they learn in school can help them find their place in life, in society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As adults, we all know that life is not just about work and career.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is about responsibility for oneself, for others, for family, for society, and for the environment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we discourage the young from confronting difficult questions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We take away opportunities for them to learn critically, to be intelligent, creative and innovative.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The skills you learn might not be of use some time later.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I prefer another term, the pursuit of "学问" – "学" is to learn, "问" is to ask.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In "The Book of I-Ching", or also known as "The Book of Change", "君子学以聚之，问以辩之" – learn and accumulate knowledge, and ask so as to be critical about what you learned.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are so afraid we will offend others by what we ask and what we say, when, actually, we need to learn how not to be so easily offended.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be able to have a constructive voice that seeks to improve our shared environment and future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We will continue to coexist, but never be truly inclusive.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In our rapid-pace development, we need to spend so much time catching up, that if we do not find time to slow down, we may just lose our sense of being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday, Zaobao, 新汇点, or Crossroads, a weekly page about new migrants and foreigners living and working in Singapore, interviewed a permanent resident, Christophe, a French native.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He said in the interview that after getting used to living in Singapore, he started to feel a sense of nostalgia.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A new resident here, feeling a sense of nostalgia.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this interview, written in Mandarin, he said: “在西方国家，即使过了四五十年都没有察觉多少变化。可是新加坡一直不断在建设，原本惊叹的心情，现在已出现变化." What he said was that in the West, you would not notice any changes even after 40 or 50 years.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But, in Singapore, because it is constantly building and constructing, when initially he was amazed by it, but now he feels differently.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, now, Christophe is beginning to be interested in discovering what would make this place a home.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He started by participating in arts, and in discovering heritage places.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, what keeps us grounded, helps us take stock, reminds us we are human, we are people living in one place?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not fear alternative viewpoints or cave in to strident voices without listening to others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, we do not have the answer immediately, but asking the right question is a step closer.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of saying there is no time, let us make time for it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And instead of saying no space, let us make space for it.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Kok, you are well within your time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These schemes build upon the foundation set by existing programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Aside from the funds set aside to support our families and communities, we must encourage more Singaporeans to be active volunteers as many of the problems within our communities cannot be solved through funding alone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteering is an important part of active ageing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is an activity which allows the elderly to stay engaged in the community and derive a sense of satisfaction from giving back, and in turn, enable the community to tap upon his years of very rich experience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Research has also shown that elderly who have meaningful relationships and are engaged in their communities are happier and healthier as a result.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteering indeed gives them a deep sense of purpose.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, getting our seniors to volunteer on a sustainable basis is not easy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Attracting a group to one-off projects is easy but beyond that, keeping them motivated to come out of their comfort zones is challenging.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to propose incentives to draw more elderly to our community volunteering programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to recruiting and attracting seniors, we should also design programmes such that our younger generation can be involved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The PA can assist by facilitating the arrangements between schools and seniors' groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, many students benefit from the exposure to serving their communities due the Community Involvement Programme (CIP) requirements by their schools.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Using the same LPA example, seniors can accumulate hours of volunteer service to exchange for a LPA waiver and application assistance from trained student volunteers from an Institution of Higher Learning (IHL).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An assigned student can assist him in understanding the requirements and benefits of the LPA, and then guide him through the process and assist him with the application.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The student can even help the elderly locate an accredited medical practitioner in his estate to certify his LPA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think this is a good example of how two volunteers, one young and one senior, can bond through meaningful intergenerational interaction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should endeavour to promote interracial and inter-religious bonding through similar volunteer programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteering for a common cause is the best way to get people of different backgrounds to realise that beneath the labels of race and religion, we have a lot more in common as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need the cooperation of our religious organisations to organise such interactive activities between different religious groups to promote mutual understanding and tolerance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While these initiatives may, sometimes, feel unnatural or contrived, we must persevere and resist retreating into our own cliques.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More importantly, we must be mindful that we have to conscientiously put in the time and effort to create better relationships for a better home and a better nation for all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another area of concern is the health of our elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our rapidly ageing population, it is of utmost importance to encourage our seniors to take preventive measures, such as making lifestyle and dietary changes to improve their health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Good lifestyle and diets should start as early as possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Making changes when one is even older and possibly more set in one's habits will be very much more difficult.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I hope the Health Promotion Board (HPB) will consider offering incentives to encourage the elderly to lead active lives and exercise more.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This was a very good way to encourage citizens to live an active and healthy life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If HPB can introduce more similar long-term programmes targeted at the elderly, I believe the response will be very good.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through these platforms, HPB can work together with businesses to provide discounts to the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Suitable business partners could include Foodfare, shops which sell spectacles, hearing aides and mobility aides.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, to encourage the elderly to make healthier choices, the discounts should only be for "Healthy Choice" dishes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Maintaining good health is particularly challenging for women.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Generally, more women than men are the main caregivers to the children and elderly in their families and they tend to neglect themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more women also out in the workforce, they have a tough time balancing career and family demands and usually, their own health takes a backseat.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Budget deserves the support of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Listening to Finance Minister's Budget Statement, three things came to mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, transformation will be extremely uncomfortable but without it, we cannot metamorphosise into the figurative beautiful "butterfly".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And third, partnership is necessary to effectively effect economic and social change.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are relevant and much needed in today's context and I sincerely hope that the measures announced in the Budget will succeed, because this is an important first step towards Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Much of our past growth was dependent on manpower growth, which we logically know cannot be sustainable, given our limited land area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The schemes in this Budget are clearly aimed at supporting innovation, with a focus on technology, and I look forward to the positive changes with great hope and anticipation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If I may offer some humble suggestions to the chorus of recommendations from Members of this House.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is already done but such emphasis must continue throughout the year and over several Budgets.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Anchor this belief of adaptation and lifelong learning in the conscious and subconscious minds, so that it becomes our way of life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, as with any transformation, there will be sacrifices and pain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While businesses should ideally learn to thrive on their own with minimal Government intervention, I fear the reality now is that businesses are so used to Government support that a strong initial push is necessary before the transformation can take on its own momentum.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the Government has to facilitate this as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But as a next step, it is important to help SMEs benefit fully from these schemes and realise that it is achievable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nobody will bother trying if they think these are too difficult or impossible to achieve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, helping SMEs to make quick wins when they enrol in the schemes would help to make the bitter pill more "palatable" for the SMEs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Partnering trade associations is a good move and these associations can not only help to coordinate industry-wide changes but also multiply the outreach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, they can help to actively share the quick wins and successful examples to motivate others to push on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now that we have begun our journey to transform, there is no turning back.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we have to give it our best shot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite limited resources and manpower, the demand for social programmes continues to rise and hence, effective partnerships are needed to ensure a more optimal application of resources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we also need to rethink how we offer care for the more vulnerable, especially our elderly and our young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to innovate – whether it is through leveraging technology or changing the way we care for our vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Allow me to begin with the care for our elderly first and in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Caring for our elderly is important for building our society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to gear ourselves to enable a graceful and meaningful retirement for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, we need to recognise that our elderly can be an asset and not a liability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should harness their wisdom and strengths to help Singapore grow economically and socially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need to put in place the infrastructure and programmes as early as possible, because these take time to take effect and take root.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are setting the tone and example for our younger generations and our decisions today will determine the values that will guide our society in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am heartened by the slew of pro-elderly measures introduced over the past years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to achieve a truly caring society, we cannot solely rely on the Government or a few charitable organisations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I see this initiative as fulfilling two objectives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Currently, the elderly are often confused by the myriad of social and healthcare schemes offered at the national and local levels.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, they cannot master the differences between the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) and outpatient subsidies, the uses of Medisave, MediShield Life and Medifund, and so on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some are automatically administered, whilst some require application.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, there is a tendency for well-intentioned organisations and volunteers to focus on rental blocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is necessary and has to continue because the elderly living in these blocks are genuinely more vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we also know that vulnerable elderly do not reside exclusively in rental blocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, even the more abled elderly need to be included socially, live a fulfilling life and have opportunities to continue to contribute.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can leverage on technologies to enable our elderly to live safely and independently at home, but whilst doing so, let us also make sure that the human touch is not inadvertently lost.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must prevent the elderly from dropping out of their social networks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I see this Community Networks for Seniors as a good way of putting that human touch back into their lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In light of challenges and expected needs in caring for an ageing population, I would like to make two suggestions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we move towards a "Smart Nation", this has to be given priority.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government should also take the lead in this area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the high demand for services and tight labour situation across all sectors, I doubt there will be enough workers to do what is needed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have to review our manpower model more creatively.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my opinion, the way ahead will be that more Singaporeans, young and old, have to take on more responsibilities in the community – we need everyone to play a part anyway to make a caring society possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to recruit more Singaporeans to volunteer to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we also need to make sure that jobs are meaningful and the "job scopes" are better defined.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There should be a central coordinating body within the respective communities for optimal manpower deployment – a function that perhaps the Community Networks for Seniors can assume.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Next, I would like to touch on support for our young and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am heartened by the continued investment in the children of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must continue to give our young a good and more equalised start in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I feel very touched by her impassionate call and I would also like to reinforce that call.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: KidSTART too is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This longer-term and more holistic approach towards children of less privileged backgrounds is welcomed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope it will also focus on children from vulnerable backgrounds, such as single parent or very complex family situations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the end, by giving the children of Singapore a good and more equalised start, it is really making sure that the future of Singapore also starts on a better footing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, it is also very heartening that the Government is determined to support families in Singapore and has implemented measures to help young Singaporeans achieve both parenthood and career aspirations, reducing their need to make trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women have also been incentivised and encouraged to stay employed, even after being mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is progressive and we must continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are still some challenges that we must solve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government is very actively working on this area but there is still some way to go.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we consider alternatives other than care centres and familial support, which not everyone has?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, organise and tap on "informal sources of labour", such as nannies and volunteers within the community to supplement infant care and childcare centres.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are many experienced women, or we know them as "aunties", or trained part-time caregivers who want to take care of infants and children and earn an income at the same time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government can help match demand with supply by creating an online directory to facilitate this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Interested parents who cannot secure a placement at the infant care or childcare centre can look to this platform for potential caregivers within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Basic profile and credentials of these caregivers can be published in the directory.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Parents and caregivers can then negotiate the price privately.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In essence, whatever the format is, make this additional option more easily available for parents to consider.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two, we should continue to support working mothers and not discourage them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is already challenging for women to succeed in corporate life, given that women are often the minority in the boardrooms and within senior ranks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With children, they have to perform the additional juggling act of being a responsible mother and a performing employee.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, it is extremely challenging for working mothers, a reality that can also be off-putting for young women who are still unsure if they should have children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In response, the Government had introduced a variety of measures to encourage childbirth and support working mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I think there is one part of this year's Budget that risks becoming a disincentive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They feel aggrieved not so much because of the reduction in disposable income, but more for the signal conveyed through this move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Those who had enjoyed the working mother relief now feel penalised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some wonder if the Government is asking them to have fewer children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some wonder if it is really worthwhile to continue working hard to advance in their careers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some wonder if this signifies that senior job roles are not meant for mothers or that mothers should not have higher career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I think there are strong emotions evoked with this move and there is a need for some airing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope that the Finance Minister can help to shed some light and share what was the policy thinking behind this move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, if I may boldly submit the following questions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Would the Minister help to share the thought process and the options considered?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I wonder if the gain from this move to make the tax system more progressive is worth the tangible and intangible costs inflicted on these working mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, could the Government have increased revenues via other means that may encourage healthier lifestyles and behaviours, for instance?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As I look forward to my queries being addressed and the policy insights being shared, I would like to raise and reinforce two suggestions, with the hope of alleviating the challenges faced by working parents, especially working mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will signal the need for a more equal sharing of parenting responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It will also mitigate the perception that mothers are a liability at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This can enable fathers or even grandparents to enjoy greater flexibility at work and hence, spend more quality time to help care for the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The family can then work out an optimal schedule amongst themselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Initiatives to encourage employers to adopt flexi-work arrangements have already been in place for some time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I think it is worth pushing it further and reinforcing the message more frequently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, the Government could perhaps emulate what it is already currently doing with the industry transformation, and that is to adopt a more targeted approach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot have everything in one year's, Budget but I have confidence that over a few Budgets, much can be achieved.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A lot of money will be spent on transforming our economy through enterprise and innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is crucial to ensure that Singapore remains relevant and competitive, so that there is growth.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Growth will enable us to realise our aspirations and fund our essential programmes like education, healthcare and defence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But there is another important aspect of this year's Budget, and that is the social element, making sure that Singaporeans have a stake in our country and share the ownership of this place we call home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have a special empathy for our seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Like our parents, our senior citizens have worked hard for us.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do not have the exact figures but, judging from my house visits and friends in the medical community, the scheme has helped many residents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But as our population ages, our healthcare expenditure can only go in one direction – up.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We are already feeling the impact of the increasing number of seniors in my constituency.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During my house visits, I have encountered more aged living on their own.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Of course, many are productive, helping look after their grandchildren and generally living a happy and fulfilling life after retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But going forward, I feel that there is more we can do to make sure our healthcare budget can be better spent in three ways: first, we can make better use of primary care resources; second, we can better leverage on technology; and third, we can encourage active ageing and emphasise prevention rather than cure.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Singapore has a good healthcare system with world-class hospitals and specialty centres, such as the National Heart Centre, Cancer Centre and Eye Centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While we have a highly sub- Page: 11 specialised system, I believe we can make better use of our primary care system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last December, while on a break in Australia, I met up with a Singaporean doctor practising in a suburb of Melbourne.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In our discussion, we spoke about coordinated care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a family general practitioner (GP), he would be the one assessing his patients' needs for surgery and coordinating with the specialist.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After surgery, the specialist would send a soft copy of the patient's files and x-rays and the GP would follow up.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I learnt that the role of the family doctor is important and useful for the long-term care of the patient.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Currently, 80% of our GPs and family physicians work in the private sector.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The remaining 20% work in our polyclinics and hospitals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In a recent visit to a public hospital, I was told that 80% of their cases are referrals from the polyclinics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is common knowledge that our polyclinics are operating at near full capacity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can we make better use of the 80% of GPs and family doctors in the private sector?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can we enable these doctors to handle the consultation with support from the specialists?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This will make it more personable, build better patient-doctor rapport and also ease some of the loads off the public doctors in the polyclinics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Next, can we use technology to create a better experience for our increasingly ageing population?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Minister had shared in his speech about how robotics in our hospital pharmacies is improving accuracy and speed of services.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the marketplace today, there are robots that can perform simple chores around the home, health bands that can monitor the state of the elderly, remind them to take their medication and send alerts when the users' health is compromised.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Isolation is one of the biggest problems for senior citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, many Internet services help people stay more closely connected with family and friends.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Should we harness the power of technology to help our elderly stay engaged?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One example is a virtual retirement village where tech-savvy elders can connect, look out for and keep one another active and engaged.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The first one is from our Tampines Pioneer Generation Ambassadors' (PGAs) house visits.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last July, our PGAs visited Mdm M and her husband to explain the PG package.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two weeks later, our PGAs received a call from Mdm M informing them that her husband had passed away.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our PGAs rushed to the pioneer's home and activated ambulance services for assistance.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our PGAs continued to befriend Mdm M and give her support to cope with her husband's demise.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is one of the many examples of friendship made possible through personalised outreach and the good work of our PGAs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that the newly-launched Community Network for Seniors can have the same personalised outreach as our PG programme.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope they can also engage our seniors who are not in the PG programme, to explain MediShield Life and understand their needs and interests.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is important that our seniors are aware of the medical assistance that is available to them while they are well so that if and when they are not well, they will know how to seek medical help.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said that she used to have body aches and pasted many "koyok" plasters to relieve the discomfort.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Since joining the centre, she had been doing morning exercises and activities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She was so happy learning simple addition and subtraction.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I implore our seniors to stay engaged and active with us and, together, we can continue to make our home, our Singapore, the best home for all of us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At every Budget, like many Singaporeans, I ask the question whether the focus of the Budget addresses the right areas for Singapore and the segments that most require support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Over the years, I struggle with another nagging question: "Is the Government doing enough or is it doing too much?" While we want the Government to provide support for those who need it, we also must ensure that it does not lead to dependency on the Government that blunts our own abilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, what is the role of the Government?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Building an environment and climate of stability and security for continued economic growth, providing quality education, training and enabling jobs − that is what I believe the Government must continue to do.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng, in delivering his maiden Budget speech, reminded us of Singapore's first Budget and its mission, which remains unchanged: "It is to find the ways to create opportunities for Singaporeans to grow, defend our home and our people." Budget 2016 and its priorities do outline the strategies to achieving this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What Singaporeans and businesses that operate in Singapore have to do is to apply ourselves to these opportunities to make an impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A common thread in Budget 2016 is that of "Partnership".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng reminded us of what Mr Lee Kuan Yew had said: "For it is your job and mine… to make sure we survive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If Singapore is to have a future, we have to work hard at it – together".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my maiden speech in this Parliament in 2006, I had touched on the point of "Hope" and what gives hope to Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I like the overt efficiency and effectiveness of Singapore and the fact that things work here.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What I hold special though and what I value for myself and my children is the knowledge that there will be opportunity to participate and succeed in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget is also seeking to deepen partnerships to support the Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) to build Page: 13 capability through the strengthened Local Enterprise and Associations Development (LEAD-Plus) Programme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Against this backdrop of Partnership for Budget 2016, I would like to touch on a few areas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Against a backdrop of economic slowdown and the need to transform our businesses to address low productivity growth facing Singapore, we need to address the concerns of ensuring opportunities − and not just opportunities, but opportunities for quality jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pace of advances in technology and the disruptions that technological developments are having on jobs, we need to develop quality middle-income jobs, given the profile of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many in this House have already spoken about the growing concerns about mature PMEs on job opportunities and the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) latest Labour Force Report on the redundancy rates.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I am not going to elaborate further on that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I would say that the trends are of concern because this group forms the bulk of the workforce and, at the same time, their re-entry into the workforce after redundancy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The trends on that have been a concern.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, we need to address the growing anxieties over the slowing economic growth and employment trends.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2016 did outline the "Adapt and Grow" initiative, which is, and needs to be more than, just wage or employment support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the focus must still be to help PMEs get good jobs, they require help to adapt to changing job demands and to grow their skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The important thing about this programme is that it helps workers settle into their new jobs and it requires employers to provide structured on-the-job training or to send them for external training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the part of PMEs, they need to apply themselves to take on the challenges to acquire new skills to be able to take on these new job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I still think that more can be done, in partnership with employers, to address employment opportunities for workers, especially PMEs, while also helping employers to address their manpower needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the Opening of this Thirteenth Parliament, I had outlined the need for employers to make deliberate bets on building a strong Singapore Core, given the rapid changes we are seeing in the workforce and to make a bet on Singapore talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With a high level of literacy and education in Singapore, the Singapore workforce is a strong talent base for companies to tap on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Singapore workforce is also known for strong work ethics and trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
