text: So, while we require employers and workers to develop and reskill, what we need is also for the Government to provide support to employers to make these investments to building the Singapore Core.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we drive a more concerted effort to accelerate and leverage the programmes, like LED and CSP, to provide quality employment for Singaporeans, especially the growing base of PMEs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do we ensure that we allow and stay open while at the same time build that Singapore Core by allowing companies a little bit more leeway, like in the LED programme, during the transition to have a little bit more flexibility on the workforce?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On this point of simplification and understanding the various schemes available, I think we can do a more effective job here.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I am pleased that there has been a deliberate shift to move from a scheme-centric to an enterprise-centric approach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This, hopefully, will improve access and drive greater awareness of the many available schemes for businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But again, I would say that more can be done because I have got feedback from various residents who have tried to access some of these schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will just give an example of a PME who tried to access the Skills Upgrading Programme and was trying to upgrade herself.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She was registering herself for a training programme last December.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She paid the registration fees and did the necessary documentation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But like many other service providers that she worked with, this training service provider, when she asked what she qualified for, how much would she be funded for, she was told: "You wait and see.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Of course, being relentless, she decided she would go directly to the Workforce Development Agency (WDA) and she did.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She found out that she did qualify, and she found out that she had to educate the service provider on how to ensure that she qualified for it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad she was perseverant and wants to upgrade herself and is doing that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But clearly, this shows that the schemes are there, but how do we ensure that those who need it have access and are able to use it?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now, I would like to touch on the point of the middle income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many did understand that this is not a broad-based programme, and that the support was meant for the lower 20% of Singaporeans aged 65 and above.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But they still had expectations, as this is an ongoing support and features in our social support system.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do agree that there is a need to limit who gets the support and to ensure affordability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The criteria of lifetime wages and level of household support are already quite stringent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The use of housing type did fuel the sentiment of why that was necessary, given that there are already stringent criteria.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While support via the schemes may not be the answer for these middle-income Page: 15 retirees, I would ask that more be done to look at how support can be given to this group to unleash their fixed assets, as there are concerns.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many of them are running out of savings and are very anxious.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, to ask them to sell off their assets seems to be the logical answer, but is probably pretty harsh.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I think some Members of this House have also spoken about it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Not directly related to Silver Support, but on the point of using housing type as a criterion for means testing, I would request that we relook at this criterion as housing type itself may not be the best because, in some cases, family support is provided and people do live with relatives in private housing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They do not own these assets, but in the means testing, they are still included in the assessment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am reading a book by Stephen Covey, titled "The Speed of Trust".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A point made in this book reminded me of what has made Singapore successful and will continue to do so, and this is the point of "Trust".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Trust is a function of two things – character and competence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: People and businesses put their trust in Singapore because we have a track record of making things happen and many describe us as a country that is safe and reliable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This has not been easy to achieve and to continue to earn that trust, we need to continue to deliver on the trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Stephen Covey, in the book, stressed that while it is natural for us to think of trust in terms of character, equally important is competence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, Madam, people have made Singapore and what we have achieved possible.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is our people that will continue to make the difference for Singapore in the next 50 years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we move to write our story for the next 50 years, let us remember that it is not only about what each of us will do but what all of us must do that will matter.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while we cannot predict the exact outcome, we must be bold, dare to dream, prepare for it, work together and execute well.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many have put their minds to the question of how Singapore can make a good living in this changing volatile world, and many have put their hearts into the question of how we can support Singaporeans to live with strength, confidence and fulfilment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I value and appreciate this, as do my Ministerial colleagues, who will take up the specific issues during the Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We want a future where our economy is abuzz with innovation and enterprise, and where our Page: 16 society is alive with caring and resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: After listening to Members, it is clear to me that not only do we know where we are heading, we are committed to getting there together.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have rallied to the call for partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The urgency and conviction behind Members' support for partnership have been palpable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is most encouraging and promising for our future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also know where we come from, the road we have journeyed to get here.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Heng Chee How is right about our hard truths: we have very real limitations as a small, resource-less country.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But resource-less though we may be, we have inherited a legacy of resourcefulness from our Pioneers whose wealth of experience and hardiness serve as our down payment for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can be held back by our limitations, or we can be like our Pioneers and break through our limitations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our Pioneers have shown us that when there is a will, there is no way you will stop a hardworking Singaporean from doing the extraordinary for family, home and country.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is the in-between, the getting-there, that is full of "unknowables".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan shared, vividly, how the world is changing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The changes are coming so fast and furious that no one can say what the road ahead will be like.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But even if we cannot tell the lay of the land ahead, there are many things that are up to us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How will we conquer each obstacle before us?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How will we pick ourselves up when we stumble?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And how will we help our fellow travellers to go forward?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this Debate, I have been struck by how many Members spoke about our values, our mindset and our culture, and I certainly appreciate these points.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is the spirit in which we do things, the spirit within which we take this journey, that will keep us true to where we came from and carry us through to where we want to go.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From Members' speeches, we can sum this up as the spirit of enterprise and caring.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Enterprise – to not be held back by what appear to be limitations, to overcome challenges, innovate, stay resilient and seize opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Caring – to keep our Singapore a warm and giving home where we help one another through our personal challenges where we can each achieve our best, reach our dreams and go on to inspire and serve others.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we are committed to moving forward together in partnership, in a spirit of enterprise and caring.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, I will speak on how Budget 2016 enlivens this spirit of enterprise and caring for our journey of the next 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Page: 17 Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Ms Sun Xueling, Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Dr Tan Wu Meng talked about global trends affecting Singapore and how our economy must remain outward-looking and forward-looking.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin spoke on short-term challenges facing our economy and the impact these will have on our businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Saktiandi Supaat provided suggestions on how we can transform our economy and what role the Government ought to play − a point which Ms Jessica Tan also raised earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These are all very valid points and I thank the Members for their thoughtful views on the subject.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa said that "to achieve better lives and a stronger nation, we need to have the means and resources to get there".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have spoken in support of our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The success of our SMEs matters to our people's jobs and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: SMEs provide a range of services that are important for our daily life and add buzz to our neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some will grow to be our future large firms.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even if they do not, our society will be the richer to have the opportunity where people just try to do something.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We want our SMEs to do well, we want them to succeed and we want a vibrant SME sector.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But in order to support SMEs, we must recognise that they range from micro-enterprises in the heartlands, to fairly sizeable firms with an international presence.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some are in sectors that are doing well, while others are facing difficulties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Hence, as many of you pointed out, we cannot have a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Louis Ng noted, different people have taken away different messages from this Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Reactions across the different news outlets have also been different; even the headlines.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A business leader once asked me this very intriguing question.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He said, "In every place, from the poorest neighbourhood in Africa to the richest precinct in Silicon Valley, there are firms that succeed and firms that don't.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Last year, both the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) honoured companies and business leaders from our founding days.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The SBF award recipients include longstanding names, such as Shaw Theatres and Yeo Hiap Seng.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The SCCCI award recipients include the founders of Lim Teck Lee, Pan-United Corporation and Sing Lun Holdings.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Page: 18 These companies and pioneers started out in an environment with few grants, incentives and agencies to support them; a point which Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also raised.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In many cases, they started from scratch or, as the Chinese say,"白手起家".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, whether you look across countries or time in our own history, why do some firms succeed while others do not?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The common element for success is this: the spirit of enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the critical element needed for economic vibrancy, in Singapore and anywhere in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Running a business is a complex thing because you will be faced with a myriad of unforeseen problems.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The more problems one solves, the further one gets ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Solving problems also allows the entrepreneur to develop the entrepreneurial instincts to then see opportunities where others see problems.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan hits the nail on the head when he said that the principles that have propelled us since Independence are "self-reliance, openness and a determination to remain updated and relevant".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These are what nurture a spirit of enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: One element of this spirit of enterprise is the need to look outwards and forward, to see challenges and opportunities in the world around us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I am very encouraged to hear Members speak of the implications of these changes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan reminded us of how robotics is shaping the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Which country in the world buys the most industrial robots?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Well, the country with the most people in the world – China!

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, if even China, at their lower level of wages, is automating, what does this mean for us?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing related how e-commerce is changing the face of retail.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I have heard of many people who go to a shop to view, feel and try products, then go home to purchase it online at a lower price.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I do not know whether Members here do that, too, but you must have heard of people who have done so.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But some in the sector are looking ahead into the future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, Funan DigitaLife Mall, known for years and years for selling IT products, is closing to reshape itself to become "an experiential creative Hub".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa cited insourcing trends in both the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This means that the global supply chain which we are a part of is shrinking.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: China and the US will produce more and more of their goods at home.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, how do we continue to create value within the world, amongst the world's biggest markets?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this regard, Mr Heng Chee How and Mr Lee Yi Shyan reiterated that economic transformation is urgent and critical.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must, indeed, support our businesses' spirit of enterprise to look outward to the world and forward to the future, and take this task of transformation urgently.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, many Members, such as Mr Saktiandi Supaat, spoke of the challenges faced by our SMEs in the near term.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Members, such as Mr Ang Hin Kee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Zaqy Mohamad, have asked for more support for SMEs in this period.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our people's livelihoods could also be at stake.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members, such as Mr Ong Teng Koon, have expressed support for this support package.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some members, such as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, spoke about rental costs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I appreciate that the experience can be different for different firms in different locations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, that is why we are careful to shape overall macroeconomic conditions to be supportive of growth to make sure that we do not price ourselves out of the global market.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We released more space, implemented anti-speculative measures and calibrated our exchange rates carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These are medium-term measures and we are seeing results.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are seeing results in terms of supporting firms even in the cost area.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Others, such as Dr Lily Neo, spoke about manpower costs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Wages have been rising, which is good for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our workers do look forward to rising wages but it puts pressure on businesses, especially those with lower margins.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must understand where these cost pressures come from – they are fundamentally based on demand and supply.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our supply of land and labour is limited.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the demand for our resources is growing, which, in fact, indicates that our economy is still growing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, while we should be careful not to price ourselves out of the global market, we must accept that we cannot be a low-cost location.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even China, which used to be a cheap place, with its vast land and population – 1.3 billion people – is experiencing rising business costs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Their businesses are automating, their businesses are moving out from coastal regions to inland, as well as to cheaper locations outside China.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All firms, large or small, in whatever sector, must compete on productivity and innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the way to reinforce the spirit of enterprise and to build vitality in our firms for the long haul.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Enterprising firms understand this and build their business models with these hard constraints in mind.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It will ensure that our finite resources will not be trapped in "zombie" businesses, as Mr Ong Teng Koon warned.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And, our workers will not be trapped in firms and sectors with poor prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our concern about restructuring is, ultimately, a concern for our workers, our people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this regard, several Members have spoken at length on what we should not do to undermine the spirit of enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Ang Wei Neng cautioned that Government support should not become a crutch.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And as Dr Lim Wee Kiak pointed out, firms should not have the impression that the Government will eliminate risks and bail out any firm in trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Vikram Nair also cautioned against institutionalising subsidies to industries as they can be difficult to remove.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I appreciate Members' comments on how we can best support our firms in this period of weakness.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But a business leader, Mr Steven Koh, put it to me this way.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He said, "Government support is like push-starting a car that has gotten stuck in a difficult patch – it can get the car going again, but the Government cannot be pushing the car for miles and miles.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It will run out of Page: 20 resources.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, once the car is moving, it has to rely on its own engine to go for the long haul." Wise words from a leader who has been in business for a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To go back to the question of why some firms succeed, we also observe that some economies and some regions of big countries produce more winners than others and have been able to create many more good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Well, in these economies, the governments have played an important role, an enabling role – enabling enterprising individuals and businesses to go further than they could have on their own.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Jessica Tan just touched on this point and said it well.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They have created a stable political and business environment, with clear policies and regulations, invested in R&D and first-class infrastructure and most of all, in their people through education and lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They have also partnered business to grow the economy, while allowing market forces to work to channel resources to the most productive firms.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In these countries, businesses and governments have come together to achieve external economies of scale – or, as academics put it, the Marshallian externalities – a point which Prof Hoon Hian Teck and I recently discussed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In short, the governments work to strengthen the spirit of enterprise in their firms and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For our people, we seek to support the development of deep skills and match these to growth areas.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah sums it up well on how we can support the spirit of enterprise and how we can aim for long-term vitality.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I quote, "In the short term, Singaporean firms might rightly expect some fish from the Government to keep their workers fed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But, ultimately, the country will run out of fish if they don't develop bigger, smarter and faster fishing ships to get fishes from international waters." And, indeed, the Government can help businesses to develop bigger, smarter and faster ships but ultimately, the captains of industry must navigate the ships and help our firms go the distance.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we move to the next phase of our restructuring journey, we will adopt a more targeted approach to helping firms.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To drive real transformation, we need to calibrate our support to the needs of each firm and each sector.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, Ms Denise Phua made a similar point about "not taking a cookie-cutter" approach.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, several Members spoke on the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) – was it effective, or was it abused?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From the start, PIC was designed to raise awareness among SMEs about productivity and importantly, to get SMEs to undertake basic productivity efforts, to get started.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With this broad-based take-up of productivity initiatives, we are now ready to move on to the next phase of restructuring, through the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some may ask whether we are sure that the Industry Transformation Programme will succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I said before, there is no textbook answer to policy; there is no textbook answer to innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, in Government, we, too, need to embrace a spirit of enterprise – we have some clear ideas of where we need to go, what we need to do.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must be humble and we have to figure it out dynamically, learning, improving and improvising as we go along, and working in partnership with businesses which know well what are needed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we do not dare to try, we will certainly fail.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we have the guts to try, we have a good chance of succeeding.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And if we go at it together, we have the best chance of succeeding.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Members have asked whether there is a spirit of enterprise in Singapore firms; is it well and alive in our firms and in our people?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is Wee Meng Construction, a local steel fabrication SME serving the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Like other SMEs, they could not attract young and skilled Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, they mapped their productivity gaps to identify improvements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, now, new Singaporean employees join the firm, and they reduce their hiring of foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Their next step is to secure overseas steel fabrication projects.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Wee Meng Construction is a good example of how we can automate, develop our people, scale up and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The technology that Wee Meng Construction has adopted is scalable across the sector and we will support such capability upgrading.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By turning adversity into opportunity, they embody the forward-looking resilience and enterprise that have carried Singapore this far.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another good example which I came across recently is Jean and Jeremy, a mother-and-son duo who own JMD Pacific, very near here, at Peninsula Shopping Centre.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A traditional retailer, growth was slow and e-commerce was drawing sales away from brick-and-mortar stores such as theirs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, Jeremy, who graduated from university, suggested to his mother to list her products online and use social media to do marketing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This immediately opened up access to a wider group of customers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Jeremy also helped to bring in sports and lifestyle products new to Singapore, and Page: 22 they became the exclusive distributor for some brands now carried by big stores, such as Challenger, Courts and Guardian.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As sales moved online, they digitised their processes and ventured into overseas markets and into new product lines, such as sports and lifestyle products.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is an inspiring story of the transformation of family businesses and how even a retail store can take advantage of technology and e-commerce to move ahead.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the industry level, successful transformation can benefit all firms within the industry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I spoke of the spirit of partnership in the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Firms can achieve more when they work together on common goals.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some people have asked – after I raised this – why competitor firms would find it in their interest to cooperate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Firms can cooperate and compete all at the same time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They can compete in ways to differentiate themselves from one another, in different niches of the market, with different views on who has the best product or service.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But they can cooperate on ways to help them all drive down costs, grow the markets and grow global mindshare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An example is the Collaborative Industry Project on 3D Additive Manufacturing where companies come together to share access to the state-of-the-art equipment at the Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology (SIMTech).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: SIMTech also works with companies to identify key technologies that can drive their future growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The system has now gained interest from several other manufacturers, and Wavelength Opto-Electronic has been transformed from an equipment trader and component manufacturer to an Original Equipment Manufacturer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a good example of how industry-focused institutions can generate value for firms in their respective sectors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For us to have more such efforts, strong sector institutions with committed leadership are needed to drive collaborations and build up shared resources in each sector.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By working with industry, the reach of this programme can be greatly expanded.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If private actors in each sector are willing to step forward to do something for their industry, the Government is very willing to support them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, there are over 300 TACs, some with more capabilities than others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan highlighted the Singapore Furniture Industry Council as a TAC, which has been effective in helping the entire industry to upgrade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with many of you that not all TACs are playing the role that they could to reach out to firms in their industries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But where they are willing to step up, we will support them in their capability development through schemes, such as LEAD and LEAD-Plus.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Separately, Mr Leon Perera suggested that a tool to benchmark productivity would be useful for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, there are productivity calculators available to firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, SBF, in partnership with DP Info, recently launched the Holistic Industry Productivity Scorecard (HIPS).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These tools help companies measure their productivity based on key indicators and allow them to benchmark themselves against the industry norm.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Since the launch of HIPS four months ago, 80 companies have used the scorecard.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is an example of how an industry association or business chamber is Page: 23 taking the lead in transformation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, while I appreciate that many Members have called for the Government to do more, I think we should also celebrate such efforts by industry associations that are not told what to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They take leadership, they take ownership, they know what the industry needs and they work together to create value for their members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Dr Teo Ho Pin spoke about how some SMEs may have difficulties attracting talent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Singapore-Industry Scholarship is another joint initiative between firms in multiple industries and the Government that addresses the issue of talent recruitment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I launched it in 2012 because I felt strongly, like many of you in this House, about building Singaporean leaders in industry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Incidentally, one important criterion which I used for having firms on this is that it is not about a scholarship but about mentorship.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Are you willing to develop the talents that you have?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you are, you are on board; if you are not, then we will not admit you to this scheme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am also very encouraged that business leaders themselves have been avid about mentoring and sharing experiences.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, the Bosses' Network set up by Mr Hong Ting Liang which brings SMEs together; second, the Workforce Advancement Federation, started by Mr CB Chan of Goodrich Global, which focuses on learning and building a sustainable workforce; and third, the Business Leaders' Alumni Club, run by Ms Susan Chong of Greenpac, which organises sharing sessions with CEOs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I want to thank Ms Denise Phua for her suggestion of flexibility and enlightened partnership, and the need to have a targeted approach and the "3As" framework.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, the "3As" framework is a way for us to look at how we can support the spirit of enterprise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I would also like to thank Assoc Prof Randolph Tan for cautioning against the risks of entrenchment of sector-based interests.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even as firms cooperate, they must not engage in anti-competitive practices.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members, such as Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, said, quite rightly, that building a culture that supports innovation is critical, that culture comes before strategy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am optimistic that we can do this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Last Friday, I visited The Hangar by NUS Enterprise as well as LaunchPad@one-north, two innovation zones which bring together professors, students and innovators.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I quite like the name of "Hangar" in NUS because it is where ideas take flight.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There, I met people working together to build exciting startups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They seek to make a difference for children seeking medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: She designed a patient engagement device in the form of a toy Page: 24 rabbit that explains medical procedures to children in a medically accurate but relatable and comforting way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For this, Esther won the Shell LiveWIRE Top 10 Innovators Global Award.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The second example is WaterROAM, which seeks to make a difference to those in disaster and rural areas in need of clean water.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They are a startup that has developed a potable water filtration system that can turn dirty water into drinkable water in the same time it would take to run it from the tap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The young man who showed it to me gamely drank the water to show me that it worked.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This has allowed it to be deployed in disaster and rural areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What struck me about both startups is that their innovation started with the aim of meeting a human need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the case of Rabbit Ray, the innovation was less in the technology than in the design, with a focus on improving the lives of children seeking medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Esther is now working on a doll that helps children who have to undergo chemotherapy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the case of WaterROAM, it is to meet the need for potable water for residents of disaster-hit zones and in rural areas, in the poor areas of the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am very happy to have young people like them who understand that innovation is not just about technology or gizmos but really about meeting human needs, making the world a better place and how they can make an impact in the lives of others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many other examples of creative people with the desire, skills and belief to make a difference.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, how do we nurture this creative environment that allows innovations to flourish?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with Mr Azmoon Ahmad and several others that curiosity needs to be stimulated from young and, indeed, we will be making changes to our education system to nurture this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Meanwhile, we must continue to improve the environment for innovation to thrive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we also placed resources in the revitalisation of the heartland.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is never about confining innovation to enclaves, as Assoc Prof Daniel Goh seems to suggest.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To paraphrase Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, the process of innovation is not a precise science.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is an art that requires us to be patient, take the long-term view, persevere and continuously adapt.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need to change mindsets, as many of you have said, but it is an art and we have to be patient.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Members have spoken about the impact of the economy on people and jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several, such as Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Mr Zaqy Mohamad, have asked whether there will be good jobs available as our economy evolves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Others, like Minister Chan Chun Sing and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, were concerned about whether our people will have the skills to take up good jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and others also spoke on how we can help retrenched workers or new entrants into the workforce find the right jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, all over the world, people are concerned about jobs as major economies grapple with job losses and structural unemployment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 25 In other places, such as the US and Europe, under-investment has held back economic and employment growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Under-employment and structural unemployment due to skills mismatches are issues that many economies are grappling with.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are in a better position because we have invested in creating jobs and enabled our people to acquire relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our overall unemployment rates are low compared with other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim said that the 1.9% figure for the unemployment rate does not tell the whole story.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But the picture does not change much even if we look at resident unemployment or any other indicators.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The ratio of job vacancies to job seekers remains above one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, if you go to job sites, whether it is Indeed.com or the MOM Jobs Bank, there are many jobs being advertised, including, of course, in the classified advertisements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I understand the anxieties of Singaporeans about jobs because it is not just about jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We cannot take for granted that there will be good jobs and incomes in the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To address these concerns, we need a coherent approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, create the right jobs; second, develop the right skills; and, third, enable the right match.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, it is about right jobs, right skills, right match.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, creating jobs and more, creating the right jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan said, "It is no mean feat to continue to generate jobs in an increasingly sophisticated economy packed into one of the most congested cityscapes in the world." Indeed, this is no mean feat.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We not only need to create jobs but given our high-cost structure, given the high level of wages already, to create jobs of high value that meet the aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To do that, our firms must be competitive and productive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I showed this slide when I presented the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This scatterplot shows average productivity and average wage per worker.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The higher the productivity of the firm, the higher the wages that they pay to each worker.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It shows that productive firms generally pay higher wages.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is why industry transformation is so important.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is why we need to transform enterprises, transform industries and transform through innovation, because Industry Transformation is the engine, the means for us to create better lives and better jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these changes will require changes which will require us to create new companies and jobs which will require new skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 26 Some Members have asked whether the Industry Transformation Programme is just about helping firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some workers have asked, "Does it help us?" I want to emphasise this very important point that, ultimately, this programme is about helping our workers and our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As part of this transformation, firms must also redesign jobs and develop their staff.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members, such as Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Melvin Yong, pointed out how important it is for firms to automate and redesign jobs and train their staff in an integrated way, so as to bring out the best in every employee and allow everyone to catch up.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Take Feinmetall, a precision engineering firm I recently visited, where I met Mr Winson Ng, a young polytechnic graduate who joined Feinmetall after his course in mechatronics at Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: After working for five months, he was sent by Feinmetall for advanced training in Germany.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Upon returning to Singapore, Winson noticed that one of the processes used to bend needles for semiconductor wafer testing could be done better.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He conceptualised a way to automate it, then worked with a systems integrator to develop a machine for it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The machine also reduced the training time required for the process, from nine months to one week.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is impressive: investing in one young man by sending him to Germany and when he came back, the firm increased productivity four times and reduced training from nine months to one week.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The other staff are now redeployed to higher value-added jobs within the firm.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Winson's training at the polytechnic and in Germany, combined with his on-the-job experience, enabled him to generate insights and innovate successfully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why I have been emphasising that employers play a very, very critical role in enabling the development of their people, not just in upgrading their firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Firms that take care in making such investments, ultimately, see dividends.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A man like Winson, a young polytechnic graduate who is able to conceptualise a machine that has such impact, gets better prospects in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must continue to build a conducive workplace environment that empowers staff to continue learning and improving.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that all firms will invest in their people, young and old, and start a virtuous cycle of higher skills, higher productivity and higher wages, which can then be reinvested to develop the firm further.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While firms create the right jobs, our people must also develop the right skills to take on these jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Preparing our people for the future starts from an early age, when our children develop the fundamentals and a love for learning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Darryl David, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and other Members have said, we must build the confidence of our young, broaden their learning and stimulate their curiosity as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a powerful force that will keep them learning and help them overcome challenges in their lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To deepen lifelong learning, we launched SkillsFuture with a focus not just on the skills of today, but also on skills for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have met many people who are pursuing part-time courses, and I know it is not easy to juggle the demands of work, family and studies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Their Page: 27 spirit of resilience and lifelong learning is most commendable.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The success of SkillsFuture depends on everyone playing their part, not just employees, but also employers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government will provide support and resources for those who are willing and motivated to acquire new skills and deepen their skill sets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some of you will be happy to know this – accounts will be given to students from Primary 5 and upwards so that they can begin to plan for their future learning and skills development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are taking the comments made by Members about starting young quite seriously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These initiatives will equip our young people with critical skills for the workplace and the capacity to learn throughout their lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have touched on right jobs and right skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Jobseekers can avail themselves of a suite of employment and training assistance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These include Professional Conversion Programmes and the Career Support Programme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: WDA and NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute help match workers and jobs and provide training to improve the employability of workers through their Career Centres.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They successfully placed over 14,000 job seekers in 2015 – quite an impressive number.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We understand the anxiety of some who have been displaced and that is why these programmes are being enhanced and its outreach doubled.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for Manpower will speak further on this at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As new industries and new types of jobs emerge, we will need to take our skills and job matching efforts even further.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We, too, have to innovate in this area.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we launched the TechSkills Accelerator for the ICT sector.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It will pilot a new model for how Government partners major IT employers, associations and industry to offer training, certification and job matching services, three-in-one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It will also reach out to those without ICT background.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some of you might ask if it is possible to develop ICT skillsets without any background.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Well, there are certain specific areas that IDA had identified, such as user experience and user interface design.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If this pilot succeeds, we will replicate it in other sectors, as many of you have suggested.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What is critical is to sustain the long-term vitality of our labour market.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members have listed the various market innovations over the years – in managing our dependence on foreign manpower, promoting local employment and helping vulnerable groups of workers to find jobs and supplement their incomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan proposed auctioning the right to hire foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Desmond Choo suggested broadening the apprenticeship system and partnering the labour movement on career guidance for young people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Zainal Sapari suggested further ways to help our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested enhancements to the Career Support Programme and setting up a support network for unemployed PMETs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin suggested setting up Centres of Excellence for SkillsFuture learning, in partnership with trade associations and professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Azmoon Ahmad and other Members spoke about providing retrenchment benefits to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 28 I just want to echo a point which Assoc Prof Randolph Tan also made.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must be careful about how we intervene in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We cannot simply copy one bit from one country and then another piece from another and hope to make sense of it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There has to be a clear philosophy and a clear sense that the various measures must cohere to be effective over the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And importantly, we must not undermine the sense of independence and efficacy and the spirit of self-reliance and resilience in our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, let me end this section by sharing a story that Mr Heng Chee How and many other Members will find inspiring.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I met Mr Sundaram Velosamy and Mr Ong Moh Hong when I visited Pan Asia Logistics (PAL).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Sundaram is an interesting story because he started working in the logistics sector in 1989 with an "O" level certificate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He has a keen desire to learn and upgraded himself by studying part-time for certificate and diploma qualifications, building up to a degree in 2013.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: After he joined PAL in 2012, he was sent to Germany for training to understand how to use the automated storage and retrieval system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When he returned, he applied what he learnt and increased the productivity significantly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Ong joined the firm in 2014 at the age of 66, just as the firm was implementing a new IT system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Age was not a barrier either for Mr Ong or his employer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Interestingly, Mr Ong has been doing logistics work for 29 years, all the while in manual positions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When I asked him how it feels to join a firm which is just starting a new IT system, he replied that it was a great opportunity to learn.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, he learnt new IT processes when he joined the firm at the age of 66.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, Mr Ong and Mr Sundaram are role models for the team and help mentor younger staff.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Sundaram said, "There is no use if I keep it to myself.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I must pass on the knowledge to others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I must mentor them, so that they can do better and also mentor others." This is a very good example of lifelong learning, of mentoring and of a company that invests in developing its staff.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And importantly, of treasuring senior workers and believing that you can continue to train older workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Ong said, older workers also have a long runway.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I commend both Mr Ong and Mr Sundaram for their pursuit of lifelong learning and PAL for creating an inclusive culture of constant development for their staff.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our approach to enable our people to access good jobs and stay employable can be encapsulated in one phrase: "Right Jobs, Right Skills, Right Match".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Creating full employment and good jobs is a major challenge, a difficult journey.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I am confident that we will be ready for the future because I have confidence in Singaporeans, I have confidence in Singapore and I have confidence that we will work together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Members, including Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Joan Pereira, highlighted the importance of empowering our seniors to lead active and engaged lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Faisal Manap, Mr Darryl David, Mr Christopher de Souza and a number of Members talked about Government support for families and the needs of the young.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am heartened that many Members, including Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Henry Kwek, support the initiatives to encourage philanthropy and volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will focus on three main topics – strengthening social support, reaching Singaporeans in need and building a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about the need to support low-income families, especially those with children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We invest in all our children to help them achieve their potential, Page: 29 paying particular attention to those from less advantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Housing subsidies that help low- and middle-income families own their homes have been increased.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Fresh Start will help some families own a home again if they are willing to work hard for a second chance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are going further for a small group of young children who may need even more support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, there are now more resources for families, regardless of income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By the way, this is in addition to tax reliefs and other leave benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A child from a lower-income household would receive more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are also substantial subsidies for all Singaporean students at our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and bursaries for those from lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I must also point out to Mr Dennis Tan that apart from the CDA grant, the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and the MediSave grant for newborns do not – I emphasise, do not – require co-matching.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Moreover, our preschool and education subsidies benefit all, but are especially generous to children from lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you look at it in its entirety across all the different schemes, substantial support is given to parents to have children, especially for the middle-income households, and with even more targeted support for those who start with less.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While the CDA First Step is $3,000, we must not forget that there are existing Baby Cash Bonuses of $8,000 or $10,000, plus MediSave grant of $4,000.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Jessica Tan earlier raised the issue of assurance for seniors in retirement, and several Members have also spoken on this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me now touch on this subject.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the last 10 years, we have strengthened the four pillars of our social security system; namely, home ownership, healthcare assurance, CPF and Workfare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In particular, we have provided our seniors with greater assurance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through CPF LIFE and MediShield Life, we are increasing risk-pooling to provide more support in the face of life's uncertainties and also during retirement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) has been further enhanced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Besides Workfare, the Pioneer Generation Package provides a special generation with additional support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Adding up our transfers to retiree households, healthcare subsidies, S&CC rebates and the GST Voucher, we provide substantial support for retirees living in 1- and 2-room HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: About 70% of this is in healthcare subsidies and amounts to substantial support for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Silver Support is a major enhancement to our social security system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In implementing the scheme, we are mindful of the impact Silver Support can have on our society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Singaporeans are proud to be able to provide for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Silver Support is not meant to replace other forms of financial support for our seniors, including personal savings, CPF, family support as well as the Pioneer Generation Package.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must be cautious that Silver Support does not undermine values, such as filial piety, or lead to a divisive mentality among citizens.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Thus, Silver Support is not the only source of help for the neediest seniors, whose basic needs are served by Public Assistance, which has been enhanced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The second point I want to make is this – no single criterion is enough to identify seniors in the bottom 20% to 30%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is, therefore, reasonable that we combine three criteria of lifetime wages, housing type and household support in our assessment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We acknowledge that there may be some seniors, as highlighted by Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Darryl David and several others, who may need help but do not qualify automatically.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Seniors in these exceptional circumstances can request CPF Board to review their eligibility for Silver Support and we will consider the merits of each case.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It starts off with $320 million a year and will increase as our population ages.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: From the outset, we should ensure that the scheme remains sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether payouts can be made monthly instead of quarterly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, it is a forward payment, which gives seniors the flexibility to manage their expenses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we move to monthly payouts, we will reduce such flexibility.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members requested greater support for caregivers through some form of monetary compensation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, I recognise that it is not easy to be a caregiver.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have met many and I have great respect for what they do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But, as a society, we have to be careful not to monetise relationships.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this is a subject that would have to be carefully studied.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: MOH and the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) will elaborate on the relevant efforts at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I would also like to commend Ms Chia Yong Yong for her very moving plea for all of us to better understand persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I strongly agree that we should continue to empower them to realise their full potential.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: MSF will elaborate on the third review of the Enabling Masterplan in the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Azmoon Ahmad asked why there is no tax rebate or, more broadly, measures targeted at the middle income, in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 31 To begin with, about half of our workers do not pay any income tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The income tax burden is low for the majority who pay, including the middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I had earlier spoken on our efforts to strengthen existing measures that benefit middle-income households and provide active support for housing, education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these measures are not as direct as putting money in people's pocket, but it has a meaningful long-term impact on the careers and future of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The most important support for all Singaporeans, including the middle-income, is employability and good jobs, a point which Ms Thanaletchimi mentioned in a recent TV programme, that the best social security is job security, and I would add that the best way to ensure job security is deep skills and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we are investing in those areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even though I devoted a considerable amount of time in this Budget to explain the Industry Transformation Programme and measures to support our SMEs, our aim is very clear – to enable Singaporeans to have good jobs, more opportunities and a better life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have to go for the long haul and these are important ways to support all families, especially middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Providing a tax rebate from year to year is not enough to address the fundamental concerns of our middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must, as Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef pointed out, preserve a spirit of resilience and self-reliance and focus on a sustainable way to build better lives for all.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we spend more, we must take extra care to spend well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I welcome Miss Cheryl Chan's comments on the importance of improving the way care is delivered, especially for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To better serve Singaporeans, we have made some moves to improve service delivery in the "last mile", especially to the elderly and vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The first is reaching out proactively to those in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A good example is the Pioneer Generation Ambassadors (PGAs), which Miss Cheng Li Hui spoke about.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our ambassadors form a close relationship with our Pioneers, explain Government policies to them and help them access the various schemes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An example is Mr Shahul Hameed and his wife.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Shahul is 74 years old with a heart condition and usually stays at home.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our ambassadors visited him to explain the benefits of the PGP and MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They also took the chance to introduce Mr Shahul to active ageing programmes in his community to help him make friends while keeping fit, while taking care of his heart condition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are practical ways in which we are reaching out proactively.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The second move is to bring help closer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Previously, those looking for short- and medium-term assistance under ComCare had to approach one of the five Community Development Councils (CDCs).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is an important milestone, but we are still striving to bring help closer to those in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And with more experience, we will do better.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Agencies can better calibrate their support to help each citizen and better address their needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Administrative hassle, especially paperwork and forms with multiple agencies, will be reduced for citizens.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I think this is especially important for those who need help, as Dr Tan Wu Meng has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we can do even better in partnering the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was extremely heartened by my visit to the Henderson-Dawson ward and the Thong Kheng Seniors Activity Centre last week.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This area is one of the older estates, with almost one in six of the residents aged 65 or above.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important to ensure that every neighbourhood is a good neighbourhood for seniors to age with dignity, lead active and healthy lives and stay engaged with the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Well, I am glad it resonates with all of you.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Every neighbourhood is a good neighbourhood for seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Henderson-Dawson is an example of how various parties come together, with good leadership of advisors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It was difficult at the start but, over time, the various partners built trust to work together and pool resources to better meet seniors' needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These include activities for seniors, like morning exercises, free lunches and educational talks on topics from nutrition to fire safety.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The elderly themselves contribute to these efforts, to help care for one another.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They demonstrate a keen sense of collective responsibility and feel a strong obligation to the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I echo Ms Joan Pereira's and Ms Tin Pei Ling's call for more senior citizens to volunteer as a good way to stay active and engaged.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth will provide an update on the Silver Volunteer Fund, which encourages seniors to give a part of their time for good causes, in the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Her husband passed away a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, she discovered new meaning in life when she started volunteering at the centre.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: She said, and I quote in Mandarin, because she spoke in Mandarin, "来自社会，归回社会. 这样也是应该的. 除非我真的不可以动, 我才没有办法. 我可以做的我就一定帮忙的".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: She said, "Having received from society, it is only right that I give back.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Unless I cannot move and I have no way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Whatever I can do, I will definitely continue to help." This is the great feisty attitude of an elderly − great resilience and great sense of care for others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must all step forward to care for our fellow Singaporeans and renew our shared commitment to building a better society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this is particularly important as our population ages.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Community partnership will be a major area of focus moving forward.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Community Networks for Seniors pilot will bring local stakeholders and agencies together to study the needs of seniors and help them take preventive care.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Looking ahead, as several Members have suggested, we can do even better to plan our estates and social services, as well as crowd in the community to make Singapore a model for social Page: 33 service delivery as well as successful ageing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ultimately, it is not about Government schemes but about building a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Kok Heng Leun said, "We must all pitch in to take care of one another and solve community problems together." This is the only way we can nourish the ties that bind us together as a society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am delighted that this has generated significant donations from the public.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singaporeans have shown great generosity in spirit and we hope that this can be sustained.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to encourage charitable giving by matching, dollar-for-dollar, any additional donations through SHARE to ComChest.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Besides providing resources, businesses have a role in helping the social sector and supporting employee volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Quirk, a local integrated marketing communications agency, supports Project Dreamcatchers, an initiative by the National University Hospital to empower youths living with chronic illness.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The youths will be producing artwork that will be showcased in an exhibition later this year and Quirk is assisting with the branding and collaterals.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A group of drivers in ComfortDelGro are active volunteers, delivering meals and driving around those in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are all examples where businesses and employees use their expertise for good causes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I acknowledge the issues raised by Ms Denise Phua, including possible crowding out of cash donations, over-subsidising volunteerism and the cap that affects IPCs that really need help.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We studied these issues and decided to pilot the scheme to encourage businesses towards volunteerism, but with appropriate caps.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our larger intention is to kickstart a movement beyond cash donations, to get businesses and to mobilise resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I would like to stress that it is not only about tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the end of the day, it is about businesses seeing themselves as responsible corporate citizens and becoming more active partners in building a caring society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will make it easier for Singaporeans to enrich our society with ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As many Members have pointed out, it is not through the Government's efforts alone, but a collective effort, that we can build a caring and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We hope that Singaporeans from all walks of life will step forward.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the past few days, several Members, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Henry Kwek, have spoken on the importance of fiscal sustainability even as we tackle Singapore's economic and social challenges.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Members have pointed out, Singapore's spending needs will grow in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the next 10 to 15 years, we will experience a rapid ageing of our population.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In some areas, such as Outram, the future is already here, with one in five residents aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An older population will invariably mean an increase in healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For instance, the hospital admission rate for elderly today is three to four times that of younger people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Countries, such as Japan, went through a similar experience.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the last 25 years, Japan's healthcare spending has doubled as its proportion of elderly doubled.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore's experience will not completely mirror Japan's, but our healthcare spending will certainly rise and we must prepare adequately for our needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, we will need to refresh our infrastructure and build new ones, to create new economic opportunities and better homes for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For public transport, we will be investing significantly more over the next five years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes the doubling of the rail network from 178 kilometres today to about 360 kilometres in 2030.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Changi Airport's T5 will be developed to enhance our connectivity to Asia and globally.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, we must continue to invest in our defence and security, which underpin our economic and social prosperity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza and Dr Lim Wee Kiak have noted, the threats of terrorism and cyberattacks have grown.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To keep our homes safe, we must invest.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As our "must haves" and "good to haves" increase over time, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin correctly pointed out that we must continue to uphold the principle of "living within our means", so that we create enduring benefit and not enlarging burden for ourselves, our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While our spending needs are growing, our revenue growth will be slowing as our economy matures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The experiences of many advanced countries warn us how easy it is for spending to become unsustainable and impose a growing burden on future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: How then should we ensure that our spending needs are met?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, we must place priority on building a vibrant economy, which will then grow our revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A vibrant, competitive economy creates opportunities and jobs for our people and generates the revenue to meet our needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, we must spend prudently and spend right.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is about being efficient and being effective, so that each dollar reaches out to the right groups to help them in the right way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, we must design our overall fiscal system so that it is fair and progressive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must tax and spend in a way that is progressive without disincentivising enterprise and efforts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our system of revenues and expenditures must always be fair and progressive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Only then can it be sustainable across generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members have asked if our personal income tax relief cap, which serves to increase progressivity, runs contradictory to encouraging procreation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
