text: There are 15 personal income tax reliefs, each serving a worthy objective.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Taken together, however, they can unduly reduce total taxable incomes for a small proportion of individuals.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: After studying the reliefs, we concluded that we needed to moderate the effects of large amounts of reliefs claimed, in order to preserve equity in our tax structure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes those with more children – slightly over eight in 10 individuals claiming WMCR on two or three children are not expected to be affected by the cap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the years, we have added and significantly enhanced various schemes to support parents in having children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I touched earlier on our substantial support for Marriage and Parenthood, including the Baby Bonus Gift, MediSave grant, the CDA and now, the First Step grant.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I have pointed out, subsidies to all Singaporean children for education in school, at preschool and the IHLs are all very significant.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With all these measures, it is clear that the Government remains committed to supporting Singaporeans in fulfilling their marriage and parenthood aspirations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, our support for families also extends beyond monetary support and includes our wider push to make it easier for families to balance their work and life commitments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes our recent efforts to extend parental leave.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah pointed out, it is about having the right mindset.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Fundamentally, having a child is about the joy of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo, in charge of the National Population and Talent Division, will elaborate more on our marriage and parenthood strategy during COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: From time to time, we will have to make adjustments to our schemes in order to continue targeting our support at those who need it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we should not be evaluating Budget measures solely from the individual's perspective in a particular year, which would be narrowly focused on the individual winners and losers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must avoid thinking, as Ms Kuik Shiao Yin eloquently put it, that we are in a "high-stakes competition of win-lose" and that there is "no win-win".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Instead, our larger goal is to make every Singaporean a winner in the long run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this must be our goal; it cannot be otherwise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we help one group, we are actually helping others, too.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we support our SMEs, we are supporting good jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we support our seniors, we are helping the families who are taking care of them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we invest in our young to help them maximise their potential and seize opportunities and have a good career, we are also helping to ensure that they have the means to support their own families when they start one as well as support their loved ones, their parents in their retirement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we keep our tax burden low, especially for the middle income, everyone benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have to see things in totality and over the long term and not set one measure against another, or one group against another, and one year versus another year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It has to be seen in totality over the long run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I come back to our journey together towards the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are in this to keep Singapore going and thriving for the long, long haul.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To take this journey, we have to keep our eyes on the road, keep our eyes on the horizon, and keep our eyes out for the people we journey with.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 36 Keep our eyes on the road.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Every journey, even the longest journey, is taken one step at a time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And so, too, with a country – though we keep our sights on the distant future, we move towards it one Budget at a time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we gaze upon the distance and do not look at the road immediately in front of us, we risk falling into a hole.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Or we will take injury and recovery before we get there.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this Budget, we have taken targeted steps to address short-term pressures to make sure that we do not fall into the hole.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I urge Members to help those who are facing pressures to make the best use they can of the measures which we have announced.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Apart from keeping our eyes on the road, we have to know our direction and we have to know ourselves, too.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And do we have it in us to go that distance?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We cannot use up all our supplies at the start and we have to have ways to grow our store of supplies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have to spend more as our needs grow, too.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we must continue to grow our economy so that we can have resources to spend more on growing needs and we must continue to spend those resources wisely.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not possible for the Government to keep handing out goodies for everyone, year after year, as several Members have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Instead, each Budget must build on the previous ones to carry forward the momentum to future Budgets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: How do we keep our eyes on the horizon?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our firms need to look outward and look forward – to find new markets, grow capabilities, transform.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Look ahead, see opportunities where others see only problems.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Each of us, too, must continually learn, get the skills that the world needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must have the resilience to overcome personal setbacks and adapt to change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope Singaporeans will make full use of SkillsFuture and that all employers do their part to redesign jobs, facilitate learning and build a better future not just for their companies, but for the people who help their companies to run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ultimately, the Government must know when to step in and when to step back.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must not inadvertently undermine the spirit of enterprise and the natural workings of markets, or undermine the spirit of caring and resilience such that we weaken the bonds of family and community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Instead, we must reinforce critical values and our spirit as a society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Resources, hard won and wisely managed, will nourish us for the road ahead.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our values and our spirit – these are what will truly energise our journey.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The purpose of this journey is to journey together and to reach our destination together, as one united, cohesive people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To me, there is no meaning to this journey, unless it is a common journey.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must look out and care for one another as we journey.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What can we do to keep all of us going together?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the heart of this, we must recognise that every Page: 37 member of our society is not just valuable, but precious.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must have that resilience in us to face each challenge as an opportunity to learn and grow, to emerge from setbacks better and stronger.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must have that humility in us to respect and learn from everyone, no matter their paper qualification or job title.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we must have the generosity to share, be it in actual things, time or ideas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I do believe, Madam, the more we share, the richer we are for it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And keep our eyes out for one another.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It will be bumpy, it will be full of unknowns.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Amongst the unknowns are not just challenges but victories.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many innovations ahead of us that we cannot yet imagine, many personal and shared triumphs, many moments of humanity, unity and beauty that will keep defining our Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through all the good and bad unknowns of the years to come, I hope our spirit of enterprise and caring will run strong.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am honoured, and excited, to partner fellow Singaporeans on this journey.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: We have a bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have one clarification for the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In my speech, I mentioned many suggestions which have been raised by various Members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said that all these suggestions will be studied carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I also mentioned that we have to have coherence in our policies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not about one or two specific measures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we see this as a critical national priority, then that would argue for the whole-of-Government approach, similar to the approach taken, for example, for climate change, for population and for ageing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the first question on whether there will be one SME centre and so on, this issue has been raised in this House on many, many occasions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, not just in this House but among business leaders.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a subject which will always be studied but, as I had said, let us take a very practical approach at this point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have mentioned the Industry Transformation Programme in the Budget speech and spoken about how we are appointing agencies to take the lead in every sector.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In each sector, you have companies large and small and they interact very intensely in their particular way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As to the second question, again, this issue has been raised by several Members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will leave this to the Minister in charge of MSF to address during the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the years, we have, on the one hand, added or enhanced various reliefs and the end result is that we now have quite a large number of reliefs for which individuals can claim a significant amount of tax reliefs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That reduces the amount of taxes that are paid.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the other hand, in the case of support for raising children, we have also been increasing a whole range of different support, be it the Baby Bonus, MediSave grant, preschool subsidies, childcare subsidies, schools and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, if you look at the support that has been given, we studied it very carefully and we think that it is time for us to review, so that the tax system, both in terms of expenditure and revenue, remains fair and progressive; that we have to be equitable across different groups and that those who have higher incomes will pay more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think it is absolutely critical that the productivity schemes we put in place will bear returns.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Clearly, this road that we are charting is a new road but how are we going to do this next journey in a much more deliberate, much more proactive way, so that when we are down the path and we think that we need to change course, we have KPIs to guide us to do so?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I recall vividly Ms Foo raising this issue during her speech, along with many interesting suggestions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, in terms of whether there are KPIs, let me say that in designing any scheme, first and foremost, we do our best to try and make sure that these schemes will achieve the intended objectives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For particular schemes, whether it is for productivity or innovation, it is not easy to have one single measure to say that, "Well, we succeeded because of this or because of that." The nature of the workings of the economy is such that various factors interact to produce certain outcomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In many cases, you do not see immediate results.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 39 If you take, for instance, investments in R&D, if you look at the example in the US, there are some very basic findings that found their way into application many, many years down the road.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And so, this is something where we have to be patient and where we should not measure the wrong thing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having said that, we are very careful in the design of all our schemes to make sure that they have the best chance of success and to make sure that, as far as possible, that the private sector also has a stake in this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Public investments ought to be made in areas for which there are what economists called "market failures", where there are externalities for which the Government will invest in.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But at the same time, we have to do it in a way that catalyses private investment and private spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are ways of going about doing it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We measure specific schemes from time to time, looking at particular areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you ask me, at the end of the day, does it work?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Do we continue to grow the economy and create jobs?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Not over one or two years but, as I have said, over the long haul.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Low, I distinctly recall that you were here when I delivered the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I recall you sitting through a number of the discussions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As for Mr Louis Ng's question on whether we will start the consultation earlier, first, let me say that my round-up speech does not allow me to address every suggestion that Members have put up.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Do bear with me because, I think we had 13 to 14 hours of debate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If I addressed every point, you may end up hearing me for 13 to 14 hours!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Throughout the year, we gather feedback, we study data and we look at what needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We gather feedback from businesses, from people and various sectors, not just the Ministry of Finance (MOF) but every agency, every Ministry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We also have various feedback mechanisms, be it REACH or the various exercises that we hold.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This year, we even did something special – we had SGfuture dialogues as part of the Future of Us exhibition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, it is not as if the Budget process only starts a month before; it cannot be.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have tried to ask for earlier feedback but many of the businesses said, "That would not be appropriate." I would like to assure Mr Ng that this is not a last-minute exercise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a lot of focus on sexy and exciting startups, which is fine and good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what about the brick-and-mortar, traditional kinds of family-owned SMEs that we have?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can they connect with these innovation hubs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am wondering whether the Centres of Innovation can also be co-located in, let us say, the Jurong Innovation District and One-North, so that the SMEs can have an avenue and channel to tap into the expertise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First of all, I do not understand why Assoc Prof Goh connects what I said about innovation with it being about new and sexy industries and new things.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If he had followed my Budget speech carefully, seen the video that I showed on the Jurong Innovation District and heard all the examples I had given both then and today, he would know that I devoted a whole section to talk about innovation and made a number of points.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, I said innovation has to be pervasive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, every firm should be innovative, whether they are large companies or SMEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, they must innovate, regardless of the business that they are in.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a point that Mr Thomas Chua picked up when he spoke about there being no sunset industry, only sunset thinking.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If Members could look at the examples I have quoted, every single one of them is an SME, including the mother-and-son team in JMD Pacific, which is a gift shop that has now turned to e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I had given examples about Feinmetall, Pan Asia Logistics (PAL), Wee Meng and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are not what you would regard or would call the "sexy" industries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the Budget itself, I gave the example of a food manufacturer, and I spoke at length about how the food manufacturers have come together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are all SMEs, but they innovated, and not only innovated, they came together, integrated and internationalised.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I must say that I am a little surprised that somehow the Members got the impression that all I am talking about is “sexy” industries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, as to the Member's point about whether the innovation centre should be in the Jurong Innovation District, I recall that the Member mentioned in his speech that innovation should be pervasive and we should be spreading out the different centres.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you look at our innovation centres, they are all over, including the Polytechnics and research institutes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, I personally find it very inspiring that in the examples that I have given, businesses, large and small, in different industries all over, are innovating.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Page: 41 Many Members, including Mr Azmoon Ahmad, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, have all spoken up that, at the end of the day, it is about our mindset and it is about an approach, and we must encourage that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that we do not perpetuate this wrong impression nor give a wrong representation of what I said in this House.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I tried to be very clear that innovation has to be pervasive across all sectors, across all firms, large or small.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, keep it short, please.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I appreciate the representation that the Minister has corrected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The question really is how the SMEs can tap into the innovation research and expertise of the Universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, I am not saying that the Government is not promoting innovation in the SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But the question for me is quite specific – how the SMEs can connect to the innovation research and expertise in the Universities, and can the Government facilitate that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Goh's specific points – how do SMEs connect with innovation, research and expertise?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Again, I actually devoted a large part of my Budget speech and today's summary to how this is being done but perhaps let me explain it again.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, in the Budget speech, I mentioned a number of things.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I gave examples of how the research institutes are reaching out to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, I quoted two examples from the Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology (SIMTech).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: SIMTech and various centres of innovation in our polytechnics, universities and research institutes are reaching out to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, I mentioned The Hangar in NUS and what is happening in the universities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even new small businesses that are starting up are making use of this space.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And LaunchPad is another example where new SMEs are going.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many help schemes for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I also devoted a lot of time, as well as in my other media interviews, talking about the need for us to have industry-level transformation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It means that we study the entire industry.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We look at the common problems where you can have a common solution and, with that common solution, everyone benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, again, I gave the example of the national trade platforms as one of those things that we are building but, of course, that will come in a few years' time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, SPRING and other agencies have a number of schemes that are already helping SMEs access technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, the work in R&D and technology adoption is not only ongoing but will be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I actually spent a lot of time, both in my Budget speech, this round-up speech and my public comments between the Budget and the round-up, on what needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I hope that Assoc Prof Goh has followed my speech, as well as my public comments.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are putting a lot of hope in SkillsFuture and I do believe it is a potential game-changer.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would just like to clarify: who are the stakeholders who are involved in ensuring the quality of the SkillsFuture courses?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is because my staff and I have attended quite a diversity of WSQ courses ourselves and the quality can be quite varied.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is there Page: 42 also a whole-of-society approach to who feeds back on what are the kinds of SkillsFuture courses we are offering and how that can be changed?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is also about how the polytechnics and ITEs work with companies to place students in the Earn and Learn Programme to develop their skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is also about employers – how employers need to play a role.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I feel very strongly about this, that employers need to play a very important role in developing their people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And not just developing their people but, as Mr Ang Hin Kee pointed out, that it is about integrating what they are doing, for example, in automation, with how they are developing their people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The company sent this young man for training and he came back, continued to learn, continued to be mentored and made a breakthrough for his company.
